This is the most tempting wrong answer, because Robert does say the people are nostalgic for the distant past. But Marc never says which part of the past. And "*most* nostalgic for the things *farthest* back" is a ranking neither of them makes. Robert only says distant rather than recent, not that nostalgia grows the farther back you go.

The author never says this in one sentence. It's what you get by joining two pieces of the second sentence: teaching well requires keeping up with new developments, and keeping up requires research. So (A) follows from the premises, but it's a step on the way. Its job is to support the last sentence, which is about what a lack of funding does to a university. (A) doesn't mention funding at all.
"The root of ineffective teaching" makes lack of funding *the* cause of bad teaching. The author only says it *adversely affects* education, which leaves room for plenty of other causes.
This is the first sentence, reworded (and nudged from "educate" to "effective teaching"). It's there to tell us what "central mission" means. It supports the conclusion; it isn't it.

Line it up:
- "Lack of funds for research": a lack of funds for research.
- "reduces the quality of education a university provides": adversely affects how well a university fulfills its central mission (educating).

The only work required is swapping "central mission" for "education," which is exactly what the Goal step set up.
The author never proposes a fix. She only says underfunding hurts education. Calling for new funding sources is a What Next answer: something the author might say next, but didn't.

A subsidiary conclusion has to be supported by something and then support something else. Ask "why should we believe a diet can affect heart attacks?" The argument never says. It's given, not concluded.
The argument says we do *not* hold heart-attack drivers responsible. The diet claim helps show we don't blame them *even though* free choice was involved. (B) points it the other way.

This is the most popular wrong answer, and it's the conclusion flipped. The author argues free will's role is *not* the same in all situations. The diet claim helps show the difference. (C) says it shows everything should be the same.
The argument never disputes that criminals should be held responsible. It agrees they should. And the diet claim is about heart attacks, not criminals.

The diet claim is support. It puts a free choice into the heart-attack example, so the example can show that free choice doesn't always lead to responsibility. That supports the main conclusion.

The most common correct answer on Role is some version of "premise." When the claim has nothing supporting it and it helps the conclusion, the plain answer is usually the right one.
One material is bad, two are good, so use a good one. That's choosing between options. There's no problem with two sources, and nothing keeping those sources busy.

Map it:
- Problem: damaged furniture. (Sleeplessness.)
- Two sources: claws or teeth. (Left or right half of the brain.)
- One activity occupying both: toys to claw *and* bite. (Counting sheep, which uses both halves.)
- So the problem is prevented.

Every ingredient lines up, including the idea that the fix works by giving each source something else to do.
Two equal routes, so either one works. There's no problem being blocked and nothing being occupied. The "two" here is two options, not two sources of trouble.

This is the most tempting wrong answer, since it also has two things and a way to prevent harm. But the recipe is different. In (D), the problem only happens when the two chemicals come *together*, and the fix is to keep them *apart*. In the original, each source can cause the problem on its own, and the fix is to keep *both* occupied. Separating vs. occupying: different recipe.
Two harbors, one ruled out, so use the other. That's process of elimination, not blocking a problem at both of its sources.

Can we make our objection? "Sure, Robin can't solve it, but Robin's friends, as a group, might"? Not quite. The argument goes from one individual to *other* individuals, not from members to the group they form. It's flawed (why assume Robin's friends are no smarter than Robin?), but it's a different flaw.

Hank hasn't won a race, so he won't help the relay team win. That's reasoning about one person's contribution, not "each member can't, so the team can't." It's also arguably reasonable: a runner who never wins probably won't help much.

This is the most popular wrong answer, because it talks about individuals and wrongness, just like the historian. That's the Topic Trap. Look at the direction: it goes from what's wrong for *one person* to what's wrong for *other people in similar circumstances*. Individual to individual, not individual to group. And it's a reasonable principle, not a flaw.

Parallel Flaw questions love a wrong answer that copies the *topic*. Match the flaw, not the vocabulary.

Same objection works: "Sure, no single member can afford a tent, but the club, pooling everyone's money, might."
- No individual member can afford a tent. (No individual should hold the power.)
- So the club, a collection of members, can't afford one either. (So society, a collection of individuals, shouldn't hold it either.)

Same flaw, same direction: part to whole. It fails for the same reason too. Members can pool their money, just like a society can pool its judgment.

This goes the other way: society might be mistaken, so every individual might be. Whole to part. That's a flaw too, but it's the mirror image of the historian's. It also only concludes that being mistaken is *possible*, which is much weaker than the historian's firm conclusion.

Necessary versus sufficient would require the ad to argue, for example, that because moisture is required for healthy skin, applying Dewyfresh guarantees beautiful skin. It does not make that formal move. Its evidence is the earth analogy.
A common cause would explain why two observed events happen together. The ad does not report two correlated events and infer a shared cause. It compares two different things.

The argument does not claim that changing beliefs changes physical reality. The opening addresses people who doubt moisturizers, but the evidence is about drought, not a change in what people believe.
“Infusion” is used to mean an input of moisture in both places. The conclusion does not switch from a process to its product. The questionable switch is from ground to human skin.

Test the analogy's relevant feature. Dry soil cracks without water; does human skin respond to a moisturizer in the same way? The ad gives no reason to think so. Calling earth “skin” makes the analogy memorable but does not supply the biological similarity the conclusion needs.
Whether the company's survival is good does not show that the two listed measures exhaust its ways to prevent further loss.

This sounds tempting because bankruptcy is mentioned. But the president's *only options* claim concerns stopping the decrease in profits. A way to survive after profits keep falling would not be a third way to stop that fall.

The president says decreased demand explains this year's low profits, not that decreased demand is the *only possible cause* of decreased profits. Even if another factor could lower profits, that would not identify the flaw in the supposedly exhaustive list of two measures for preventing a further decline.
Even a slight further decrease is a decrease. Its size does not show that there is another option for preventing it.
“Other ways to stop the decrease” is exactly the omitted third route. If another route exists, reducing expansion and eliminating operations are not the *only* options. This is the False Choice flaw.
The herbalist does not warn customers of frightening consequences if they reject the juice. The doctors' warning that the herbs might be harmful is the point the herbalist dismisses.
Customers can report improved coordination while the herbs still carry a risk of harm. Those claims can both be true, so the herbalist's evidence is not internally inconsistent.

The doctors assert that the herbs might be harmful. The herbalist replies that doctors want to protect a monopoly, then concludes there is no reason not to try the juice. A motive to make a claim does not show that the claim is false. The potential harm has not been addressed. This is the Ad Hominem move.
The customer reports are not phrased to assume the juice is safe. The error occurs in dismissing the warning, not in wording the evidence as the conclusion.

The report that coordination improves *after* drinking juice might invite a post hoc objection if the conclusion were that the juice caused the improvement. The conclusion is that there is **no reason not to try** it. The live objection is the possible harm raised by doctors, and the herbalist attacks the doctors instead.
“Originators” means the people who proposed or created the legislation. The stimulus identifies people supporting it. We are not told who originated it.

The columnist assails the law because some *supporters* have questionable histories or face charges. That attacks the source of support rather than the legislation's merits. A charge is not even a conviction, but the flaw remains even if the character allegations are granted.
The columnist names no people who would be adversely affected and makes no plea on their behalf. The appeal is against allegedly bad supporters.
The argument says nothing about the number of supporters inside or outside the legislature. It targets their character, not their count.
The columnist never claims the supporters depend on manufacturers' success or act inconsistently. That would be a different attack on them.

The reply reports an absence of helpful evidence but does not establish how that absence arose. Destruction remains possible. A denial of the current evidence's existence is not a denial of the alleged earlier destruction.
Calling the charge an exaggeration would require a reason to believe there was no destruction or that its scale was overstated. The reply provides neither.
The attorneys could have information about destroyed material. The government's statement tells us nothing about what the attorneys know.
There might be no evidence because a search found none, because none ever existed, or because it was destroyed. The reply alone does not prove a failure to search.
Even if the reply is true *now*, it does not disprove that helpful evidence existed and was destroyed. The alleged coverup is a possible explanation for the reply's truth.
The mother's illness and dependence are not a paraphrase of “the policy should pay.” They are distinct facts, albeit irrelevant to the contract timing.

Pity for the mother is understandable, but it does not answer the insurer's contention about when coverage began. The argument swaps an emotional reason to want payment for a reason the contract requires it.
The representative makes no comparison between family obligations and business obligations. The defect is that family hardship does not determine the insurance contract.
No person is attacked. The representative invites sympathy for the mother.
No cause-and-effect relationship is reversed. The dispute is over the time at which a policy took effect.
P does not cite other unpopular views held by the opponent. P cites a predicted consequence of the specific tax proposal.
No claim about the opponent's character appears. This is not Ad Hominem.

The view is that the government *must* raise taxes for these services. P calls it mistaken because doing so would reduce taxpayers' buying power and upset them. Unhappiness is compatible with an obligation.
Taxpayers' buying power is related to a tax increase, so the issue is not wholly irrelevant. The problem is the inference from that negative consequence to no obligation.
P rejects the claim that an obligation exists; P does not insist an obligation exists.
A later corrective upgrade could help later users. It does not show how many problems the current upgrade causes now.
Severe problems would matter to the consumer, but the argument estimates *likelihood*. Seriousness does not show that more people have problems than the number of calls suggests.

If many people had problems without calling, reported calls undercount actual failures. The company's inference from “few calls” to “few problems” then collapses. The reusable question is whether the method of counting captures the event the conclusion is about.
Problems without the upgrade do not tell us whether this upgrade causes problems for its users.
If some reported problems came from users' mistakes, even fewer reports would count as defects caused by the upgrade. That does not expose the company's undercount.

This asks whether DNA understanding is *enough* for good choices. The argument needs to show that DNA understanding is *required* for good choices. Even if some DNA experts make poor choices, the inference about people without DNA knowledge remains the target.
The conclusion describes what individuals know. It does not establish a particular quota of informed people needed for policy to be good.
The argument does not infer policy skill from personal medical skill. It draws both conclusions from lack of DNA knowledge.

To infer that the 80 percent who cannot understand a DNA story also cannot make informed personal or policy decisions, DNA understanding would have to be essential to those decisions. The evidence never establishes that requirement.

The 90 percent self-report might imply that many overestimate their knowledge *if* the DNA criterion were valid. But the objection concerns whether the criterion itself is required for informed choices.
“Unusable” need not shift between permanent and temporary meanings. A program can be unusable for several reasons under the same ordinary meaning.
An unplugged mouse *can* cause unusability. The argument treats unplugging as though it *must* be the cause whenever such a program is unusable. This is the illegal reversal of the conditional.
The general fact about required peripherals is related to the conclusion. It just does not establish that this specific peripheral was unplugged.
The generalization may be perfectly true. The flaw is applying it backward, not making it too broad.
Fred's program explicitly requires a mouse. Whether other programs need no peripherals has no bearing on why this one became unusable.
The argument is about Marion's particular schedule, not a problem mistakenly treated as hers alone.
Marion knows the bridge is closed. The flaw is not that she overlooks a consequence of a known fact; the author overlooks her ability to choose the train despite disliking it.

This choice tempts because Marion's preferences matter to the story. But it proposes that *people generally* want to avoid being late, while the argument's evidence is specific: Marion hates taking the train. Even if she wants very badly to be on time, she still has the train option. The flaw is converting dislike of that option into its impossibility, not projecting a general human preference onto Marion.

Her hatred of trains is evidence she may choose not to take one. It does not exclude that alternative. A disfavored option is still an option, and taking it could defeat the conclusion that she cannot avoid being late.
The train is a possible route whether or not Marion has a “good reason” to take it. The issue is availability, not whether an occasional choice lacks a good reason.

The survey asks whether respondents graduated from high school, so dropping out before reaching high school may sound like a counting issue. But such a respondent would still be a nongraduate. The central problem is whose schools the nongraduation reflects. Someone who left school before high school in another city is still no evidence about Center City's schools.
Finishing high school early still makes one a graduate. The survey already asks whether the person graduated, not how long it took.

The survey counts Center City residents without separating those educated in Center City from those educated elsewhere. A dropout in another city's schools cannot establish a dropout from Center City's schools. The report labels its sample as if it measured the target.
The report makes a claim about current or past dropout rates; predicting how publicity affects future rates would not validate that claim.

Changing diploma standards could affect what graduation means, but the first defect is that many surveyed residents may have no connection to the schools whose dropout rate the report claims to measure.
“Messages” has an ordinary role here: communications received from extraterrestrial origin. Defining it more tightly would not make silence prove the absence of intelligence.

The argument infers that no neighboring system contains intelligence from our lack of evidence that one does. The missing responses have several possible explanations. Absence of proof is not automatically proof of absence.
The conclusion concerns neighboring systems. Intelligence farther away is compatible with the conclusion and would not challenge it.
The issue is whether anyone in neighboring systems is intelligent, not whether humans have also sent spacecraft recordings.
Even if most systems are uninhabited, the conclusion says *none* of the neighboring systems has intelligence. A high general probability cannot establish that absolute claim from silence.
Whether most people can diagram sentences is about people's skill. The premise says *a sentence can be diagrammed*, not that ordinary speakers can draw its diagram.

If some ungrammatical sentences are diagrammable, X's diagrammability does not establish grammaticality. The author cannot use the “grammatical → recognized” rule without first establishing that X's sentence is grammatical.

This sounds close because it mentions recognized and diagrammable, the words on both ends of the argument. But it runs *recognized → diagrammable*. The author needs *diagrammable → grammatical* before the existing *grammatical → recognized* rule can be used. Even if every recognized sentence is diagrammable, a diagrammable sentence may still be ungrammatical and unrecognized.
“Only if diagrammable is it grammatical” already says every grammatical sentence can be diagrammed. Repeating a premise cannot fix its reversal.
Some ungrammatical sentences being recognized as ungrammatical says nothing about whether X's diagrammable sentence is grammatical.
The facts about the firm's specialty and Dalton's specialty can both be true. There is no contradiction until the author assumes every member shares the firm's primary specialty.
Dalton may practice without a firm, but that does not establish he does. The error is ruling out membership based on his specialty.
The law firm as a whole primarily does criminal defense. Dalton primarily does divorce. Those facts can coexist with his being a member. A group's dominant trait need not be shared by each member.
The conclusion is about Dalton's membership, not whether the firm's criminal-defense wins are evenly spread among attorneys. The 90 percent figure is background.
The author does not generalize from a selected subset of lawyers. The error is applying a characteristic of a firm to an individual attorney.

The criminal cases and the proposed exclusion might make this seem like a cause-and-effect claim. Check the actual conclusion: it says no wealthy person should be appointed, not that wealth caused crime or that a committee appointment caused an outcome. The evidence is about a *number* of wealthy criminals, and the conclusion bars *all* wealthy people. The change in quantity, not cause and effect, is the problem.
Nothing is said to follow another event in time, and no causal inference is made from a sequence.
No action's unintended consequence is at issue. The conclusion is a hiring exclusion.
Criminal conduct and an ethics rule are the stated grounds. The problem is how far the evidence extends, not whether those standards are subjective or objective.

“A number” of wealthy criminals may be exceptional. It cannot justify a ban on *every* wealthy person. This is the Sampling or Hasty Generalization move: the observed cases may not represent the wider class.
Maurice calls the proposed policy censorship, but his causal objection is not that an unpopular policy cannot work. Popularity never enters his evidence.
The exchange is about a causal factual claim, not a confusion between private moral judgment and objective social fact.

Youth violence existed without television and movies. That only shows those media are not required for *every* instance of youth violence. They might still contribute to violence now. Maurice rejects a possible cause because the effect once occurred without it.
The historical claim may be verifiable. Even granting it fully, Maurice's inference remains flawed, so verifiability is not the criticism.
“Violence” has the same basic meaning in Jane's present-day claim and Maurice's historical comparison. The error is about what that comparison proves.

The examples are physicians, attorneys, physicists, and engineers; they support the premise about professional evaluations. Even if that premise were true across professions, the transfer to school exams would still need a justification.
The recommendation is not premised on raising students' scores. It is premised on making exams resemble professional evaluations. No score increase is required for that rationale.
Professionals' past exams without books do not settle what tools present-day students should have. The analogy hinges on what current exams are trying to measure.

Professionals' longer study might make their use of books different, but the argument does not depend on equal levels of subject mastery. The sharper objection is that the *purpose of evaluation* may differ. Even equally trained people could be tested for different purposes.

If professional evaluations test realistic practice and school exams test independent mastery, their different purposes explain why one allows references and the other may not. The analogy needs similarity in the respect that matters for the proposed policy.
The author need not think freedom is the most valuable thing in every comparison. The narrower error is treating one exceptionally severe loss of freedom as proof about *every* risk to freedom.
Whether physical rebellion is possible does not address the value judgment that taking a life risk is always worthwhile.
The bare room is one extreme case. It might justify a life risk for that person without justifying a life risk whenever *anyone's* freedom is at stake. “Always” outruns the example.
The conclusion concerns one's *own* freedom. The value of risking one's life for others' freedom is outside its scope.
Whether people dare take a risk does not tell us whether the risk is worth taking. Someone can lack courage for a worthwhile action, or take a brave but unwise risk.

This is the most attractive distractor because Sid does shift the scenario. But Micki's original statement already concerns a consequence: whether one person's crossing *hurts* the grass. Sid also talks about a consequence: the grass dying after universal crossing. He does not exchange a statement about consequences for one about actions themselves. He changes *one person's action* to *everyone's actions*.

Micki says one person's crossing does not hurt the grass. Sid argues about what happens if *everyone believes* that and crosses. The effect of universal belief and behavior cannot by itself disprove the claim about a single crossing.
Sid can consider a hypothetical belief held by everyone without personally believing it. The error is using the hypothetical mass behavior to rebut Micki's one-person claim.
Micki does not claim that harming grass is justified in some circumstances; she claims one person's crossing does not harm it. Justification is irrelevant to whether her factual claim is false.
Sid does not criticize Micki's character. He criticizes what he takes to be the effect of general acceptance of her statement.
Other kinds of dangerous radiation do not challenge the conclusion about the radiation crews actually absorb. This would help only if crews were exposed to one of those other kinds.
A dental X-ray might offset some other risk, but the evidence says the X-ray itself does negligible harm. The conclusion concerns radiation harm, not total health benefits of dentistry versus flying.
Higher-intensity X-rays may be harmful. The argument compares an ordinary dental X-ray to an ordinary flight; it does not claim that every X-ray exposure is harmless.

The more often and longer someone is exposed, the more radiation that person can absorb. Crew members' repeated flights could cause nonnegligible harm even if the radiation from a single flight is as harmless as that from a single dental X-ray. This is the missing difference in the comparison.
Additional risks of flying may matter to airline crews' overall health, but the conclusion is limited to harm from radiation. An objection needs to make the radiation conclusion doubtful.
Eighty-nine percent is plainly a large majority. Quibbling over the word "overwhelming" would not expose the national sampling problem.
Wanting to finish and dropping out can coexist. The two conclusions concern students' desire and a possible explanation of a dropout rate, not logically conflicting outcomes.
The argument says *if* the national dropout rate is high, lack of desire cannot explain it. It does not need a high rate actually to exist to make that conditional claim.
Students can want to finish and still leave school. The author does not contradict himself by discussing both possibilities.

The respondents are from three schools in one medium-sized city, while the conclusion covers high school students nationwide. Even a large, randomly selected sample can be unrepresentative when drawn from the wrong population.
The speaker explicitly notes that almost no new businesses have arrived. The mistake is extending the departure rate backwards, not ignoring incoming businesses.

A rate of four departures per week and a stock of at most 1,000 businesses are different quantities, but comparing them *would* be informative if the rate had lasted long enough. The unsupported move is assuming that it did.
The president does not attack the Board's interests or motives. He attacks its estimate with a numerical argument.

"Leaving ... at the rate of about four a week" reports a rate now. The president calculates as though businesses had been leaving at that rate for an extended time. That historical premise was never supplied.
The president calls the estimate a gross exaggeration, not merely imprecise. His reasoning does not depend on pretending that "about four" is exact.

The physician need not believe hormones are the *primary* explanation. The conclusion says testosterone and estrogen *tend* to influence heart disease, which allows other factors to be important or even dominant.
Nothing here requires these to be the only relevant hormones. Another hormone could also promote or inhibit disease.
The speaker compares men and women at different life stages to suggest effects of hormones. The argument does not need young high-testosterone men to have higher risk than postmenopausal women.

The observed hormone differences and heart disease patterns are correlations. To conclude that testosterone promotes and estrogen inhibits the disease, the physician assumes those correlations reflect causal influence. A shared cause or another sex-related difference could instead explain the pattern.

Hormone levels could vary substantially within age and gender groups while the described average patterns still hold. The causal inference does not depend on identical levels among all people in a group.
Whether the game tests *other* cognitive abilities does not help assess whether it can detect differences in perception and memory.

If card games are among the hardest cognitive tasks, equal performance could be stronger evidence against the alleged decline. The author needs the game to be sensitive enough; this answer makes that more plausible.
Perception and memory may interact, but the alleged flaw concerns whether the game can reveal a reduction in either. Interaction alone does not explain the tied scores despite a decline.
The origin of the belief, even prejudice, would not by itself show that the belief is false or that the study's game can detect an actual decline.

If perfect play takes only fairly low levels of the two abilities, both age groups could play perfectly even though eighty-year-olds' levels are significantly lower. A test with a low ceiling cannot rule out the decline the argument denies.
Some people could prefer nondiatonic music while diatonic scales still dominate most music. Individual exceptions do not address whether social conditioning contributes to the broad pattern.
The conclusion explains diatonic music's popularity, not how innate dispositions affect appreciation of nondiatonic music.
A theory of why diatonic scales are popular need not explain the existence of every scale. The argument's issue is the exclusivity of the proposed cause.

Innate dispositions and social conditioning might jointly influence popularity. The failure of the anthropologist's prediction for a *purely* social explanation does not show that social conditioning contributes nothing.

The argument concerns patterns in human music and the human mind. Animal appreciation of nondiatonic music would not settle whether social conditioning helps explain human preference for diatonic scales.
"Evidence" is used consistently as support for a historical link. The archaeologist disputes how strong the pyramid comparison is; no second meaning of the word drives the inference.
The argument cites design and function, not an emotional reaction intended to replace evidence.
The premise is about differences between pyramids; it does not simply restate the claim that there was no historical link.
The terms are sufficiently clear for the argument's purpose. The problem remains even if every feature and use is defined precisely.

Differences between the pyramids at most challenge one proposed indication of contact. The categorical conclusion assumes there is no other relevant evidence of an early link. That assumption is unsupported.
Anyone may report an emotional response. The question is whether trained connoisseurs' responses can inform authenticity; public access to the same kind of response does not show they cannot.
Rembrandt is introduced as an example of the claimed method, not as evidence that only his work has variable impact. The central premise is about artworks' impact across people.

Even if people generally react very differently to art, connoisseurs might agree widely about the impact relevant to attribution. If so, public variation would not justify dismissing the connoisseurs' assessments.
The speaker does not say emotional impact is irrelevant to authenticity. The complaint is that responses vary, which allegedly makes the proposed method unreliable. Those are different claims.
The example contrasts a Rembrandt with a student's work, but the argument never compares Rembrandt's emotional skill with other painters'. Its reasoning turns on variation among observers.
The speaker presents one article as saying coffee is dangerous and another as saying it has benefits. He does not adopt the first article's conclusion as a premise.
The argument says expert guidance is useless, whether or not people always want such guidance. A desire for advice is not the logical bridge at issue.
The conclusion is about health decisions, so expert opinion in other areas cannot repair or expose the coffee-based inference.
The author is skeptical of experts. He does not infer that all expert opinions are trustworthy because one is.

Coffee could be harmful in some respects and beneficial in others. The articles would then report different true facts, not contradictory advice. The argument's starting point for dismissing experts would fail.

More ticket sales might or might not make the route viable. The pundit does not assume that they will; the town officials' recommendation suggests that possibility. The pundit's flaw is dismissing their advice by pointing to their behavior.

The airline may have options besides suspension and continued losses. The pundit's inference about whether residents should follow the recommendation does not rely on a two-option view of the airline's choices.
Who paid for the officials' trip does not determine whether encouraging residents to fly is sound advice.
A general comparison of ground and air transport prices would not establish that the officials' advice should be ignored. The route's profitability is the relevant issue.

The pundit uses the officials' failure to follow their own recommendation as the reason to reject the recommendation. That is a version of the ad hominem mistake: hypocrisy can be real while the advice remains sound.
A planet being fit to sustain life does not guarantee that life arises on it. The conclusion concerns *fitness*, not the actual origin of life.

The argument extrapolates from our system's one-in-nine ratio to numerous other systems. That inference needs many other systems to be similar to ours in the prevalence of life-sustaining planets. Without that, the local ratio tells us little about the universe-wide count.
We need not understand how life begins to assess the premise's stipulated judgment that Earth is fit to sustain it. The projection across systems is the gap.
The argument does not require Earthlike life to evolve elsewhere, or require life to evolve at all. It counts planets capable of sustaining *some form* of life.

Other systems need not have exactly nine planets. They need a comparable frequency of life-sustaining planets for the extrapolation to work. Nine is the denominator in our system, not a required size for every system.
The politician may be prejudiced against apartments, but describing the opponent's residence does not establish that motive. The flaw we can verify is reliance on an irrelevant personal fact.
Where apartment buildings can be built does not address whether the opponent's home undermines his argument. His proposal can be assessed without this suburban-versus-center comparison.
Knowing the politician's own living arrangement would not make the opponent's argument more or less sound.

Whether the opponent lives in a country house has no bearing on whether zoning laws should encourage more varied housing. The criticism attacks the advocate's lifestyle while leaving the policy reasoning unanswered.
The opponent need never have lived in an apartment for his present claim about zoning to be sound. A past apartment residence would not be the missing defense of his argument.
Legislators need not be great leaders for the activist to urge them to follow the conduct attributed to great leaders.
The conclusion recommends how legislators ought to vote, not a prediction of whether the bill is likely to pass.

The economic drawback may be outweighed by noneconomic reasons to support the bill. Without comparing the costs with potential benefits, the activist cannot conclude that sound policy requires voting no.
Whether legislators *usually* consider economics does not determine how they ought to vote on this bill. The gap lies in the omitted reasons for passing it.
The activist explicitly grants that the bill is popular while arguing that it is economically harmful. He does not infer harm from popularity.
Customers without complaints might matter if we knew how many there were, but their *interests* do not explain why Moore received all filed complaints.

There may be few or no competing plumbers. If Moore performs almost all the plumbing work, all complaints naming him would be unsurprising and would not establish that his work is unusually poor. The argument needs a meaningful comparison.

A small business can still produce enough jobs to support a judgment. The specific gap is the number of other plumbers and jobs available for comparison, not a bare question about whether Moore's business is "too small."
Complaints about electricians, carpenters, or other tradespeople would not tell us whether Moore performs plumbing work well.

If more dissatisfied Moore customers failed to complain, that would make the known complaints undercount dissatisfaction and could strengthen the criticism. It does not expose why *all filed plumbing complaints* point to Moore.
Reliability of ground shipping does not explain the customer's belief that it cannot arrive tomorrow.
The coordinator did say air express would arrive tomorrow. That guarantee alone does not rule out ground carrier also arriving tomorrow.
Ground carrier is less expensive. That fact explains why the question is a choice, but not why the customer thinks ground cannot meet tomorrow's deadline.

"Unless air express, not tomorrow" means that air express is necessary for tomorrow delivery. That is exactly the customer's mistaken interpretation. The coordinator said ground might arrive tomorrow, so the supposed necessity is false.
The customer need not believe every more expensive shipment is faster. Her mistake concerns the specific alternatives and the certainty of next-day arrival.

Technical knowledge could be acquired without formal schooling. If so, even a much higher knowledge requirement today would not refute Maria's claim that formal education is unnecessary. Frank treats one route to knowledge as the only route.

Improvements in schools since Edison's day might make formal education more useful, but Frank's conclusion says it is *necessary*. School quality does not close the gap between knowledge and credentials.
Both speakers use "crucial contributions" to mean consequential technological work. Their dispute is over what preparation that work requires today.
Frank does not need to assume Edison was uniquely productive. His response concerns today's knowledge requirements, regardless of other inventors in Edison's era.

Frank can grant everything Maria says about Edison and still argue that today's conditions differ. His flaw lies in the inference about formal education, not in failing to challenge the historical example.
Being well qualified does not show that age was the deciding factor; Sullivan might have lost to an even better qualified candidate.
That age was *one* factor keeping Sullivan from promotion is consistent with it being the deciding factor. The number of other factors does not rebut the manager's argument.
Some people associate age with good judgment, but that does not show how age worked in Sullivan's promotion decision or in the cited promotions.

If the older promotees had no younger competitors, their promotions do not show that an older applicant would beat a younger one. Sullivan could still have lost because he was much older than the competition in his particular contest.
Confidential deliberations might make the true reason hard to know, but secrecy does not explain why the manager's evidence fails to rule age out.
The editorial does not analyze a particular implementation of spending cuts and predict its failure. It dismisses the proposal by invoking the advisor's past.
The editorial is not promoting an alternative proposal by stoking fear of its rejection. It is arguing against the advisor's proposal.

The source's youthful embezzlement conviction is used to discredit the present economic claim. Whether wasteful spending can be eliminated sufficiently requires evidence about budgets and services, which the editorial does not examine.
The writer does not merely say there is no evidence for the advisor's claim. He offers a personal reason to distrust the advisor, then treats that as grounds to reject the claim.
The premise about a conviction does not restate the conclusion about tax cuts and services. The reasoning is flawed, but it is not circular.

The author is not using one Egyptian cup to generalize about what most Egyptians did. The cup establishes an instance of alcoholic beer in Egypt by 2000 B.C.; the issue is whether that instance was the world's first.
"Alcoholic beverage" includes wine and beer in both the evidence and the conclusion. The argument compares dates, not two meanings of the term.

The author does not say Babylonian wine production depended on Egyptian beer production. Being earlier than one known Babylonian example is offered as evidence for priority, not for transmission of technology.

The cup is older than the cited Babylonian evidence, so Egypt has the earlier *known* example of the two. Another society might have made alcohol even earlier without leaving evidence we have found. The oldest discovered instance need not be the first historical instance.
The author supplies the 1500 B.C. Babylonian wine date as background. Even if that date were well documented, the Egyptian cup would not establish that no society produced alcohol before Egypt.
Willett need not think all growth is good. He can oppose this particular restriction while accepting that some growth has costs. His stated reason is the earlier rejections.
Willett does not attack Benson's character. He attacks the age of the proposal and cites past council decisions.

The idea of restricting growth can be old while reasons supporting it are new. Changes in the past five years could make today's regulation warranted even though earlier councils rightly rejected earlier restrictions.

Many factors may affect quality of life, but Willett does not attempt a full quality-of-life analysis. The flaw in *his* argument is using the oldness of the proposal as if it ruled out new justification.
The council ten years ago may have been well qualified and correct in its own circumstances. That still would not decide whether present reasons support new zoning rules.

This tries the "groups not fair to compare" objection, so test it. The volunteers are compared with their *contemporaries*, people of roughly the same age. A few nonvolunteers being somewhat older than a few volunteers would not explain gaps in money, social resources and outlook across the whole group. The comparison is fair enough on age. The real problem is the direction of cause, which is what (E) supplies.

This is about the charlatans: exposing a few frauds does not show that everyone lacks ESP. The fortune-teller does rely on that idea, but it is a reasonable idea. Negate it and you get "proof that many lack a trait shows everyone lacks it," which is plainly false. Relying on a true principle is not the flaw.
The fortune-teller does not need the number of failed attempts to be the *only* relevant factor. She treats it as enough, but she would be just as wrong if other factors mattered too.

The studies she mentions are attempts to *disprove* ESP that failed. If some of them reached inaccurate conclusions, we learn nothing about the leap from "not disproven" to "proven." The flaw survives untouched.
She says the attempts so far have failed, not that no scientific method could ever settle the question. Her conclusion would be just as flawed if a perfect test existed but had not yet been run.

"It has not been proven that there is no ESP" becomes "some people have ESP." That treats a claim's not being shown false as proof that it is true. This is the classic unproven vs proven false flaw, run in the positive direction.

This one is close, so check the wording. The evidence and conclusion are about an *increase* in theta waves. (E) is about people having *low levels* of them. Someone could start with moderate theta levels, get an increase from music, and still not be creative. The gap is whether an increase guarantees creativity, which (D) states directly; a claim about baseline levels does not capture it.
The columnist says music is *enough* for creativity, not that it is *required*. Pointing out that people can be creative without music agrees with everything the columnist said.
If live music or a phone speaker also raises theta waves, that is perfectly consistent with the argument. It would only widen the conclusion, not undermine it.

The rule is creativity → more theta waves. The columnist runs it backward: more theta waves → creativity. Ask, "Could theta waves rise without creativity showing up?" If yes, music can raise theta waves and leave you no more creative than before. A fever comes with a rising temperature, but warming up in a sauna does not give you a fever.
The hippocampus is just one place theta waves occur. The argument's leap is from theta waves to creativity; no claim about the hippocampus causing anything is needed.

The link from rain to mosquitoes to encephalitis is given as a premise ("typically leads to"). The argument does not infer that link from the order of events, so there is no post hoc move to criticize.
Nothing in the argument depends on whether a lower threat is desirable. Obviously it is, but the question is whether it is possible.

The threat may depend on rainfall *and* on mosquito control, standing water, protection from bites and more. If so, being unable to change the weather does not stop us from lowering the threat through the other factors. One factor we cannot control is not every factor.

The argument does not claim encephalitis disappears without heavy rain. Even if the threat existed in dry years too, the author would still conclude that it cannot be reduced. Negate (D) and nothing changes.

"People cannot change the weather" is already a premise about what is possible. The argument moves from one claim about possibility to another. The problem is the missing factors, not a jump from actual to possible.
If an exciting debate raises turnout, that boosts voting generally. It does not say more of those voters choose the debate's winner, so it does not show that winning helps.

Non-watchers can learn who won through news reports. If those reports shape their votes, winning a debate can matter a lot even though the viewers themselves are committed or confused. This names exactly the group the evidence left out.
Disagreement over who won fits the author's point that uncommitted viewers are unsure of the winner. If anything, it makes "winning" seem less able to move votes.
Unpredictable effects do not favor the winner. To weaken the conclusion, we need a reason that *winning* helps, not just a reason that something unpredictable happens.
Committed voters sticking with their candidate after a loss supports the claim that the debate result does little to change votes.

The letter attacks the critics' lifestyles, not the substance of their criticism. Whether the critics live up to their own standard does not affect whether middle-class lifestyles cause ecological damage. This is the "you do it too" version of ad hominem.

This tempts because the letter does point to inconsistency between the celebrities' words and their lives. But the letter never draws a conclusion about how *sincerely* they hold their views. It uses the inconsistency to dismiss the criticism, which is (A).
The letter never examines the critics' grounds at all, adequate or not. It dismisses the criticism by looking at who makes it.
No evidence in the letter backfires on its conclusion. The celebrities' lifestyles are a different topic from middle-class families' damage.
The letter does not generalize from a few people to everyone. It describes one group of critics and then dismisses their argument.

For the creatures to reveal a fear *of the horse*, they must represent the horse in people's minds. They might represent people, riders or something else entirely. The argument never shows which, yet its conclusion depends on it.
Whether the fear is reasonable does not matter. A fear can be both justified and unconscious. This would not cast doubt on the claim that the myth expresses that fear.
The argument speaks only of myths *expressing* unconscious thoughts. It never mentions suppression, so it cannot confuse the two.

The stimulus calls the developments "apparently independent." Even if one culture borrowed the myth, the borrowed version could still express fear of horses. Borrowing does not touch the gap between creature and horse.
The argument relies on the fact that myths express unconscious thoughts. It does not need to explain *why* they do. An answer asking for more explanation of a premise is not the flaw.

To get from "not the highest" to "not sufficient," the politician must assume sufficient profits have to be the highest among all industries. Nothing justifies that. Negate it (sufficient profits need not be the highest) and the conclusion no longer follows.
The politician does not criticize oil companies at all. The argument defends them from tighter regulation.
The argument is conditional, not causal. It does not infer a cause from two things occurring together.
The politician has actual data: profits are not the highest. That is evidence, not an absence of evidence. The problem is what the data are taken to show.
The data concern the whole oil industry compared with other industries. No single example is generalized.
Ranking generosity against other virtues has nothing to do with whether the generosity is permanent.
The columnist does not attack anyone's character or contrast the donors' values with his own. He draws a conclusion about how lasting their generosity is.

The columnist moves from "donors give only intermittently" to "their generosity is rarely permanent." That works only if generosity exists only when it shows up in a donation. Negate it, so that a trait can persist between its displays, and the argument falls apart.
The evidence is about *most* donors. There is no small sample here; the problem is what intermittent giving says about character.

The columnist hedges: donating "may be" a sign of generosity, and "any generosity it may demonstrate" is the subject. He does not need most donors to be generous. Negate (E) and his reasoning about permanence is unchanged.

Whether publishing requires prying does not matter to the argument. Negate it (publishing such stories does involve prying) and the author still reaches the same conclusion, since he has brushed the prying objection aside.

This bridges the gap exactly. The evidence establishes a right to publish; the conclusion claims an obligation to publish. Negate (B) (having a right does not entail an obligation) and the conclusion no longer follows.
The conclusion is conditional: *if* a story is not libelous. The author allows that some stories about private lives might be libelous.
This runs the link the wrong way: obligation → right. The argument needs right → obligation.
Libelous stories are set aside by the conclusion's "if not libelous" condition. No weighing of the two rights is involved.
The author never says the right is violated only when elections are held solely by mail. This garbles the argument rather than describing it.
Whether the right will continue has nothing to do with *how* it should be exercised. The author takes the right as given; the question is mail vs in person.

The sole support for rejecting mail voting is that voting has "always" been done in person. That is an appeal to tradition. "Sacred right" tells us voting matters; it does not tell us mail voting threatens it.

The author argues mail voting should not be *allowed* at all. Saying the council might never use the power does not touch that reasoning. The argument would be just as flawed if the council certainly would use it.
The premises and conclusion fit together without conflict. Voting has been in person, and the author wants it to stay that way. The flaw is weak support, not a contradiction.

If misbehaving dogs are the ones that get disciplined often, the correlation is explained without discipline causing anything. It could even be that discipline helps, and those dogs would be worse without it.
Dogs learning how owners react does not explain why frequently disciplined dogs misbehave more, and it does not offer a rival cause.
The conclusion is about dogs. Other animals do not matter.
The study compares kennel club members with each other. How they compare with other dog owners tells us nothing about the correlation inside the club.
Same problem as (D). Members versus nonmembers is not the comparison the argument rests on.
The principle says nothing about a chance to repair. Fraud under it depends on knowledge and the seller's statement.
The price is irrelevant to whether the principle applies. An answer asking for a number is almost never the flaw.
"Defective" means the same thing in both places: the item does not work properly. The brakes were defective in that sense.
The principle does not require the buyer to believe the seller. Fraud is defined by what the seller knows and says.

Wilton asserted the bicycle was sound without good reason to think so. That is not the same as asserting it while *knowing* it was defective, which is what the principle requires. The application treats careless assertion as knowing falsehood.
Whether Bruch wants to belong is beside the point. The question is whether the document proves it does not.
The conclusion requires the list to be complete. If the document names only some members, Bruch's absence proves nothing. The journalist never shows the list is complete.
How the document was sent has no bearing on whether it lists every member.
Bruch's possible reasons for secrecy do not affect what the list shows.

This tempts because the representative did have a reason for secrecy. But the representative only confirmed that the listed companies are members, and the journalist's inference about Bruch goes wrong even if that confirmation is perfectly accurate. The gap is the list's completeness.
A conservative estimate already predicts gridlock. Higher estimates would make doing nothing look even worse.

Building an expressway and doing nothing really are mutually exclusive, so taking that for granted is fine. The problem is not that the two options overlap but that they are *not the only ones*. Watch the difference between "exclusive" and "exhaustive."
Gridlock arrives within ten years either way. A slower increase afterward does not rescue the do-nothing option or help any alternative.
The economic cost of gridlock would, if anything, add to the case against doing nothing. It does not reveal the missing options.
The mayor offers only two choices and never explains why others are off the table. Eliminating one of two options proves the other only if those two are all there are.
Robinson's evidence is about these particular props and costumes. He is not generalizing from anecdotes.

Wexell's argument turns on artistic significance outside a performance. Robinson talks only about availability. Even if display is the only way to show the items, that does not answer whether they are worth showing.
Robinson does not mention anything about Wexell personally.
Robinson never claims Wexell's evidence is insufficient. He offers new reasons of his own, which happen to miss the point.
"The only way" might suggest necessary vs sufficient, but there is no reversed conditional here. The trouble is relevance, not a scrambled condition.

"Everyone I know" is a sample chosen by who the speaker happens to know, not by any method that reflects the nation. It is likely to share the speaker's views, so it cannot show how the country voted.
The premise (the speaker's acquaintances voted no) is different from the conclusion (most people voted no). The argument is weak, but not circular.
The speaker attacks the results, not the people who announced them or voted for the proposal.
The argument is about how people actually voted. "Should" never enters it.
The speaker is not appealing to popular belief. If anything, he rejects the majority result. His mistake is the sample, not an appeal to what most people think.
The only reason given for clearing the sharing services is that the intermediaries are at fault. Both can contribute to musicians' losses, so blaming one does not excuse the other.
The editorialist does not promote any behavior by citing its popularity.
The editorialist does not attack the musicians' character. He grants that they are deprived of royalties.
No undesirable consequence of the musicians' view is used against it.
There is no conditional rule about blameworthiness here to scramble. The error is treating blame as if only one party could have it.
The premise already says aspirin helps *prevent or reduce* heart disease. The argument does not need to infer prevention from reduced severity.

A disease can top the list and still threaten only a minority. If most people are not at significant risk, most people would not be healthier from protection against it. That breaks the step to "most people."
The argument never claims aspirin helps with other diseases. People helped against heart disease are healthier even if nothing else changes.
Aspirin does not have to be the *best* measure to make people healthier. A good measure can still help.
The conclusion is about industrialized nations. Studies done there would fit the conclusion, not undermine it.
The author never says no other changes are needed. The argument is about what follows when the changes do not happen.
The author says circulation will rise *less quickly*, not that it will fall. The argument keeps those apart; it just draws the wrong conclusion from the slower rise.
The conclusion is not a restatement of a premise. It is drawn, badly, from the conditional.
There is no general claim refuted by a counterexample. The argument misuses a conditional.

Continuing the past rate *ensures* the magazine becomes the largest. The argument treats it as *required*, so that missing the rate means missing the goal. Those are different, and the magazine might reach the top by some other path.
No conditional about harm is reversed. The critic is not reasoning about what makes something harmful at all.
The critic does not claim anything is true for lack of contrary evidence. The reason offered is Fillmore's self-interest.
The only reason to reject Fillmore's argument is that it serves Fillmore. A self-serving argument can still be sound. The critic attacks the arguer's motive instead of the argument.
The critic is not relying on Fillmore's authority; the critic is rejecting Fillmore's view. Nobody's questionable authority supports the conclusion.

Granting a premise while rejecting the argument is not inconsistent. You can accept that children learn from television and still deny that television is harmless. The critic's claims fit together; they just do not support rejecting Fillmore.
The studies were "numerous" and covered "every airport" that exceeded capacity. Nothing suggests too few cases. The problem is their age.

If safety at higher traffic depends heavily on *which* technology is in use, results with 30-year-old technology do not predict results with today's. The editorialist treats "latest" then as the same as "latest" now.
Whether council members know about the studies does not affect whether the studies support the conclusion.
The editorialist does cite evidence against the claim: the studies. The weakness is that the evidence is outdated, not that the argument mistakes a lack of evidence for evidence.
The conclusion is only that safety would decrease. Whether a decrease is worth it is a separate question the editorialist never raises.

The study shows a correlation between species count and a plot's ability to support plants. Good soil and growing conditions could be what allows more species to grow. The author assumes the direction runs from species to soil without considering the reverse.
An argument can establish a cause without explaining how it works. Asking for the mechanism is not the flaw.
The study compares many plots, and the conclusion is about prairies in general. Nothing hinges on one plot standing in for others.
We are given no reason to think the plots studied were unusual.
No proportions appear. The study counts species and measures growth.
Percentages work the same whether the town has 100 houses or 100,000. Size does not create or remove overlap.
A drainage problem already counts as a problem in the resident's math. Whether it also makes a house unsafe does not change how many houses have a problem.
Ease of repair has nothing to do with how many houses have problems now.
The resident's own claim leaves up to 40 percent with neither problem. "Many houses have neither" fits the argument and does not touch the addition error.
If some houses have both problems, they get counted twice. With overlap, fewer than 60 percent of houses have a problem, so "at least 60 percent" fails.
Kao has the *sufficient* side (running for office) and the conclusion is the other side (golfer). The direction is right. The weakness is that "most" does not mean "all." That is a different flaw.
There is no conditional at all. This is a prediction from comparative strengths, not a reversed rule.
This infers a cause from one coincidence in timing. The voter's argument is conditional, not causal.

Rule: negotiating a loan → go to the bank. Thompson went to the bank. Conclusion: Thompson is negotiating a loan. Same reversal, same shape: people visit banks for many reasons, just as prime ministers travel for many reasons.
This treats a claim not proven false (never committed a crime) as proof of its opposite. That is the unproven vs proven false flaw, not a reversal.
The pundit need not say university graduates lack these traits. Graduates could have them too; the question is whether university adds anything for people who already have them.

If corporations also require an attribute available only through university, such as a credential or specific training, then attending helps get the job. The pundit's evidence covers only the attributes valued *most*, not everything required.
The pundit does not need corporations to hire *only* people with these traits. The argument fails because other requirements might exist, not because of how strict these ones are.
The conclusion is limited to job prospects. Other reasons for attending university do not bear on it.
The pundit points out that many graduates *already* have the traits. Whether study can produce them does not matter for those graduates.
The columnist is not reversing a conditional. The error is about how much a proposal must accomplish.

Some electrocutions without overhead cable lines show only that the ban would not end electrocution entirely. The activists only claimed the lines raise the risk. Rejecting their argument because it does not solve everything holds them to a standard they never claimed.
The columnist rejects one argument for the ban. Other benefits the ban might have are beside the point of whether *this* argument works.
The columnist says nothing about the activists themselves.
No other proposals are mentioned.
An unrelated leg-rotation condition doesn't affect whether the shoes treat flat-footedness.
The conclusion is about adults. Teenage smoking rates do not bear on it.
The percentage of adults who smoke *is* a measure of the whole adult population. Nothing is generalized from a part.
The survey is recent, and it tracks changes across the last twenty years. The conclusion is about that change, not about statistics that are out of date.
Restrictions on advertising other products would not explain a drop in smoking.
Many other factors could have lowered adult smoking in the same decade. Without ruling them out, matching timing does not show the restrictions made a significant difference.
Williams draws no distinction between confrontational and entertaining teaching. He talks about Thomas's motives.
The argument is weak, not circular. Williams does not assume Thomas is wrong in order to prove it.
Williams treats the report as Thomas's own view, which it is. There is no characterization mistaken for endorsement.
Williams attacks Thomas's possible jealousy and frustration rather than the report's reasoning. Even if Thomas is jealous, York might still be too confrontational.
This tempts because Williams clearly sides with York. But Williams never denies outright that York could be too confrontational. The flaw is *how* he resists the report: by attacking Thomas.
The writer never says social reasons are the only legitimate ones. The writer only says relying on them does no harm.

Map the abstract wording. "A behavior" is accepting arguments for social reasons. "A particular endeavor's goals" are science's goals. "Comparable behaviors in other endeavors" is social influence on every human endeavor. The writer treats the fact that social influence is everywhere as settling whether it obstructs science. It does not.
If scientists also weigh the evidence, social reasons are less likely to harm science. That helps the writer rather than exposing a flaw.
Whether scientists notice their social motives does not affect whether those motives harm science.
The writer reasons from other endeavors to science, not from science to other endeavors. Nothing is concluded about whether the behavior harms anything else.
The manager does not treat any factor as individually necessary. He relies on one research finding.
The research is relevant; it is about loose versus tight groups. The problem is that it applies only under a condition the manager never establishes.
The manager does not need flexible teams to be better *always*. His mistake is ignoring the research's own limit, not exaggerating its size.

The research applies only when a common purpose is shared. If independent workers who avoid tight groups struggle to commit to a common purpose, the finding does not apply to them, and "bound to succeed" collapses.
The manager does not mix up his own goals with the team's shared goals. He simply never shows there will be a shared goal.
No condition for producing a result is confused with one for preventing it. The argument weighs effects, not conditions.
"Would very likely not be harmed" is a prediction, not a value judgment. The flaw is in the prediction.

The regulations tend to discourage landowners from protecting species. They also block construction on land where those species live, a stronger protective effect. The developer looks only at the first effect, so removing the rules could harm species overall.
Developers' and landowners' interests do not decide whether species would be harmed.
Landowners without endangered species are not affected by the rules in question, so their reactions do not bear on harm to species.
Postmark and entry form are *requirements* (necessary conditions). Missing one means no acceptance. That reasoning is valid, so it cannot match a flawed argument.

One combined rule (organized + good cook → delicious), then a failed result, then blame placed on one specific part. The contrapositive only gives "not organized *or* not a good cook." That is a different error from negating two separate triggers.

Exercise → fitness improves. Quit smoking → fitness improves. Bob does neither, so his fitness will not improve. Same structure: two separate sufficient conditions, both absent, outcome denied. Bob could improve his fitness by eating better or sleeping more.
The rules say the police are *allowed* to ticket. The conclusion says they *will*. The flaw is treating permission as certainty, not negating two conditions.
This mixes "most" and "some" statements. The structure is quantifier-based and does not deny an outcome from two absent triggers.
Multiple authors would not change the issue. The question is whether we can know some feelings were not intended.
The "most readers" claim is Abner's evidence about how the translation affects people. The translator does not appeal to popular opinion.
If the poem was not meant to produce any particular feelings, then the translation could hardly produce the "wrong" ones. That would help the translator, not expose a flaw.
"As Dr. Abner should realize" is a jab, but the translator rejects the criticism on the grounds of what we can know, not because of Abner's circumstances.

The translator moves from "we don't know what feelings the author intended" to "we can't say the translation produces unintended feelings." Some effects can be ruled out even when the specific intended effect is unknown.

The premise "a product as good or better would cost as much or more" holds only if price reflects quality. Grant that, and the most expensive product is automatically the best. So the premise assumes what the conclusion asserts. Circular answers are usually wrong on Flaw, which is what makes this one hard: here the premise really does depend on the conclusion.
The conclusion is about products currently available. Whether a better product could be made does not matter.
The spokesperson never claims anything causes the high price or results from it. There is no causal claim to reverse.
The argument is about the company's products, not the company as a whole. No part-to-whole move appears.
The premise and conclusion fit together perfectly. That is the problem: they say the same thing. They are not in conflict.
The two reasons are compatible. "Not proved" and "even if proved, they are hypocrites" can both be offered at once. "Even if" signals a fallback, not a contradiction.

This is the other kind of ad hominem: attacking someone's motive. Competitors might gain if KlopperKidz is pulled, but the manufacturer never says so. The stated reason is that competitors do not follow their own advice, which is (D).

This tempts because the manufacturer says the allegations are not proved. But the manufacturer never concludes the toys are safe or the allegations false. The conclusion is that the argument does not merit attention.

The competitors have not withdrawn their own injury-causing toys, so the manufacturer dismisses their argument. Failing to follow a recommendation does not make the recommendation wrong. This is the "you do it too" flaw.
No conditional about what makes a toy unsafe is reversed.

Schmidt criticizes a method of enforcement. Chandha responds as if Schmidt had criticized the rules themselves. Showing the rules are valuable does not show neighbor reporting is a good way to enforce them.
Chandha says nothing about why Schmidt holds the view. The response is about the rules' value.
Neither speaker discusses the rules' detailed provisions. Schmidt's complaint is about enforcement, which (A) captures.
Chandha does not reason from "likely sometimes" to "always." "Could degrade" is a possibility.
Chandha never discusses bad feelings among neighbors at all, so there is no cause and effect to confuse.
There is no sample. The argument reasons from general facts about sodium nitrate and sodium.

The obvious risk of dropping nitrate would be spoilage, and the argument already says nitrate does not prevent it. Losing the pink color is the only cost mentioned. The real gap is the leap from "excessive" to "never."
The government is never mentioned. The argument is a recommendation, not a policy about consent.
The evidence only shows that *excessive* use is a problem. Limiting the amount would address that problem and keep the color. The argument never explains why a total ban is better than moderation.
No economic justification appears. The reasoning is entirely about spoilage, taste and health.
How many strong achievers versus others do extracurriculars has no bearing on whether both rural and urban students are among them.
The principal claims only that *some* of each group participate, not that one group outnumbers the other.

The students who do both lunch and extracurriculars might all be rural, or all urban. The mix in the lunch program says nothing about the mix in that overlap, so the principal cannot conclude both groups are represented.
Other ways of spending time do not affect whether some rural and some urban students do extracurriculars.
"Participate" means taking part in both uses. The meaning does not shift.
The paleontologist never says the theory is true because the skeptics' argument fails. He says only that their reasoning is misguided. So this does not catch any move he makes.
If older maniraptors could have lived without leaving older fossils, the missing fossils are even weaker evidence against the theory. That supports the paleontologist.
The paleontologist does not claim older fossils would prove the theory. He only says their absence does not disprove it.
The paleontologist addresses one piece of reasoning. Other evidence against the theory would not show his response to *that* reasoning is flawed.

The skeptics refuse to *accept* the theory because the evidence found so far looks insufficient. That can be reasonable even if the missing fossils might exist. The paleontologist treats their position as if it required proof that the fossils do not exist.
Smokers exercise less. Less exercise is bad for the heart, so this is a non-nicotine difference that fits the frame.
Something in chewing tobacco blunts nicotine's effect on the heart. Same nicotine, less damage for chewers.
Chewers eat better. A healthier diet protects the heart, which separates the groups.

Cancer is not heart attacks or blood pressure. A chemical in chewing tobacco that causes cancer says nothing about why chewers have *fewer* heart problems. If anything, it is one more harm for chewers, and it fails the frame.
Something in cigarette smoke, but not in chewing tobacco, raises blood pressure. That gives smokers extra heart risk on top of the shared nicotine.
Cheaper ad rates would explain the fall in ad revenue. They do nothing to explain why more magazines than ever are succeeding.
Television audiences do not tell us anything about magazine revenue or magazine success.

Only the biggest magazines live on advertising, so the ad slump threatens them. Everyone else lives on circulation, and more people are reading, so more of them succeed. Both halves of the stimulus now fit.
If readers cut subscriptions and borrow copies, circulation revenue falls too. That makes the record number of successful magazines even harder to explain.
New magazines surviving is one more sign of success. It repeats the surprising fact instead of explaining it.
Sharing the music builds a supportive community. Belonging is a source of joy, even when the songs are about pain.
This compares *success* between two kinds of musicians. It says nothing about why performing sad songs brings joy or hope to anyone, so it does not touch the conflict.
Irony and wit give perspective on troubles. Laughing at hardship is one way sad material turns into affirmation.
Hearing that others share your plight helps you cope. That turns songs about trouble into comfort.
Turning sorrow into art can be cathartic for both performer and audience. Release is a direct route from sad lyrics to a good feeling.
"Some kinds of plants" do better among other species. We are not told alfalfa is one of them, and this does not give a mechanism for its year-to-year decline.
This explains how alfalfa adds usable nitrogen. It confirms the expectation that alfalfa should not run short, so it makes the decline more puzzling.
Alfalfa produces substances that build up in the soil and poison it. Each year in the same field, more of the toxin is there. That is a reason for decline that has nothing to do with nitrogen.
Alfalfa adds nitrogen only when certain bacteria are present. The stimulus already says alfalfa increases nitrogen, and we are not told the bacteria are missing, so this does not explain the decline.
No black walnut trees are mentioned. A sensitivity to their leaves cannot explain decline in an ordinary alfalfa field.
How likely an attack is near dense versus sparse vegetation does not explain where a startled bird flies.
If some feeders are far from houses, birds there have even less reason to hit windows. It does nothing for the birds that do.
Bird size is not part of the puzzle. Large and small birds alike hitting windows leaves the behavior unexplained.
Being startled by noise rather than predators might change a reaction in general, but it does not explain flying *into windows* rather than into the vegetation.
If the windows reflect the surrounding plants, a fleeing bird sees what looks like cover and flies toward it. It is behaving just as the first sentence says birds do.
This is about the placebo group. It does not explain why people in the *vaccine* group got symptoms.
Who recognized their symptoms does not change who had them. Vaccinated people still showed symptoms.
Overall fitness might affect how sick someone gets, but a completely effective vaccine should prevent infection regardless.

The vaccine prevents infection; it cannot undo one that already happened. With a 60-day delay before symptoms, people infected before the shot would show symptoms afterward. The vaccine is still completely effective.
Faster recovery says the vaccinated people were still infected. That is the puzzle, not the explanation.
Tasmanians once had these practices and dropped them. That is the "lost it" route.
If Tasmanians developed boomerangs and spear-throwers *before* the split, they should still have had them. This adds to the mystery of why they lacked them later instead of explaining it.
Polynesians brought these innovations to Australia after the bridge disappeared. Tasmania was cut off by then, so Tasmanians never got them.
Australians invented the boomerang and spear-thrower after the split. Tasmanians could not have received them.
The innovations existed before the split, but only among northern groups the Tasmanians never contacted. Separation then kept them out.
A gap that has grown over 30 years does not explain why two measurements taken now give different numbers.
Women in identical jobs earning about the same as men is about full-time pay. It does not explain why including all workers lowers the ratio.
More women in well-paid full-time jobs would raise women's averages. That works against a lower all-worker figure.
A larger share of women work part time, and part-timers earn less. Adding them pulls the women's overall average down more than the men's, which turns 80 percent into 65.
Figures from other countries cannot explain the gap between two figures about Naota.
The eye overcorrects while healing and becomes farsighted. That patient now needs lenses for a new problem.
RK works less well on severe nearsightedness. Severely nearsighted patients may be left needing lenses.
Uneven healing leaves the two eyes different, which only lenses can fix.
Uneven healing can cause astigmatism that requires lenses, even in patients who started with mild nearsightedness.
This compares RK patients with people who skipped surgery, before surgery. Being equally nearsighted beforehand says nothing about why some patients need lenses afterward.
Cliffs resembling other sparse places tells us nothing about why trees there live longer than forest trees.
Fires are frequent where these cedars grow, and they reach forests but not cliff faces. Forest cedars burn before they get old; cliff cedars survive.
Losing bark after a few hundred years would happen to old cedars wherever they grow. It does not separate cliff from forest.
This explains why cliff cedars stay short. The puzzle is why they live longer, and height limits say nothing about age.
Occasional furniture use might lead to some cutting, but the choice does not say forest cedars are cut more than cliff cedars. It does not explain the age gap.
