Students started both reading and arithmetic before computers. That applies to two of the subjects alike, so it cannot explain the split.
Arithmetic's exactness makes it the best fit for computer-assisted learning. That gives a subject-level difference that matches the ranking: arithmetic most useful, the others less.
Teacher reluctance would affect every subject. It does not explain why one subject did well and the others did not.
Interest in the newest computers applies to all programs equally.
More programs in reading and writing should have made computers *more* helpful there, not less.
Antilock cars are driven more carelessly. The drivers, not the brakes, account for the extra accidents.
Antilock brakes fail more often than regular brakes. Brakes that fail cause accidents.
Without expensive maintenance, antilock brakes are worse than regular brakes. Many owners will skip that maintenance.
Most drivers do not know how to use antilock brakes properly, so they do not get the safety benefit.

This says where the brakes were meant to help and where the worst accidents happen. Highways affect cars with either kind of brake, and "most serious" is about severity, not number. It does not explain why antilock cars have *more* accidents.
Diet while breast-feeding does not explain why the recommended pregnancy diet seems not to work.
If babies of poorly fed mothers have no serious problems later in childhood, diet looks even less important.
Babies of mothers without a nutritious diet have more first-year problems. Most babies have some problem either way, but the diet lowers the number. The recommendation is still sound.
How serious first-year problems are compared with later ones does not show the diet helps.
Doctors repeating their advice is not evidence that the advice works.
If gas and dust come weeks *after* breakup begins, the comet should have split before it brightened. That runs the timeline the wrong way.
Why gas and dust brighten a comet does not explain the gap between brightening and the visible split.
Cracks can release gas and dust without the comet breaking all the way through. The comet began cracking in September, brightened, and split into pieces in November.
A steady increase in gas and dust does not say why the pieces were not visible until November.
This explains why the comet broke up. It does not explain the delay between the brightening and the visible split.
Lead-free paint being harmful in other ways does not explain more *lead* being ingested.
Better uses for the money say nothing about lead levels after removal.
Other sources supplying most of the lead might make removal pointless, but not harmful. It does not explain an *increase*.
Removing the paint spreads lead dust, which children swallow more easily than paint on a wall. The law causes the very exposure it aims to prevent.
Other hazards being worse does not explain how removing lead paint increases lead intake.
Comparing this corn to its ancestors does not explain why people preferred it to the other grains despite the health problems.
Modern corn being more nutritious has nothing to do with people thousands of years ago.
Without meat or milk, people had no other way to make up for corn's poor nutrition. That makes sticking with corn harder to explain.
If some alternatives grew in poorer soil, switching back would have been even easier.
People learned that adding readily available nongrain foods fixed their health. They could keep corn's higher yield and solve the nutrition problem at the same time.
Animals on calcium supplements rarely get new stones. That repeats the surprising result without saying why it happens.
Adding oxalate while cutting calcium is a different change from adding calcium. It does not explain why more calcium helps.
An inherited cause of stones does not explain why extra calcium lowers recurrence.
More dietary calcium means more calcium leaves through the intestines and less is left for the kidneys to filter. The urine is less concentrated, so fewer stones form.
Stones made of uric acid are not the calcium-oxalate stones the stimulus is about.
People shocked by others' powerful views become afraid to voice their own. Unrestricted speech has silenced them, which is exactly the claim.
More views, some offensive. Being offended is not the same as being silenced, so this does not show speech is inhibited.
This recommends restricting speech. A recommendation does not explain how unrestricted speech inhibits speech.
The salary comparison suggests the claim is absurd. That undermines the conclusion we are supposed to justify.
Offended people speak up in reply. That is more speech, not less.
Lactose tablets do not help people who have lost the ability to absorb lactose.
Lower milk consumption everywhere does not separate tropical from nontropical people.
Abundant sunlight makes the body produce vitamin D, which helps absorb calcium. Tropical people get calcium absorption another way.
A slight rise in other dairy products does not fix calcium absorption for people who cannot absorb lactose, and "slightly" could not close the gap.
Genetics deciding how much the ability is lost does not explain how bone repair stays normal.
Punishment after conviction does not affect how many victims complain in the first place.
This is about how hard complaints are to investigate. It says nothing about why there are so few complaints.
Some schemes are discovered a year or two late. Over ten years, those victims would still eventually complain, and the choice covers only "some" schemes.
Which court prosecutes the fraud does not explain why victims do not report it.
Most victims are too embarrassed to seek any remedy, so they never complain. Fraud grows while complaints stay low.
Taller dams being built as arch dams explains why many arch dams are tall. It does not explain why the short ones are the ones collapsing.
Comparing arch dams with other types does not separate tall arch dams from short ones.
Larger structures get more careful design and construction. That extra care can outweigh the greater forces, so tall arch dams hold while shorter ones fail.
Long-known engineering principles apply to arch dams of every height.
Comparing short arch dams with short dams of other types does not explain why short arch dams fail more than tall ones.
A belief about growth rates does not decide between the two fixed scenarios.
Wanting a GNP above $120 billion would favor scenario 2, which comes closer.
If GNP does not affect personal welfare, people might be indifferent between the scenarios. It does not explain a preference for the lower GNP.
If GNP is a poor measure, people again have little reason to care either way. That gives no reason to prefer scenario 1.
Citizens want F to be more economically powerful than G. Only scenario 1 delivers that, so they choose it even though F's GNP is lower.
Hatching order and brood size do not explain why adults care for every larva.

Cooperation helps the most larvae survive, but the beetles are trying to *shrink* rivals' broods. This explains why caring for everyone produces many survivors, not why beetles who want fewer rival larvae would do it.

If beetles cannot tell their own larvae from others', they cannot harm rivals' larvae without risking their own. Equal care follows from the same goal that drives egg destruction. (Eggs, presumably, they can identify by where they laid them.)
Cooperating to defend the site explains joint defense. It does not explain why beetles that destroy rivals' eggs leave rivals' larvae alone and even feed them.
If space for larvae is limited, a beetle has even more reason to remove rivals' larvae, not care for them.
Larger classes mean less attention per child, which should make things worse, not better.
Past classrooms being better equipped makes their failure harder to explain and today's success more surprising.
Today's classrooms use group projects that engage students of different ages. That replaces the one-level lesson that confused the young and bored the old.
A wider range of ages should make the old problems worse.
Whether teachers were once in mixed-age classrooms does not explain why the classrooms now work.
If two beetles bury a larger carcass, two parents would mean *more* food. That makes the result stranger.
Parents eat from the carcass themselves. With one parent gone, more of the fixed food supply goes to the larvae, so they grow larger.
Taking turns describes how parents share work. It does not explain bigger larvae with only one parent.
Larvae finding food after a week would be true whether one or two parents are present.
Two parents defending the carcass better would favor two parents, which deepens the puzzle.
Whether size shows age does not affect the chance of reaching maximum life expectancy.
Sea turtles living longer than other marine animals says nothing about captivity versus the wild.
Most wild leatherbacks die from predators, which captive ones never face. That is something bad about the wild to offset the diseases of captivity, so the two odds come out about equal.
If few people can make captivity healthy, captive turtles should do worse, not equally well.
Comparing leatherbacks with other reptiles does not separate captivity from the wild.
Another drug being better does not explain why this one's users are above average.
How often another drug is prescribed says nothing about this drug's users.
Most high-cholesterol patients being on diets does not explain the cholesterol of the people who do take the drug.
The drug goes only to people at least 30 percent above average. Lowering them to 12 to 15 percent above is a real effect, and it leaves them above average.
The balance of high and low cholesterol in the population tells us nothing about the drug's users.
The urine proteins that react with saccharin to form crystals exist in rats but not mice. No crystals, no damage, no cancer.
Faster regeneration in mice could mean more chances for cancerous cells, not fewer. It does not explain the difference.
Both rats and mice got high doses, so dose cannot separate them.
Where the crystals are toxic would apply to both species if both formed them.
Other sweeteners are not the issue. This also runs the wrong way, giving mice crystals and rats none.
Faculty salaries rising does not change what students pay; tuition per course is flat. It does not explain why students can no longer afford it.
Students must take more courses per semester, and tuition is charged per course, so their tuition rises.
Higher living costs leave less money for tuition.
Scholarships are renewed only for high grades. Students who lose them pay more.
Part-time jobs once held by students went to nonstudents. Students lost income.
The current turf has needed a lot of maintenance, but we already know grass costs more to maintain. This does not outweigh that.

Turf injuries are fewer, but each one heals more slowly and needs more expensive therapy. That cost could outweigh the cheaper maintenance and make turf the more expensive field overall, which is the kind of reason a budget committee acts on.
Whether spectators can tell the difference does not affect injuries or cost.
This lists different maintenance tasks, but we already know grass is more expensive to maintain overall.

This is a *budget* committee, so player preference is not the kind of reason that drives its recommendation. And nothing says this university's athletes have played mostly on grass, so we do not even know the preference applies to them.
The deer eat only the bony shells. That is not meat, so they can feed on turtles without digesting meat.
Killing turtles by accident explains the killing, not the eating.
How often it happens does not explain how a deer that cannot digest meat eats a turtle at all.
Competition for food might explain killing turtles. It does not explain eating them.
Turtles being slow explains how deer catch them, not why they eat them.
Not having read the books would apply under either name, so it cannot explain knowing one fact but not the other.
Everyone who knows about Clemens also knowing about Twain is consistent with the gap but does not explain why so few know about Clemens.
Most people do not know Twain is Clemens, so they cannot carry "writer" from one name to the other.
Holding conflicting beliefs about authors in general does not explain this specific gap.
"Some people" knowing the pseudonym fits the puzzle but does not explain why most do not know Clemens was a writer.
A larger population means more diagnosed cases in total, even if the rate does not rise.
Pre-cut carrots lose vitamins quickly, so people eating more carrots may get less vitamin A.
Popular cuisines use more vegetables, including carrots. More carrots eaten should mean less deficiency, so this deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.
The extra carrots went to groups that rarely had deficiency, so the groups at risk saw no benefit.
Demand rose but supply fell, so people may actually be eating fewer carrots.
Whether playwrights criticize their own society more than others does not connect the wish for empathy to inaccuracy.
Playwrights exaggerate a society's weaknesses for dramatic effect. A hostile society makes the hero sympathetic, and the exaggeration is why historians distrust the portrait.
If plays tend to give useful information about their society, the historians' skepticism is harder to explain.
This says plays often reveal their societies seriously, which contradicts the historians' view.
Popularity is never mentioned, and this does not connect the playwrights' aims to inaccuracy.
Farm size does not explain why yields failed to rise on farms that switched.
Higher yields in "some areas" restates part of the test result. It does not explain why yields did not rise elsewhere.
The hybrids were tested under much better conditions than most farms have. Their advantage depended on those conditions, so it did not show up on real farms.
Taste and sales are not yields. This does not explain flat yields.
Subsidies explain why farmers switched. They do not explain why yields stayed flat.
However many of the birds were too young to breed, the stimulus says *most* of the transplanted warblers kept the cooperative pattern. Young birds do not explain what the majority did.
Climate is not the cause the stimulus gives for cooperative breeding. A similar climate does not explain the result.
Most of the new island's land is not suitable for nesting. Usable territory may be just as scarce as at home, so the same cause keeps the birds breeding cooperatively.
Other species' reasons for cooperative breeding do not explain these warblers' behavior.
Fewer competitors for nesting territory should make it *easier* to breed alone, which deepens the puzzle.
If bacteria on old brushes speed up plaque, sterilizing should have helped Group 2. But Groups 1 and 2 ended up the same.
New bristles are stiff, and brushing wears that stiffness down over months. Only Group 3 always had stiff bristles. Groups 1 and 2 brushed with worn brushes, sterilized or not, so they matched.
A new way of measuring plaque applies to all three groups and cannot separate them.
If some of Group 3 used to brush less, they should have *more* plaque, not less.
Equal vigor rules out one difference but does not explain the result.
Why crime fell does not explain why anxiety rose.
Underreporting of anxiety does not explain why anxiety increased.
If people assess their risk realistically, anxiety should have dropped along with crime.
Anxious people living in high-crime areas explains where anxiety is high, not why it rose overall last year.
The share of violent crimes covered by the news nearly doubled. People saw far more crime stories, so anxiety rose even while crime fell.
People feel safer with antilock brakes and skip their seat belts. Each crash becomes more deadly, so total deaths can rise even as collisions fall.
Traditional brakes stopping as quickly "under some circumstances" does not show antilock brakes cost lives.
Antilock brakes being easier for new drivers is another safety benefit, which deepens the conflict.
Cost has nothing to do with saving lives.
Equal effectiveness against different kinds of accidents does not show the brakes increase deaths.
Exhibition visitors have narrow interests and see fewer exhibits, so their visits are shorter.
A plan to extend hours was considered but *not* enacted. Nothing changed, so it cannot explain any difference in visit length.
People there for prestige only need to show up, not linger.
One-hour tickets limit how long exhibition visitors stay.
Tour groups follow a schedule and cannot browse, so their visits are shorter.
Pesticide levels often stay high for decades after use ends. The ban was only a few decades ago, so the toxaphene in the lake can simply be left over from before it.
Other pesticides in the water do not explain where the toxaphene came from.
If toxic chemicals rarely travel far through the air, toxaphene from distant countries is less likely to reach the lake. This closes off one explanation.
Manufacturers opposing the ban does not mean anyone kept using toxaphene after it.
The puzzle is toxaphene in the lake's water. How easily it is detected in fish says nothing about why it is there.
Other structures having the same pattern does not explain why it happens in bridges.

Builders reinforce the high-stress points, so those points hold. The stress moves to weaker parts of the bridge and causes the fracture there. More high-stress points means more stress moved around, and so a higher chance of fracture.
If fracturing creates high-stress points, fractures and high-stress points should show up in the same place. That is the opposite of what we see.
This explains how fractures can happen without high-stress points, but not why more high-stress points still make a fracture more likely.
Bad construction explains why high-stress points and fractures go together. It does not explain why the fractures land somewhere else.
Newer tires support the experts, but this does not explain why strict places still have more accidents.
Overconfidence after inspection is a way the rules could *cause* accidents. That supports the evidence against the experts.
The strict places have far more congested, dangerous roads. They would have more accidents without the rules, so the rules can still be lowering a rate that starts higher.
Seat belts discouraging reckless driving "for a few people" supports the experts a little, but it does not explain the higher accident rate.
The accident rate is per kilometer *driven*. Having more kilometers of road does not change that rate.
Female bats catching more insects on warm nights does not explain how the bats know it is warm.
The bats can sense barometric pressure inside the cave, and that pressure moves with the temperature outside. That is their signal.
This is a reason to stay in on cool nights, but it does not explain how a bat in the cave can tell the night is cool.
Eating more in spring and fall than in summer does not explain the difference between warm and cool nights.
Knowing that more than half the bats left on most evenings says nothing about how they choose which nights.
Meteorologists understanding the factors better now does not change how many tornadoes are recorded.
Stronger tornadoes suggest something about the climate has changed, which makes the meteorologists' claim harder to believe.
A slow rise in the last five years does not explain the tripling since 1953.
Property damage depends on how much property is in the way. It does not explain more recorded tornadoes.
Many more citizens now help detect tornadoes. More tornadoes get noticed and recorded, while the number actually forming stays the same.
Distraction causing accidents does not separate busy highways from quiet ones.
This says where the high fatal rates are instead of explaining why the busiest roads have low ones.
Knowing that the drivers are commuters does not tell us why they have fewer fatal accidents.
Most serious accidents happen at high speed. Congested highways keep traffic slow, so they produce fewer of these deadly crashes.
Busy highways "do not always" carry more trucks. This does not connect traffic to fatal accidents either way.
Rock staying solid at high temperatures might explain why Venus has no volcanos. It does not explain where the heat goes.
Venus's surface is thin, so heat from inside radiates straight into space. That is a way out for the heat without volcanos or fissures.
Bigger temperature swings inside Venus do not explain how it releases heat.
Surface movement "somewhat like" Earth's is not a way of releasing heat, and the stimulus already says Venus has no fissures from that movement.
A hotter atmosphere would make it harder, not easier, for heat to escape.
Recycling trucks polluting less than incineration makes recycling look *better*.
Recycling would cost so much that the city could not afford other projects that reduce pollution. The garbage problem shrinks, but the environment loses more overall.
If the city has to burn its garbage, recycling would reduce burning. That makes recycling look better.
More use of recycled materials in manufacturing is another benefit of recycling.
Recyclers consuming less is another benefit.
Some forms being more contagious does not explain the gap between low incidence and high deaths.
The stimulus is about *residents* of Country X. Deaths among nonresidents do not explain it.

Country X seldom diagnoses the disease except in the most severe cases. Mild cases go uncounted, which keeps the reported rate low. The cases that are counted are the deadly ones, which drives up the death rate.
Year-to-year swings in the number of cases affect every country and do not explain this gap.
More potentially fatal illnesses in general says nothing about disease P.
The kind of products sold this way does not explain why admitting the affiliation helps.
This compares people who respond to mass-media ads, but it does not explain why the admission helps the campaign.
How the boosters were recruited does not affect how consumers respond to them.
Cost does not explain why one kind of word-of-mouth message succeeds more than another.
Admitting the affiliation leads to a more relaxed, in-depth conversation about the product. That benefit can outweigh any extra skepticism.
Animals being more active in warm weather does not explain why one tongue movement slows and the other does not.
How far the tongue extends says nothing about how temperature affects it.
Where the chameleons live does not explain the difference between extension and retraction.
Retraction runs on muscle, which the cold weakens. Extension runs on energy stored in an elastic sheath, so the cold does not slow it much.
Comparing the chameleon's retraction muscles with other animals' says nothing about why extension holds up in the cold.
Gum has less sugar than a meal, but it still adds sugar. This makes the gum less harmful, not helpful.
Decay being reversible if caught early does not explain why gum helps.
Chewing gum makes saliva, which reduces acid and helps rebuild enamel. That benefit outweighs the small amount of sugar.
If sugar takes 24 hours to cause harm, brushing after every meal seems less urgent. That does not explain why gum would help.
Healthy jaw muscles are not cavities.
More people drinking decaf today does not explain why it tasted bad at first.
Whether people would drink it does not explain how it tasted.
Food affects the taste of all coffee, regular and decaf alike, so it cannot explain why decaf tasted worse.
Price is not taste.
Processors used only low-quality beans for early decaf. The coffee tasted bad because of the beans, not the process.
If shoppers care more about reliability than fuel efficiency, it is even stranger that they skip the reliable cars.

Shoppers go by a model's reputation, and reputations can be out of date. A model that has become reliable may still carry an old reputation for breaking down, so reliability-minded shoppers pass it by.
Owners keeping their reliable cars does not explain why new shoppers do not buy those models.
A car that needs a lot of maintenance is not reliable by the stimulus's definition, so these models are not the ones in question.
Unreliable stylish cars do not explain why reliable cars sell poorly.
If viewers had the sound off, the bad sync would not hurt. But that only removes the harm. It does not explain why these dealers did *better*.
People remember a commercial better when the sound and picture are out of sync. The flaw made the ads stick, and that helped sales.
Who the studio's clients were does not explain why its commercials worked better.
If some commercials had no people talking, the flaw mattered less in them. That still does not explain better sales.
Most dealers relying little on TV applies to dealers using either agency. It does not separate the two groups.
Killing crocodiles that attack should reduce attacks, not increase them.
A count of crocodiles in one area does not show any change over 20 years.
Comparing Lake Victoria with the rest of Africa does not explain the increase over time.
Crocodiles being unafraid of humans is not shown to be new, so it does not explain why attacks went up.
People now fish in more parts of the lake, so they meet crocodiles more often. More contact means more attacks, with the same number of crocodiles.
The argument is about tuberculosis proteins. It does not need every protein in every disease-causing bacterium to be recognizable.
Whether skin irritation is a symptom of the disease itself is irrelevant. The test is about a reaction to an injection.
Negate it: the reaction is *not* exclusive to tuberculosis, so other bacteria can trigger it too. Then a reaction does not show tuberculosis infection, and the conclusion falls apart.
If the injection itself can cause tuberculosis, that is a problem for the test, not something the physicians assume.
This is about whether infected people always react. The conclusion only claims that everyone who reacts is infected.
Negate it: there *are* unknown anthracosaur fossils older than 340 million years. Then anthracosaurs existed before this lizard, and lizards could have evolved from them. The conclusion falls apart.
Older lizard fossils would only push lizards back further, which helps the argument. The author does not need to rule them out.
The stimulus already gives us a known lizard fossil older than every known anthracosaur fossil. The author is not assuming there are none.
Known anthracosaur fossils can be older than some younger lizard fossils. What matters is the first lizard, and nothing known is older than it.
Lizard fossils of uncertain age do not affect the argument, which rests on the dated 340-million-year-old fossil.
Negate it: this style does *not* have a comparable effect in novels and songs. Then the novelists tell us nothing about Lindsey's lyrics, and the analogy collapses.
Whether some readers miss the subtleties of modern novels does not affect the comparison with Lindsey.
Narrative structure is never discussed. The argument does not need Lindsey's lyrics to match other lyrics in structure.
The argument does not compare novels and songs with other kinds of writing.
The judgment being criticized is already about her lyrics. The author does not need lyrics to matter more than the music.
Fines might help, but the argument relies on development bringing resources, not on any specific policy.
Pollution from neighboring countries does not affect leaching from Country X's dumps.
Negate it: industrial development in Country X will *not* increase. Then the resources to tackle pollution never arrive, and there is no reason to expect the problems to diminish.
Country X is already at the income level where the problems peak, so it has already begun industrializing. The author does not assume it has yet to start.
How Country X compares with other countries does not affect what will happen to it.
Negate it: the *number* of news stories a person sees *is* the source of the confusion. That is a third cause, and poor organization is no longer the only explanation left.
The argument does not need poor organization to make understanding *impossible*, only to be the cause of confusion.
Whether seeing more stories would help is not about what causes the confusion now.
The evidence already says stories are well below what people can handle. The argument does not need people to cope with a *very* high density.
Some people being overwhelmed by too much information points toward the "too fast" explanation the author ruled out.
The argument is about whether this tax cut would make upper-income citizens invest. How their past investment compares with lower-income citizens' does not matter. Negate it and nothing changes.
The citizen predicts what this tax cut will do. It does not need past tax cuts to have worked. Negate it, "past tax cuts did not tend to create jobs," and this one still could.
The argument does not need water to be the *only* cause of erosion.
Negate it: *none* of the terraces in Dooney County were built to prevent erosion. Then the evidence about flat land and erosion terraces does not apply, and the terraces say nothing about the land.
What matters is why the farmers built the terraces, not whether the terraces actually work.
The stimulus says erosion is not a *problem* on flat land. The argument does not need there to be no erosion at all.
Terraces elsewhere in the county do not affect the argument, which rests on the terraces on farms.
Negate it: only one or two planes were scheduled for all nine flights. Then one or two mechanical problems could account for every cancellation, and there is no reason to suspect another cause.
How Swift compares with other airlines does not matter. The argument is about Swift on this day.
Flight length plays no role in the argument.
Past cancellation records do not affect what caused these nine.
Where the planes are based does not affect how many there were.
The author argues against the idea that herbs are left out because they don't work. The author does not assume they are ineffective.
When a substance is "properly" used is a different question from what physicians can recommend.

Negate it: a physician *can* recommend an herb even when it is not sold as a drug. Then the patent and approval problems do not stop physicians from recommending herbs, and the conclusion falls apart.
Other substances kept off the market for other reasons say nothing about herbs.
The cost of medical care is never part of the argument.
Breeding resistant bananas someday is not part of the argument, which relies on fungicides.
Negate it: large plantations do *not* produce most of the world's bananas. Then protecting them does not protect most of the crop, and the conclusion falls apart.
The argument relies on fungicides. It does not need the disease to spread more slowly on plantations.
The conclusion is only about Sigatoka. Other diseases do not matter.
Where the unexposed trees grow does not affect how much of the crop is protected.
The age of the patients does not affect the argument's point about their share of the population.
Whether people need a second transplant does not affect brain disorders.
Negate it: *every* degenerative brain disorder can be cured without a brain transplant. Then the lack of brain transplants does not matter, and there is no reason the share would grow.
How many deaths these disorders cause now does not affect whether their share will grow.
Research spending is never part of the argument.
The argument allows doing without as an option. It does not need a renewable replacement for every resource.
Negate it: we *can* replace exhausted nonrenewables with other nonrenewables forever. Then the current pattern never has to change, and the conclusion falls apart.
The argument does not need renewables to be impossible to exhaust.
Rising or falling consumption only changes when the ore runs out, not whether it does.
Doing without is one of the author's own options. The author does not assume it is impossible.
Negate it: the downturn *did* sharply cut the deposits banks lend from. Then banks lent less because they had less money, and relaxing the standards might not change anything.
Whether the standards caused the downturn is a different question from whether they reduced lending.
Why the standards were tightened does not affect what relaxing them would do.
The stimulus itself says lending fell during this downturn. The author does not assume no downturn comes with less lending.
If no relaxation could make up for the downturn, relaxing the standards might not increase lending. That hurts the argument.
How citizens view justice does not affect whether they can criticize experts.
The argument's requirement for justice is about citizen criticism, not the effect of punishment on criminals.
The argument does not need justice to be the system's *primary* concern.
The argument does not claim punishment and deterrence can't go together.
Negate it: citizens *without* that knowledge *can* still criticize the experts. Then the requirement for justice is met, and the conclusion falls apart.
Whether every variety of sweet-potato whitefly is a pest does not affect the search for a parasite of the silverleaf.
The argument does not need a parasite to *always* control its pest.
Better chances in the future do not tell us whether the past search was wasted.
Negate it: *some* parasite of the sweet-potato whitefly also attacks the silverleaf whitefly. Then the search may have turned up something useful after all, so it was not necessarily wasted.
If they found sweet-potato parasites that do not affect the new pest, the search could still be wasted. The argument does not need them to have found nothing.
Sheila's objection has nothing to do with how Crownsbury compares with other cities.
Sheila does not claim Robert misunderstands his own plan.
Negate it: with the bumps and signs in place, *every* driver slows to a safe speed. Then no one hits a bump too fast, and Sheila's objection disappears.
Sheila needs only some drivers to lose control, not most of the people affected to be harmed.
Nonresidential streets are not part of either speaker's argument.
This says emotions require intelligence. The argument needs the reverse: intelligence requires emotions.
The argument says computers can *never* have emotions, so how far technology advances does not matter.
Identifying one's emotions is a new and stronger requirement than having them.
The argument is about whether a computer has any intelligence at all, not how much.
Negate it: something can be intelligent *without* the capacity for emotions. Then a computer could be intelligent despite having no emotions, and the conclusion falls apart.
Popularity is never part of the argument.
The argument does not need some censoring regimes to be non-totalitarian.
Negate it: a totalitarian regime *cannot* see a loss of passivity as a threat. Then the evidence gives it no reason to censor these writings, and the conclusion falls apart.
The argument depends on what regimes *perceive*. It does not need passivity to actually be necessary for keeping power.
The conclusion says many regimes censor these writings. It does not need most of the labeled writings to be of this kind.
Negate it: words that refer to *nothing* can still have meaning. Then Ashley's statement does not make "of" and "upon" meaningless, and Joshua's reading falls apart.
Joshua never talks about usefulness.
This says referring words have meaning. Joshua needs the reverse: words that do not refer have none.
Joshua's reason for abandoning the words is that they are meaningless, not that they are not useful.
Usefulness is never part of Joshua's reasoning.
This makes serotonin *required* for a good mood. The argument only needs serotonin to *help*.
The argument says sugar can help. It does not need skipping sugar to cause anxiety.
The argument does not need tryptophan to be the *only* source of serotonin. It only says tryptophan is one.
Negate it: raising serotonin does *not* promote relaxation or freedom from anxiety. Then the chain from sugar to serotonin says nothing about mood, and the conclusion falls apart.
The argument does not need protein to cause anxiety. Protein only starts the chain.
The argument relies on North American cars being equal *now*. It does not need them to keep improving.
Negate it: Japanese drivers *are* inclined to buy left-side-wheel cars even though they drive on the left. Then the steering wheel is no obstacle, and switching it removes nothing.
A legal requirement would make the point even stronger, but the argument only needs buyers to prefer right-side wheels.
Removing *one obstacle* does not require most Japanese buyers to prefer the North American model.
The argument does not claim this is the *only* way to reduce the imbalance.
"Unfair *only if*" makes resources the single possible source of unfairness. The commentator only needs this one kind of imbalance to be unfair, not every unfair election to trace back to money.
Familiarity might be one route to positive feelings, but "only when" shuts out every other route. The argument does not need that.

Notice how gentle "at least sometimes" is. That is what you want in a necessary assumption: just enough to hold the argument up. Negate it: "more media exposure *never* makes a candidate's image evoke more positive feelings." Now buying airtime gives no edge at all, and there is nothing for the fairness law to prevent.
Whether candidates always spend to the limit does not matter. The worry is that some *can* buy much more, and that it would help them.
"Will not be elected" turns a tendency into a guarantee. The commentator only says voters *tend* to pick the candidate with the stronger image.
The argument is about whether shifting is good on balance. It does not need policymakers to lose power over ignoring *any* faction.
Democracies versus other governments never comes up. The author compares a benefit and a cost inside a democracy.

This is the weighing, stated outright. Negate it: "the harm of abandoning principle outweighs the advantage of adaptability." Then shifting is more evil than benefit, the exact opposite of the conclusion.
When policymakers appeal to principle is a different question from whether shifting is worth it.
If democracies are not actually flexible, the benefit the author relies on disappears. An author never assumes something that sinks their own argument.
Larson is already out because of her schedule. Her assertiveness changes nothing.
Negate it: "the task *can* be assigned to someone outside the shipping supervisors." Then knocking out Larson and Franks does not leave only Parker, and "must" falls apart.
What would happen in a world where Franks were more assertive does not matter. In this one, he is out.
The argument only needs Larson's conflict, which is unavoidable, to rule her out. It does not need every conflict of every kind to disqualify someone.
This rules out outsiders for one reason only, assertiveness. An outsider could still be barred for some other reason, so the argument does not need this. It needs the broader point in B.
Whether painting was the dominant art form says nothing about whether war existed before it.
The argument says agriculture led to warfare. It does not need every Neolithic war to be about farmland.
Negate it: "there *was* warfare before the first war paintings." Then the lack of earlier pictures proves nothing, and warfare could predate agriculture.
"Inevitable result of civilization" is a much bigger claim than the author makes or needs.

This is the most popular wrong answer, and it is tempting because it seems to tie farming and war together in the art. But the argument does not care when people started painting farms. Negate it: "paintings of farm life began at a different time than paintings of war." The argument is untouched, because it rests on when war paintings appear, not farm paintings.
Thieves taking some of both kinds does not affect where the extra security should go.

Stated from the other side: the less valuable pieces are not in demand. Negate it: "less valuable pieces *are* very much in demand by wealthy collectors." Then thieves target them too, and there is no reason to shift security toward the most valuable pieces.
How well a museum is secured overall is a different issue from which pieces inside it to guard.

This is the top trap, and it sounds like a premise for "focus *more*." But the recommendation works from any starting point. Even if museums already favor their valuable art, the argument says to favor it further. Negate D and nothing breaks.
What collectors do with stolen art afterward does not affect which art gets stolen.

Negate it: "literary language is *no more* likely to be misunderstood than non-literary language." Then designing against misreading gives no reason to strip out literary merit, and the conclusion loses its support.
Which documents are more important never comes up.
Comparing lawyers with novelists does not connect misinterpretation to literary merit.
Who finds these issues interesting has nothing to do with how the language reads.

This is the most tempting wrong answer, because it echoes the idea of care under high stakes. But the argument is about how the language is *designed*, not about people's general caution. Negate it and the argument still runs on the design point.
Where parents got the idea for directed learning does not affect whether it helps.
If children struggle to adapt without parental guidance, directed learning may be exactly what they need.

This is the most popular wrong answer. It mentions the right things (directed learning, general opportunities), but it points the wrong way. If directed learning enhances learning opportunities, it would *improve* a child's education. Patti would never assume that.
Negate it: "directed learning *is* a necessary part of growing and adapting." Then it is part of how children learn that enormous amount, and Patti cannot say it fails to help.
Formal schooling comes after preschool. The argument is about preschoolers.
The natural beauty of the materials is a different explanation for plain sculpture, and the argument does not need it.
Negate it: "modern sculpture has *not* been influenced by beliefs about ancient sculpture." Then the misunderstanding about the ancients cannot explain why modern work is monochromatic.
This is the top trap, because the stimulus talks about moisture washing paint away. But how modern sculpture holds up to moisture has nothing to do with why it is made without color.
Paintings that show sculptures might be a clue someone missed, but the argument does not need that clue to exist.
This predicts the future. The argument explains the past, and works whether or not sculptors change course.
Negate it: "the technology *will* become prohibitively expensive." Then buildings stop using it, the savings shrink instead of growing, and $200 billion a year is out of reach.
Another oil crisis might raise prices, but the argument does not need one.
If buildings become a smaller share of energy use, savings from buildings would matter less. The author would not assume that.
This restates the conclusion in different words. An assumption is something the argument relies on to get to the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

This is the most popular wrong answer, and it feels right: how else would savings grow so much? But growth can come from using today's technology in more buildings. The argument does not need brand-new science. Negate E and the prediction can still come true.
If genes can change in a few years, a genetic explanation becomes *more* plausible. That hurts the author.

"Not necessarily" is soft, and soft is exactly what a necessary assumption should be. Negate it: "new behaviors that appear in a few years *are* genetically predetermined." Then the hot spring habit came from genes, not social learning, and the conclusion falls.
This sets a rule for concluding that genes changed. The author is concluding the opposite.

This is the most popular wrong answer, and it is easy to see why: it sounds like the conclusion. But the author says the macaques are not *complete* captives of their genes. That leaves room for genes to matter a lot. "Completely independent" goes far beyond what the argument needs.
The argument is about the ability to adopt and pass on behavior. It does not need this habit to last for generations.
Pay has nothing to do with qualification.
Other contractors being worse would not change whether this one's technicians are qualified.
Negate it: "some technicians who lack certification *are* qualified." Then the 60 percent figure is not a count of unqualified people, and the outrage loses its basis.
Who installed the old systems says nothing about the contractor's workers.
Personal ties might be another reason to object, but the editorial's argument is about qualifications.
Other bidders do not matter. The question is whether the city could have kept the money itself.
Negate it: "the city *could not* have raised parking fees." Then the company's extra profits came from something the city could never have done, and that money would not have gone to the city.
"Always" handle it directly is a sweeping rule. The pundit only claims this one sale was a mistake.
Other factors in setting rates do not affect whether the city could have earned this money.
If private companies collect fees more efficiently, the city might have earned less than the company did. That is a point against the pundit.
The Hydro does not need to be the best-seller, only to be gaining while others lose.

Negate it: "the Hydro is *not* recognizable as environmentally friendly in any way its competitors are not." Then the urge to look green helps every competitor just as much, and it cannot explain why only the Hydro is rising.
A better safety record is a different explanation for the Hydro's success, which works against the author.
Whether neighbors drive Hydros is beside the point. The question is whether the car signals anything to them.
The argument is about *appearing* environmentally conscious. How much buyers actually care about the environment does not matter.
Wild bees never come up. The argument is about commercial bees.
Whether the damage can be undone quickly is a question about the fix, not the cause.
Diversity does not need to keep falling. Being low is enough for the argument.
If threats wiped out genetically diverse populations in the past, diversity does not protect bees. That cuts against the idea that low diversity is the hidden problem.

Negate it: "lack of genetic diversity *cannot* make honeybees more vulnerable to adverse conditions." Then inbreeding does nothing to help the infections and mites along, and it is no underlying cause at all.
How steady their eating habits are says nothing about whether the habits are healthy.
Negate it: "these conditions *cannot* be unhealthy for the animals." Then the animals are healthy, the studies' assumption holds, and there is nothing to skew the results.
Animals outside the lab are not part of the argument.
What some studies take into account does not affect whether the conditions can skew results.

This is the most popular wrong answer. It flips the scientist's idea: the scientist needs bad conditions to *cause* poor health, not good conditions to *guarantee* good health. A restricted diet and plenty of exercise could still leave an animal unhealthy for other reasons, and the argument would be fine.
The economist never says anyone taxes savings. Stopping a tax that was never mentioned does not follow.
Higher savings are the *only* way to improve, but that does not make them a guarantee of improvement, let alone a rapid one.
Whether consumption taxes alone could pay for everything is never discussed.
This is the conclusion the evidence builds toward: switch the tax focus to the one that encourages savings. Every piece of the argument supports it, and it claims nothing extra.
"Detrimental" to "any country" goes well past the evidence. The economist only says income taxes do nothing for savings, not that they actively hurt every economy.
Changes to international law may or may not be involved. The argument turns on giving up power over industries.

Notice the "some ... some" wording: modest and exactly enough. Negate it: "a comprehensive solution would require *no* nation to give up *any* power over its industries." Then the reluctance is irrelevant, and the conclusion has no support.
This says willing obedience would be enough for a solution. The argument needs the reverse: no willing obedience means no solution.
Who produces the pollution and who suffers from it is never discussed.
What current laws require says nothing about what a comprehensive solution would require.
"Always" is far more than needed. The stimulus only says clay *can* be mixed into something acidic.

The argument needs only some mixtures to turn acidic, not every one.
Other plants are beside the point.
Azaleas only need to flourish. They do not need to do *as well* as they do in naturally acidic soil.
Why the government lifted the ban does not matter. What matters is what happened after.
Whether the officials believe their own denials does not affect whether the policy caused damage.
It does not matter which companies did the dumping, only that the repeal led to it.
Comparing the mining industry with environmentalists does not connect the policy to the damage.
Negate it: "even with the ban, about the same amount of waste would have reached the streams." Then the buried streams are not the policy's doing, and the facts no longer contradict the officials.

Negate it: "being informed about the consequences *does* guarantee the choice is free." Then informed volunteers are choosing freely, paying them is fine, and the defense the essayist rejects is actually sound.
"No transaction" can ever be justified by voluntariness alone? The essayist does not go that far. They say voluntariness plus payment is not enough *here* because duress is possible.
Linking every limit on freedom to outside duress is a broad claim the argument never needs.
The essayist is not saying risk-for-money is wrong in itself, only that it is wrong under duress.
"Any action" freely chosen should be allowed is a sweeping principle, and it points the wrong way for this argument.
Cost is a different reason to skip the screenings. That competes with the reporter's explanation instead of supporting it.
Negate it: "the distributors believed screenings would *not* dampen anyone's enthusiasm." Then skipping them does nothing to protect interest, and the reporter's explanation stops making sense.

Whether awareness turns into ticket sales is not part of the explanation.
A specific prediction about how many people see the film goes beyond what the explanation needs.
No theory gets a counterexample. The author is building a case, not knocking one down.
Mercury and Venus are the competing explanations, and each is eliminated with its own reason. Mars wins because it is the only one left.
Nothing compares the present with the past.
The author accepts every premise and questions none of them.
The conclusion is about these particular meteorites, not a general principle.

Split it. "An expected consequence of a supposed development did not occur": no rise in savings, which a cutback should have caused. "That development itself did not take place": spending is undiminished. Both halves match.
"Two predictable consequences" sounds sophisticated, but the author only points to one consequence (savings), and only notes that it did not occur.
Economic self-interest and misinformation never come up.
The author does not set up two alternatives that exhaust the possibilities.

This is the most popular wrong answer. It gets the shape of the conclusion right (no change is happening). But the author does not call the evidence *ambiguous*. The author treats the savings data as clear and decisive: "Clearly, however..." An answer about weighing murky evidence describes a different argument.
The paleontologist never questions the ornithologist's credentials.
The second-speaker rule applies here. The paleontologist accepts the claw evidence ("the ability to perch in trees") and attacks the step from it to the conclusion.
Chickens are the parallel case. Same trait, perching, but a different lifestyle. That shows the weakness: perching does not establish tree-dwelling.
The hypothesis does not contradict its own evidence. The paleontologist says the evidence is too weak, not that it conflicts.
Health problems other than dental decay are not relevant to resolving the apparent paradox.
The paleontologist is attacking the argument, not adding to it.
Paul does not say Sarah's argument is circular.
Paul accepts Sarah's definition. Forced service is not volunteering. He finds volunteering in what happens later.
