The evidence is about what books will do for the future, not about what past generations saved for us. Nothing says these books were preserved by anyone before us.
The argument never sets future generations against the present one. Keeping your own book doesn't cost the present generation anything the argument mentions.

"Will most likely enrich" matches "almost certainly contribute to the enrichment", "posterity" matches "future generations", and the right side is exactly the conclusion: an obligation not to destroy. Apply it to books and the conclusion follows.
This requires that the thing benefit "someone we know." Future generations are people we will never meet, so E would actually block the conclusion.
The tax goes up to raise revenue for health costs. The rule sets the tax to discourage use, and A never says use should fall.
The studies say demand won't be affected, so this tax can't discourage use. That's the one effect the rule cares about.

The pesticide contains a compound harmful to people, the tax is raised, and the point is to push buyers toward pesticides without it. Higher tax, less use of the harmful product. That's the rule in action.
The tax isn't raised at all, and the reason is tourism. The rule never weighs tourism.
The tax on a harmful product is lowered. The rule calls for a tax high enough to discourage use.

Buying a sports car threatens no one, so a just government wouldn't ban the sale. Racing it without limits on public highways directly threatens other people's health and property, so restricting that fits the exception. Both halves of A line up with the rule.
Abolishing services that don't require labor isn't restricting anyone's desires. And the rule never says what an unjust government would do.
Handing out emergency funds isn't a restriction. The rule says nothing about who gets aid.
Magazines and movies that criticize the government don't directly threaten anyone's health or property. A just government couldn't censor them.
E predicts what an unjust government would do. The rule only describes just governments, so it can't tell us how an unjust one behaves.
Juan would miss an "aesthetically pleasing experience." Missing a good film isn't considerable physical or psychological harm.
The father lies to dodge a discussion. An argument about candidates isn't the harm the rule requires.
The husband lies to avoid inconvenience. If anyone is at risk, it's the husband, who recently had severe chest pains. The lie creates danger rather than preventing harm to others.
Hearing that the mother loves the older sister more would plausibly cause the boy serious psychological harm. That harm falls on someone other than the liar. So the lie fits the rule.

This is the trap, picked by 12%. Jamal does face emotional pain, and that looks like the rule's psychological harm. But the rule protects others. Jamal lies to avoid personal pain and embarrassment. Read the rule's last two words carefully: "to others."
Theory fails here because good music is a matter of taste. The stimulus never says parenting is a matter of taste. It says parents know their own children firsthand.

The experts are dismissed because they don't care about what matters to ordinary buyers. Our experts are set aside because they lack direct experience of this particular child, not because they don't care.
The climber knows this particular mountain, and the experts don't. "Might do well to ignore" matches "should not necessarily" follow. Firsthand knowledge of the specific case beats general expertise.
This sides with the expert over the person who works the land.

This is the trap, picked by 9%. It does favor your own voice over outside advice. But the reason is that conscience "speaks with a single voice." That's about consistency, not firsthand experience. E also says it is "better to follow" conscience, which is stronger than the stimulus's "not necessarily."

The conclusion says Toril did not act responsibly, so this choice is worth reading. Does the evidence say Toril didn't make a reasonable effort to get accurate and complete information? Yes: Toril invested the company's money without investigating the risks. Investing company money is a professional act, so the principle applies. The large return doesn't matter. The rule judges the effort made before acting, not how things turned out.
This ties interpretation to the history of the period when it was made. The evidence is about color, so A doesn't connect.

This is the trap, picked by 10%. It's true to the stimulus: restoration can change colors. But that's the premise we already have. B never mentions interpretation, so it doesn't explain why old interpretations might no longer hold.

If colors are relevant to an appropriate interpretation, then learning the colors were different gives a reason to doubt interpretations based on the old colors. Evidence about color now reaches the conclusion about interpretation.
The argument is about whether interpretations are appropriate, not about who judges an artwork's value.
This judges interpretations by when they started. That has nothing to do with the colors changing.
Farmers did switch to machines. But the cause is that labor got more expensive. In the stimulus, nothing happened to the old product. A substitute just became easier to get.
New games boost sales of screens. Those products work together, and sales rise. The stimulus has a substitute pulling sales down.
A new soft drink enters the market, and people drink less of the established brand. A new substitute arrives, and the old product sells less. Same pattern.
A rule forbids playing, and the child focuses on homework. That's a restriction, not a substitute becoming available.
Neither program dominates because neither has every feature. No new substitute arrives, and no sales fall.
The parent hoped the child would imitate. It didn't work.
Example and reason failed, and repetition worked. "More readily than through other means" is exactly what the parent saw.
Reasoning failed with this child, but we don't know why. Maybe the child understood and just didn't care. "Too young to understand" makes a claim about children's minds that the story never supports.
The child didn't imitate the parent. And D's contrast between imitation and reason misses the method that actually worked.
Nothing suggests the child wanted attention or acted against expectations on purpose.

All five siblings are more qualified than every other applicant, and still none are hired. The only thing that explains the decision is that they're family. That's partial, just in the unexpected direction.
Everyone who complained gets the same gift, the employee's mother included. Family gets no special treatment.
This is a trap, picked by 7%. Never firing three siblings sounds suspicious. But maybe none of them ever deserved firing. Without knowing they performed badly, we can't call this partial.

This might be unfair, since the problems are over two years old. But the policy targets partiality, and nothing ties this employee to any family relationship. The problems also did happen, so the claims aren't false.

This is the most-picked trap, at 10%. Promoting a relative over someone else is only partial if the relative wasn't the better choice. E gives no comparison. The relative may well have earned it. A, by contrast, tells us the relatives were the better choice.
Better warranties raise market share and cut profits. No fee drives users away, and nothing is wearing out less.
The store closes overnight, not raising a fee, and its revenue rises. In the stimulus, revenue can fall while the condition improves.
Here more money comes in, and the service still gets worse. That reverses the stimulus, where less money and better condition go together.
More spending brings more visitors, and the extra revenue covers the cost. Usage goes up, not down.

Library fees rise, there are fewer patrons, and the books are in better repair even though the money for repairs has dropped. Every link matches, including the twist that less money still means better condition.

This is the trap, picked by 8%. It sounds right, since being watched can make people nervous. But both groups were being watched. What differed was what the players thought was being evaluated: the racket or themselves.
The group that thought only the racket was being judged did better. That's people performing better when they don't believe their abilities are being judged.
Both groups were equally skilled, and nothing tells us anyone's confidence.
Nobody here assesses their own talent.
Nobody is trying to please the testers. E also predicts more effort, while the stimulus is about how well people played.
Being a copy is about originality. An exact copy could still give an audience a stimulating experience.
The symphony doesn't excite the audience, yet it's called beautiful because it's performed competently. By the critic's standard, failing to stimulate is the problem.
The cube is praised for a rare material. That says nothing about the audience's experience.
This is the trap, picked by 6%. A controversial artist might seem stimulating. But D praises the painting for who painted it, not for what it does to the people looking at it.
The poem is called deficient because it has little impact on its audience. Little impact means no stimulating experience. That's exactly what the critic's principle uses to judge value.

This is the trap, picked by 11%. "Never expand" would settle the matter, but the chairperson only asks for further consideration. That leaves room to expand after all. A rule that forbids expansion outright goes further than the reasoning does.
This pushes toward expanding wherever there's profit. The chairperson is putting on the brakes.
This is the second trap, at 6%. The chairperson raises stability as a concern but never ranks it as the most important factor. They even acknowledge the profit opportunity.
"Be cautious" matches "not without further consideration," and "politically unstable countries" matches the evidence. This is the principle at exactly the argument's strength.
The chairperson says not to let incentives alone entice the board. That isn't the same as always ignoring incentives.

"Better cognizance" is the heightened awareness from the evidence. "Does not warrant a radical solution" is the wariness in the conclusion. If the statistics only show better cognizance, A tells us not to go radical.

This is the trap, picked by 10%. It sounds cautious in the same way. But the argument never doubts that the problem exists. It doubts that the problem has suddenly grown. B also covers any attempt to stop a problem, not radical ones.
The argument is wary of solutions driven by new statistics. Basing them on statistics alone is the reverse.
Nobody is manipulating the data. The numbers can be completely accurate and still reflect awareness more than a real increase.
Radical solutions might backfire, but that isn't the argument's reason for caution. Its reason is that the statistics may not mean what they seem to.
The argument puts the anxiety down to the work being hard to judge, not to anyone's personality. A makes a claim about personalities that the argument never makes.

This is the trap, picked by 5%. It mentions the creators' feelings, so it sounds close. But it says a work's value depends on those feelings. The argument says the creators' feelings depend on how easily the work can be judged. B reverses which one depends on which.
The argument explains why artists get anxious. It never says how engineers or artists should be evaluated.
Machines are things whose success is easily ascertained, and art is something whose value isn't. Engineers worry less and artists worry more. D is the stimulus stated in general terms.
The argument compares two kinds of creators. E compares a creator to the evaluators. The stimulus never says how confident evaluators are.

Raoul's trip ended with a broken leg and two weeks in the hospital. That didn't end well, so "All's well that ends well" has no illustration here. The story is an apparent counterexample, and putting "as the saying goes" after it is the misuse the principle describes.

Harold has done the same thing many times before. That's selfishness as predictable as gravity, so the quote matches the story. The friends' surprise doesn't change that Harold's behavior was calculable.
Roger won't spend the money because Roger is frugal. "A penny saved is a penny earned" is the frugal person's motto. The story illustrates it.

Sharon loves cats, and Sharon's husband, despite the allergy, still sometimes comes along to cat shows. Sharing a life with Sharon means sharing what Sharon loves, at least a little. The story illustrates the saying.

Fatima knows enough mathematics to see how much will stay unsolved. That's the saying in action: you need to know a lot before you see how little you know. The story illustrates it, so the phrase is used properly.
If further depletion is imprudent, developing the wetlands is imprudent. That supports the Wildlife Commission.
If future generations' right to wildlife outranks a nation's economic needs, the Development Commission's appeal to growth loses. That's the Wildlife Commission's side.

Regulate only after commercial development has actually been found to reduce endangered species. The Development Commission says Figoria has conserved, and its development "might not affect wildlife." So no such harm has been found, and regulation isn't justified yet. The Wildlife Commission wants regulation before any harm, which this principle rules out.

This is the trap, picked by 12%. It talks about how different nations have harmed the environment to different degrees. That's the Development Commission's theme, so it feels like their answer. But read what it concludes: regulation cannot allow for those differences. The commission's whole complaint is that Figoria's record of conserving should count. D says it doesn't.

The Development Commission insists Figoria has the right to govern its own resources. Handing regulation to an international agreement takes that right away. A works against the commission it is supposed to help.
This concludes that parents should check teachers' qualifications. Nobody is trying to avoid responsibility.

Parents shouldn't answer for older adolescents, because those adolescents have minds of their own and freely choose what to do. That's the factory's defense: we didn't make the choice, an independent party did.

This is the trap, picked by 8%. It objects to a burden, as the factory does. But the students' reason is that the material wasn't covered in class. No independent party made the choice. The structure that matters, blaming someone else's free choice, isn't there.
The appointee is excluded for a conflict of interest. That's about bias, not shifting responsibility.
This doubts a claim based on witnesses' reports. Nobody's responsibility is being shifted.

This is the trap, picked by 8%. Sally's family uses jalapeños often, so #1 roughly fits, and Sally has gotten used to them, so #2 fits. But #3 needs Sally to come to like them. All we're told is that Sally can now eat them without discomfort. Tolerating a food isn't liking it. C ends with George "very fond" of pierogis, so it hits all three beats.

This is the trap, picked by 7%. Executives favoring people who share their interests looks like personal taste. But the alternative they pass over is "the most education." Nothing says education is what serves the company best. The stimulus contrasts personal taste with the organization's interest, and A contrasts it with education.
Supermarkets choose for profit. That's choosing in the organization's interest, which the experts failed to do.
Librarians choose for the library, they pick books they enjoy, and they pass over books that serve the community the library is for. Personal taste beats the interest of those they choose for.
Students choosing their own courses are choosing for themselves. Picking easy courses is a personal tradeoff, not a betrayal of an organization's interest.
The executives pick what viewers want, which serves the network's audience. They aren't indulging their own taste.
This says not to trust one model because conflicting models can't all be right. It never says to keep looking for information before deciding.

This is a trap, picked by 11%. It warns against deciding on one factor alone. But its fix is to weigh the information you already have more carefully. The rule says that when your information is inadequate, you should go out and get more.

This is the most-picked trap, at 12%. It sounds like the rule because it urges looking for more information. But the rule is triggered by a specific situation: not enough information to make a decision. C has no decision and says "always" look, even when the researcher may know enough. That's a general habit, not this rule.
Personal experience is called an "inadequate basis," which is the trigger. Studying reliability histories from many owners is seeking more information before choosing a car. Both halves are there.
This has the trigger: not enough information. But then it says to give up and admit the meaning can't be found. The rule says to keep looking.
Both examples swap expensive labor for cheaper labor: many workers for a few, highly paid workers for fewer, less-skilled ones. A names the motive behind both.
Today's managers want to replace skilled workers with less-skilled ones. That doesn't suggest more education will keep workers competitive.

This is the trap, picked by 15%. It picks up the modern example, where skilled workers may be replaced. But the first example shows skilled workers winning, so C can't be illustrated by both examples. And managers are only "looking for" this technology. We don't know skilled workers have already lost their advantage.
Both examples cut the number of workers. Nothing says new jobs make up the difference.
The passage never mentions heavy industry or says which industries are affected.
The condition is that what Marcus does isn't bad. That doesn't tell us whether lying to Marcus's parents does more good than harm.
Lying to the police about a possible criminal might do plenty of harm. B never weighs good against harm.
A lie that affects only yourself can still do more harm than good. Who it affects isn't the test.
The lie helps Thomas and does no harm. Some good and zero harm means more good than harm, so Laila's principle makes it permissible.
The lie benefits the people deceived but "may harm others." We can't tell which side is bigger, so the rule isn't triggered.
This is meeting a supervisor's deadline, which is the kind of demand efficient employees ignore.
This is the trap, picked by 4%. It does ignore a deadline, so half the definition fits. But the time goes to routine correspondence that could wait, not a project with a big reward.

Being on time for a monthly meeting is a routine scheduled demand. An urgent call from a major customer could mean a big reward for the employer. Skipping the first for the second is efficiency as the passage describes it.
Daily meetings about workloads and schedules are scheduling, not a big-reward project.
Scheduling tasks around the nearest deadlines is exactly what efficient employees ignore.
The executive never asks what makes a publication reliable. The publications are already called reliable.

This is the trap, picked by 5%. It takes us from reliable sources to "the tinctures are ineffective." But the executive concludes something about profit, and B says nothing about profit. B also needs a majority of reliable sources, and the executive only consulted "a variety."
This says consulting publications isn't a reliable basis for predicting profit. That's exactly what the executive did, so C undermines the reasoning.
This is about adverse effects. The publications say the tinctures don't work, not that they cause harm.

The trigger is a number of reliable authorities calling the products ineffective, which is the executive's evidence. The outcome is that promoting them won't be profitable, which is the conclusion. E is the whole argument as a rule.
Long's illegal act is the punishment, stealing back, not the way Price's theft was discovered. Price confessed. Nothing about the discovery was illegal.
Shakila can't report the secretary because Shakila once did the same thing. That's hypocrisy, not evidence gathered illegally.

Takashi broke curfew on Monday, but the sighting was on Tuesday, so Takashi's violation had nothing to do with discovering Sarah. And Takashi isn't the one punishing. Sarah's parents are, and they did nothing wrong.

The conservation officer found Kuttner's illegal traps while trespassing on Kuttner's land, so the discovery itself was illegal. Kuttner admits it, and the officer, the one who would punish, can't justifiably do so. That matches the company and Ellison.
The board can't act because it pardoned others before. That's about consistency, and the evidence against Ramirez wasn't obtained illegally.
The rule never makes keeping a promise unacceptable, and owing Maria money isn't one of its conditions.
Alan was hurt and couldn't come, so Felicia couldn't tutor Alan that Tuesday. That's a circumstance beyond Felicia's control, condition 2, and the conclusion is that not tutoring was acceptable.
Owen asked to change the day. The rule says nothing about having to agree to a new request, and it never concludes that anything is unacceptable.
Without the keys, Quinn couldn't get in. That's a circumstance beyond Quinn's control, so condition 2 makes not watering acceptable. D only checks condition 1 and reaches the opposite verdict.
Ian was unable to make it, but only because Ian chose to return library books first. That was within Ian's control, so condition 2 doesn't apply, and nobody released Ian either.
This says harmed employees should be compensated. It doesn't say who is responsible, so it doesn't reach the manufacturer.

"Only" puts preventable on the right: responsible → preventable. That tells us when a manufacturer is not responsible, when the harm couldn't be prevented. It can't prove the manufacturer is responsible. Knowing the harm was preventable doesn't trigger anything.
This covers risks the manufacturer was aware of. Here it was ignorant, so C never applies.
If preventability is irrelevant, the argument's main evidence counts for nothing.
The workers are innocent people harmed by T, and the evidence says the illnesses were preventable. Both conditions are met, so the manufacturer is held responsible. That's the conclusion.
The editorial never compares spending on essential and nonessential services.

The health services are essential, so they must be funded from reliable sources. Lottery revenue could decline, so it isn't reliable. That rules out using lottery money for any part of them, which is the conclusion.
This bans being "entirely" dependent on lottery money. The editorial bans funding "any part" of the services that way. Under C, partial lottery funding would be fine.
The editorial says these health services are essential. It doesn't say every health service must be treated that way.
This saves lottery money for future shortfalls. The editorial's answer is to stop relying on lottery money for these services at all.
This says people should be told the regulations. Even if McBride should have been told, A doesn't say anything about whether dismissal would be unfair.
The issue isn't that Form 5 was hard to fill out. It's that it was the wrong form. And B says nothing about dismissal.
The incorrect action was the Bureau staff handing over Form 5, and the Bureau is a government agency. So dismissing the complaint for that reason is unfair. That's the conclusion.
We know staff handed out the wrong form, not that the procedures are too complex for them. And D tells agencies how to design procedures. It doesn't say dismissing the complaint is unfair.
This protects the nightclub. Nothing says the nightclub lacked a chance to defend itself, and the conclusion is about fairness to McBride.
Deterrence never comes up. The lawyer's objection is about who pays for what.
This compares overall penalties. The surcharge is added "in addition to any other penalties", so violent criminals may still pay more overall. B doesn't make the surcharge unfair.
Nothing suggests the money is spent on anything other than services. The lawyer's complaint is who pays, not where the money goes.
A petty thief pays for services for victims of violent crime, which is more serious than petty theft. D says that criminal shouldn't have to pay, so the surcharge is unfair to nonviolent criminals.
Fines for theft based on the value stolen have nothing to do with the victim surcharge.
Riley would have realized it with a moment's thought, so the accident was foreseeable. Rule 2 doesn't apply, and no rule says Riley escapes blame.
Oblicek had no idea the loan could bankrupt the business and couldn't reasonably have foreseen it. That's rule 2 exactly: unwitting and unforeseeable, so Oblicek should not be blamed.
Gougon worried the sauce might make people sick but had no reason to think it would. Worry isn't knowledge, so rule 1 doesn't apply. No rule says Gougon should be blamed.
The rules never say who is the only one to blame. And Dr. Fitzpatrick acted unknowingly, so rule 1 doesn't make the doctor blameworthy.

This is the tempting one. Kapp should have seen the fire coming, and blaming Kapp feels right. But Kapp didn't realize it, so rule 1 (knowingly) doesn't apply. Rule 2 only excuses. No rule here blames someone who was unwitting but should have known.
Most voters will see Grenier as insincere, and A says voters are unlikely to vote for such a politician. That leads straight to Grenier losing.
If voters don't notice changes in stance, the flip-flop wouldn't hurt Grenier. The pundit says voters will notice and react.
If voters agree with Grenier's current position on wages, this says the old views won't matter. That would help Grenier.
The pundit's reasoning is about sincerity, not whether voters think Grenier understands their finances.
The voters doubt Grenier because the stance changed, not because Grenier's beliefs differ from theirs. And E only predicts doubt. It doesn't get us to losing the election.

Protecting key industries leans the politician's way. But the argument turns on missing evidence about whether the change is worth it. A ignores that and never weighs the pollution benefit the politician admits.
Public acceptance never comes up.

"Altered only if" puts compelling evidence on the right: change → compelling evidence. Contrapose it: no compelling evidence → don't change. The politician says the evidence isn't there, so the standards shouldn't be raised.
Both options here have upsides and downsides: cleaner air on one side, jobs on the other. D says that's when policy should be changed, which is the reverse of the conclusion.
The politician lacks clear evidence that the benefits would make up for the losses. E says to assume they would, which supports raising the standards.
This is about irresponsibility. The conclusion is about dishonesty.
This supports the activists' preference for eliminating nuclear power. It says nothing about the advocates being dishonest.

Better waste disposal could keep nuclear power going, which undermines the activists' goal. The advocates still ask for it in the name of the activists' ideals. C calls that dishonest, which is the conclusion.
This is about irresponsibility, not dishonesty. And the advocates do believe nuclear power is acceptable, so D's trigger isn't met.
The advocates' ideals are no secret. The letter's complaint isn't that they hid their views. It's that the request undermines the activists' goals.
This says what to do after testing finds a risk. It assumes the testing already happened. The conclusion is about requiring the testing in the first place.
This applies to crops with no potential risk. The environmentalist says these crops are risky, so B doesn't apply.

"Unless" means "if not": if a crop might pose risks and hasn't been thoroughly tested, it can't go into production. GE crops might pose risks, so they need testing before production. That's the conclusion.
This covers crops already in production. The conclusion is about testing before production begins.
This tells us when testing can stop. It never requires testing before production.
This bans political messages in all short stories. The critic says the message could have anchored a different short story, so A contradicts the critic, and it ignores the reason, distraction.
The political message distracts from the humor, which is the primary focus. B says nothing should do that, so the message should have been left out.
The critic never mentions alienating readers.
The critic mentions an essay only to say the message deserved its own piece. How messages are developed in different forms isn't the issue.
If the message didn't matter to the story's merit, there would be no reason to cut it. The critic's reason is that it actively hurts the humor.
This is a distorted version of the evidence. The passage says people are often arbitrary, not that they never have good judgment.
This is the judges' complaint, which the author is answering.
The author argues that judges' discretion should be limited.
This is the support for the conclusion. Judges being often arbitrary is why minimums are needed.
Minimums are necessary, and the reason is to limit arbitrary judicial discretion. This combines the pivot sentence with what "that" refers to.
The editorialist doesn't say how much progress has been made, or that it is mainly due to radicals. The claim is only that radicals play a positive role.
This states the positive role: by promoting their views, radicals help produce progress. That is the claim the "for" clause supports.
This restates the evidence about fear and inertia, and adds "most effectively," which the passage doesn't say.

This is the most-picked trap. It says radicals put forth untenable positions in order to produce fear. The editorialist never says the radicals intend this. They have a positive effect, whatever their motives.
This overstates the concession at the start. It's the part the author grants before the "but."

This makes photosynthesis the whole story. The journalist's point covers pollination and seeds too, and this choice also says animals are needed for photosynthesis to occur, which the passage doesn't say.
This is part of the opening concession, not the conclusion.
This picks up only the carbon dioxide point and turns it into a claim about Earth's chemistry. It leaves out the mutual dependence.
The passage says plants would deplete carbon dioxide, not oxygen. It also isn't the conclusion.
Animals depend on plants, and plants depend on animals. That is what "the dependence is mutual" means.
This is roughly what the studies claim. The critic is arguing against it.
The critic never compares nineteenth-century images of women with current ones.
The critic's evidence, that few North Americans have seen the operas, is aimed at showing the operas haven't significantly reinforced stereotypes here. That's the unstated conclusion.
The critic talks only about these operas, not opera as a whole as a force on social attitudes.
The critic needs only that limited exposure means limited influence. "Cannot be influenced" by anything not directly seen goes much further. It's closer to an assumption than to the conclusion.
The argument does reach a judgment. It says the criticism is unfair.
This is the criticism the argument rejects.
This is part of the tax example used as support.
The first sentence says the criticism is not fair. "Unjustified" means the same.
This is the last link in the evidence chain. It supports the claim that poorer residents benefited.
The journalist doesn't say the free marketplace is in jeopardy. That's a background worry, not the claim argued for.
The value of a free marketplace is part of the support.
"Curtailed" means reduced. This restates the sentence that "For this reason" introduces.
This restates the second sentence, which supports the value of a free marketplace.
This is the closing sentence, which adds support for curtailing government power.
This is the sentence "As a result" introduces. Nothing else in the argument is supported by it.
This is close to the citizen's first claim, which supports everything after it. It's a premise, not the conclusion.
This supports the main conclusion. The legislation fails because it can't address home environment.
This restates the second sentence, which supports the claim that environment matters most.
The citizen says breed-specific legislation fails to address human behavior. The current laws are said to be adequate, not to fail at this.
This is the view the editorialist turns against with "However."
The editorialist never compares indoor and outdoor use for danger. The point is a different route of exposure.
"Determine the safety of these chemicals" means study their effects on people. That's the recommendation after "However."
Children mouthing equipment is an example of how exposure could happen, not advice to parents.

The editorialist says only that the safety needs checking. It doesn't claim the lumber is more dangerous than once believed. Testing is called for because the danger is unknown, not because it has been shown.
Tallulah offers the poor quality of fiction as overlooked evidence, not as the proven cause of novels' decline.
Tallulah never says the columnist's explanation is false, only that it ignored relevant evidence.
"Overlooked important evidence" is the same as forming a view "without considering all of the pertinent evidence."
Tallulah never claims people read as much as before.
This is part of the evidence the columnist overlooked.
The argument doesn't compare how much predictive power each science has.
The argument never ranks math's importance in the two fields.
This is what the social scientists want. The author doesn't argue for it.
With "this" filled in, the conclusion says reducing social phenomena to mathematical expressions would be a mistake. That's what D says.
The first sentence says prediction is the hallmark of the natural sciences, not that it explains their success. And it's background, not the conclusion.
This is the second sentence, the reason the focus must change.
"Unless the focus is radically changed, research will fail" translates to "If the focus is not radically changed, research won't produce true intelligence." That's the first sentence.
The author says the research will fail, not that it already has.
The argument implies noncognitive responses matter for true intelligence. It never says they matter at least as much as computation.
This is closer to something the argument relies on. The conclusion is about what AI research will achieve.
This is the assumption the counselor rejects.
This is the example of irrationality that supports the conclusion.
The counselor describes this habit as an example. Calling it irrational in these words isn't the point being argued.
With "that assumption" replaced, the counselor's claim is that personal conflicts are not inevitable.
This is the last part of the example, which supports the claim about irrationality.
This is the decision the client is responding to.
This is the owners' reason for the increase, which the client rejects.
This is the client's recommendation, the sentence "After all" supports.
This is the first part of the support.
This completes the support. The mission is in danger, so rates shouldn't go up.
This is the first sentence, which everything else supports.
This is the content of the law, given as background.
This is the first piece of support.
The argument never says the law itself must be a shared principle.
This is part of the support for why debating the law is pointless.
This is the first sentence, which the other facts support.
This shows the limit wouldn't hurt cooking. It supports the proposal.
This is the ignition threshold the limit stays below.
This shows current burners get hot enough to start fires.
The argument doesn't claim to explain why fires start. It says a limit would reduce them.
This supports the conclusion. No expertise means not a real critic.
This also supports the conclusion.
The owner grants this before the "but."
This is the claim after the "but" that the rest supports.
This is an analogy used as support.
The argument doesn't say studying history leads people to misunderstand the crises they face. It says studying history doesn't help avoid mistakes.
This restates the evidence about uniqueness, with periods instead of accidents and crises.
This is the evidence about crises never being the same. "May appear to be the same" is also an addition.
The author never says studying history is valuable for some other reason.

When an ice age begins, the polar ice caps steadily advance outward from the poles (the ice caps from the North Pole extend down through Canada to the northern latitudes of America). When an ice age ends, the polar ice caps steadily retreat backwards towards the poles.

During an ice age, as the polar ice caps expand southward, the arctic habitat expands. A polar bear might end up all the way down where New York is.
But when the ice age ends, the polar ice caps recede back towards the poles, shrinking the arctic habitat, forcing the cold-adapted animals to migrate back north where it's cold enough for their liking.
The first date came from scientists looking at a certain area like New York that is cold during an ice age but warm otherwise, so that they could see when it went from being a place where cold beetles wanted to live to being a place where warm beetles wanted to live.
The fact that warm beetles started living somewhere just means that that area because too warm for cold beetles, but that doesn't mean all cold beetles died out. Their habitat just shrunk, so they would have headed north to where it was still cold.

Necessary Assumption loves to write trap answers like this.
If the paragraph says, "Black lives matter", the trap answer says the argument is assuming "non-black lives don't matter".

We're never allowed to take a sentence and just invert its terms that way. If we say, "people who serve in the military are heroes", that doesn't mean "people who don't serve in the military are not heroes".

The critics' premise is saying, "Sure, 3 glasses of wine a day would help decrease your risk of stroke. But it wouldn't benefit your health overall because you'd be more likely to die from sudden heart attacks."

If the author is acting like "that level of consumption (3 wine / day) is associated with an increased risk of sudden heart attack", then he is attributing a consequence of binge drinking (higher risk of heart attack) to this separate plan of drinking 3 glasses of wine per day. They don't have anything to do with each other.
Someone could drink 3 glasses of wine per day, and not binge drink, and they would presumably get the decreased risk of stroke without getting any increased risk of sudden heart attack.
(Technically, the argument never said that the increased risk of heart attack was a consequence of binge drinking, so this answer is not perfect, but it's the best available and sounds the most like our complaint.)

The author isn't confusing one risk with another. He is comparing a decreased health risk (less chance of stroke) with an increased health risk (higher chance of sudden heart attack).
He is definitely assuming that for someone who has both the decreased risk of stroke and the increased risk of heart attack, that the positive is completely offset by the negative, but he isn't confusing one type of risk with another.

Since this answer begins with presumes / takes for granted / fails to establish, we can ask ourselves whether this answer truly is a Necessary Assumption.
The critics don't need to assume that wine is not significantly different from other alcoholic beverages. They are fine with believing that wine is significantly different. In fact, their argument seems to acknowledge that wine does have special benefits (consuming 3 glasses a day can decrease the risk of stroke).
The critics are merely saying that the benefit that wine drinking would provide would be negated by an increased risk of heart attack, and so there isn't any net gain to health overall.

We're fine with hearing that 3 glasses a day would confer a substantial decrease in risk. We don't need to know whether it's specifically 37% or 42%, in order to assess the logic of this argument.
Answers that are complaining that we didn't get a specific measurement, a specific statistic, or the specific names of people who may have been alluded to in the argument are almost always wrong.
It's practically never the case that a missing number / name / definition is what creates a reasoning flaw.

This names the (#1) famous flaw Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which an author presents a conditional logic premise,
Should change to online → Won't increase Costs
and then reasons via that rule in an illegal backwards or opposite fashion.
This author argued that, "Since it won't increase costs, we should change to online". That is switching "won't increase costs" from the Necessary (right) side to the Sufficient (left) side.
Or in conversational terms, the author is acting like as long as it's doesn't raise costs that's a good enough reason to switch. In doing so, the author is failing to consider other possible reasons (besides an increase in costs) that we might not want to switch.

This author isn't assuming anything about the causal backstory of why they're in a precarious financial situation.

The author is assuming that publishing an online version will not make our financially precarious position worse, but she doesn't need to believe the reason we're financially struggling is because we have a paper version.

The author is overlooking that an online version would have disadvantages over a paper version. That would be an objection, because that would help us argue against the conclusion.
But if we say, "Hey, author --- the online version has other advantages, too", that just strengthens her conclusion that we should switch to online.

Does it hurt the author to say, "Hey, author — even if we change to online, we'll still be in a financially precarious position"?
Not really, because the author was never selling us on switching to online as a solution to our financial problem. The author was thinking that we can't make the switch if it would be a financial burden, but she isn't arguing that we should make the switch because it will be a financial solution.

takes for granted / presumes / fails to establish

Say you had four buckets of Skittles. The five flavors are evenly distributed, so about 20% of the Skittles in each bucket are red. In a fifth bucket, you have like 90% red Skittles, 10% an even mix of the rest. If you combine those five buckets into one huge pool, the % of Skittles that are red will be higher than the normal 20% rate. It won't be anywhere near 90%, but it will still be elevated. There will still be a correlation of red appearing in the population. Similarly, the people with hereditary disease are the bucket of red skittles. A ton of them have a correlation between caffeine and heart disease, and when you combine these hereditary disease people with the rest of the general population (who have no correlation between caffeine and heart disease), you still end up with some statistical lumpiness that makes caffeine drinkers more likely to have heart disease than non-caffeine drinkers.

We have no grounds for thinking the sample was too small. These samples were acquired from various manufacturing locations, so we can't even say, "Sure, Factory X has a 20% rate of defects, but all the other factories have a way lower rate".

Is this author assuming that the field inspectors were just as likely to choose a defective item as they were a nondefective item? Close, but not quite.
The author is assuming that the field inspectors were randomly choosing items as samples. But, if they were randomly choosing items, and the rate of defectiveness was 20% (1 out of 5), then they would be 4 times as likely (80%, 4 out of 5) to choose a nondefective item.
So in the author's mind, where inspectors grabbed samples randomly, and 1 out of every 5 samples was defective, she would be assuming that the inspectors were less likely to choose a defective item than a nondefective item, since 4 out of those 5 times they grabbed a nondefective item.

This doesn't work as an objection. Even if a few sites are responsible for most defective items, the manufacturer is still averaging out to an unacceptable 20% defective rate.
We would need to know that the "various manufacturing locations" from which the inspectors grabbed their samples just happened to disproportionately skew towards these few "bad apple" manufacturing sites.
But since this answer doesn't give us a storyline like that, there's no way to argue that the 20% is a skewed number.

This does work as an objection. If the inspectors were trying to find items they assumed were defective, then they're not grabbing random samples, they're seeking out the ones that look bad.
In that case, the samples that make it back to the lab are not a representative sample of the items being manufactured, they are a skewed sample. Thus, the author can't go from knowing that 20% of the samples are defective to thinking that 20% of the total items are defective.

If you like probability math, keep reading:
Say that 10% of large car drivers are injured in accidents while 20% of small car drivers are. But also add the idea that 60% of large car drivers will get into an accident, whereas only 25% of small car drivers will.
Probability of being injured in large car:
60% * 10% = 6/10 * 1/10 = 6/100 = 6%
Probability of being injured in small car:
25% * 20% = 1/4 * 1/5 = 1/20 = 5/100 = 5%

Sure! It sounds like we can't trust that species that were too difficult for humans to domesticate thousands of years ago shouldn't automatically be assumed to be too difficult for modern humans to domesticate. This would hurt the author's assumption that "was true of the past is still true now".
If you're picky like me, you might hate this correct answer because the evidence says "Since that time ... we've tried innumerable times to domesticate all the ones that seemed worth it". To me, that language doesn't clearly define a past vs. present. It sounds more like over the last few thousand years we have been continually trying innumerable times, and thus it makes little sense to act like the author was saying "We tried a few thousand years ago and it was hard, so it would still be hard". It sounds more like "We've been continually trying for a few thousand years and it's been hard."
But the fact remains that this answer is the best available, since on Necessary Assumption we're going by the standard of "Which answer, if negated, most weakens". Suggesting a big disparity between how difficult it was then vs. how difficult it is now is still the best objection available in these answer choices.

This provides an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact.

It's not because that type of background makes them more likely to succeed; it's just because most of the employees have that background.
If most people are right handed, then most criminals should be right handed. That doesn't mean that being right handed makes you more likely to be criminal. It's just the idea that if we don't think two things are related, then their proportion in the general population should match their proportion in the specific population.
If 90% of people are right handed, and if we don't think that there is any causal connection between being right vs. left handed and being a criminal, then we would expect 90% of criminals to be right handed.
When things are disproportional, then we know there is some weird causal factor at play. When people of color are only 40% of drug users but 65% of people arrested for drug use, then we start to think, "is race/ethnicity playing some causal role in whether or not you get arrested for drug use?"
So if 70% (i.e. "most") of the employees at this company were born in Pennsylvania, then you'd expect 70% of the best sales reps to be born in PA.
If 70% of the employees have an engineering + no sales background, then you'd expect 70% of the best sales rep to have that background.
Since we can explain the predominance of this background among the best sales reps as a simple fact of the underlying population of employees, we have less reason to believe the author's thinking, that this background is a secret causal-difference maker that makes someone a better sales rep (which she implicitly believes, if she thinks in future hiring we should be prioritizing this type of background).

This describes the #1 famous flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which an author presents a conditional logic rule as one of his premises, but then applies that rule illegally in some reversed or negated fashion.

No. Establishing that other tests are even easier doesn't establish that this test is difficult. It only establishes that this test is more difficult.
LSAT frequently tests this distinction between Relative and Absolute language.
If I say, "This 2nd grade math test is hard. After all, the 1st grade math test is even easier", you would correctly say, "This 2nd grade math test is not hard. It's harder than a 1st grade test, but it's not hard."

This describes the famous flaw, Unproven vs. Proven False, in which an author concludes that someone's claim is wrong, merely because they unsuccessfully tried to prove it was true.
Here, the author does infer that the claim "this certification process is very difficult" is false. Does his evidence describe the argument that Plumb-Ace makes in favor of claiming that it's very difficult?
No. His evidence doesn't reference Plumb-Ace's argument for this claim at all. His evidence merely points to the very high passing rate for the written portion.

This isn't speaking to our objection that the philosophers are analyzing whether or not two claims are identical, whereas we only said they were identical in meaning, not in all attributes.
We're not trying to convince the philosopher that these two sentences are in fact identical; we're just trying to reiterate our original claim (untouched by his rebuttal) that these two sentences are in fact identical in meaning.

This has a great structure, but the ingredients are inverted from what they should be.
We linguists are saying, "Two sentences can be non-identical physically, and yet still be identical in meaning."

The philosophers were never debating whether claim 1 logically entails claim 2. That is a separate issue.
The claim that "all lions are hairy" logically entails that "some lions are hairy", but that doesn't mean that they are physically identical or identical in meaning.
So convincing the philosophers that one claim proves the other is not actually doing our intended job, which is convincing them that these two claims are identical in meaning.

This speaks to our objection that the philosophers took the conversation somewhere else. We only commented on whether two claims were identical in meaning, i.e. whether they mean the exact same thing.
We never said they were the exact same sentence. We said the two sentences have the exact same meaning.

This describes the famous Circular reasoning flaw, in which we say that the premise is restating the conclusion or assuming the truth of the conclusion.
The two premises here were "salespeople work on commission" and "salespeople steer toward products with higher commissions". Neither one of those is a paraphrase of the conclusion, which is "claims are inaccurate".

Does the conclusion infer that "some claims are inaccurate"?
Yes, it infers that "all claims made by salespeople at major health stores are inaccurate".
Does it do so on the basis of evidence that is about who is making those claims?
Yes, it tries to invalidate the legitimacy of the salespeople's claims, because they are salespeople who are steering customers toward higher-commission products out of their own self-interest.
This describes the famous Ad Hominem flaw, in which we dismiss someone's views or claims because of who they are, not what they said.
In general, Ad Hominem arguments say, "Don't listen to X. He's got a vested interest in this matter", or "Don't listen to X. His past behavior / statements don't line up with what he's telling you now."
LSAT wants us to deal with people's ideas head-on, and evaluate their legitimacy based on evidence and soundness, not based on any tangential qualities about the source itself.

This describes the famous Whole to Part flaw, in which an author assumes that a trait that's true of a collective is therefore true of each part of the collective.
Did the conclusion of this argument infer that "each member of a group of people has a certain property"?
No, we can't really match that. The conclusion was that "the claims made by a certain group of people have a certain property".

This is essentially saying that insurance companies have a higher profit margin than do lotto sponsors. In other words, with insurance companies, they're keeping more of the money and expending less on payouts to their customers.
That would make them a bigger losing bet than lotto tickets, so that goes the opposite of our desired direction: "insurance is fine, lotto is dumb".

This describes the famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, in which the author presents a conditional logic premise and then applies it in an illegal backwards or opposite fashion to reach the conclusion.
Was there any conditional logic in the premise?
Yes, there were two conditionals.
Salesperson → steers toward higher commission
Salesperson in → work on commission
major health store
Committing a Nec vs. Suff flaw with one of those conditionals would sound like one of these arguments:

This addresses whether Einstein’s theory should be credited with the discovery of the advance of the perihelion of Mercury, while the conclusion of the argument is about whether the prediction of the phenomenon should count as evidence in favor of Einstein’s theory.

This relationship would establish that if a theory was not developed with a phenomenon in mind, than that phenomenon should not count as evidence in favor of that theory. The evidence of this argument however, is that the theory was developed with the phenomenon in mind.

This principle misrepresents the evidence and the conclusion of the argument. Not accounting for all relevant phenomena is different than accounting for a specific phenomenon (the advance of the perihelion of Mercury) and the theory not being well supported is different than a specific phenomenon not counting as support for the theory.

This provides the link between Einstein’s theory likely being adjusted to account for the advance of the perihelion of Mercury with the conclusion that the predictions made by Einstein’s theory about that phenomenon should not be counted as evidence in support of Einstein’s theory.

When a Flaw answer begins with fails to consider / ignores the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows would Weaken.
Can we object to the author by saying, "Hey, bud — we earn significantly more money on each high-end computer than we do on each low-end computer"?
Sure! "How is it going to maximize our profits to sell only low-end computers, if we make significantly less money on each low-end computer?!"
If we solved the Relative vs. Absolute riddle and realized that a product with a higher profit margin might nonetheless make less profit, then we'll understand why this answer is saying this idea.
But even if we didn't work out that mathematical objection when we read the argument, we should still be able to ask ourselves, "Would it weaken this argument to say that each high-end model makes significantly more money than each low-end model? Yes, that seems to go against the author's recommendation!"

When a Flaw answer begins with fails to consider / ignores the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows would Weaken.
Can we object to the author by saying, "Hey, author — it's possible that last year the store sold as many high-end models as low-end models"?
No, the author doesn't care at all about what the ratio of high-end to low-end sales were last year.
She's trying to make a recommendation for the upcoming year, strategizing what ratio would be most profitable.

When a Flaw answer begins with fails to consider / ignores the possibility, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows would Weaken.
Can we object to the author by saying, "Hey, author — some people come into the store to buy a low-end one but end up buying a high-end one"?
No. In the author's Plan, the store will only stock low-end computers, so there won't be any people who "upgrade" from their intended low-end to a high-end.
But the author isn't saddened by a customer who is forced to still buy a low-end, rather than a high-end. The author thinks forcing that customer to buy the low-end maximizes profit for the store (since the profit margin on the low-end computer is 25% but would only be 13% on the high-end model).

When a Flaw answer begins with takes for granted / presumes, we can ask ourselves whether the idea that follows qualifies as Necessary Assumption.
Was the author assuming that "the sole objective in managing the computer store is maximizing profits"?
No, just because she mentions "maximizing profit" as a reason for following her recommendation, that doesn't commit her to thinking that "maximizing profit is the only objective in managing the store".
When someone says "we should do X", they are assuming that the upsides outweigh the downsides.
So a correct answer could have said that the author, "presumes, without providing justification, that the manager does not have objectives beyond maximizing profits that would be badly undermined by this plan".

If we're trying to argue that "insurance makes sense, lotto tickets don't", it certainly doesn't feel superficially helpful to hear "ya spend even more on insurance than lotto".
This is a difference, but not a meaningful one. As stated in my example before, the average cost of an insurance policy might be $500 (vs. a $5 lotto ticket), but the average payout of the insurance policy is also much more, $75 vs. $2.
All we know is that they are both a "losing bet" in the long run. We aren't told which one has a worse rate of losing money, but we would only care about the ratio of pay-in to pay-out (500/75 vs. 5/2).
This answer is only saying that one has a bigger pay-in than the other (but if it also has a bigger average pay-out, it could still be the wiser investment).
"Small financial risks for the chance of obtaining much larger benefits" sounds a lot like lotto tickets. This answer is saying something good about lotto tickets? No thanks.

This is definitely the most tempting answer, because it feels like it points to a salient difference that makes lotto tickets sound worse: you're way less likely to get a payout! Having reached answer choice D without having made any friends along the way, this is definitely an answer I would hold.
The problem is, this answer is talking about the grand prize. The professor's argument is about the average payout. If this answer said the odds of winning any prize in lotto are way lower than the odds of getting an insurance settlement, that would be a meaningful difference that would disrupt the professor's analogy and I'd be much more inclined to pick it. But as written, this just establishes that you're less like to win the biggest prize than to get an insurance settlement. It's still possible, in this case, that the odds of winning something meaningful are as good as the odds of getting some insurance settlement, so it doesn't have a particularly strong impact on the argument.

I hate this answer, and in many universes in the multiverse I'm probably picking it. It rewards us for having assembled the grand causal chain of
Air Poll. → Glob Warm → Big Niño → Drought → Fire risk ↑
However, we're only told that "many scientists believe" that air pollution led to global warming which led to the weirdly big El Niño.
This answer treats that as a fact and also amps up the burden of proof by saying that air pollution was largely responsible, when the safe inference would be somewhat responsible.

On Most Supported tasks, we are allowed to flip a Causal Difference-Maker and say "If it hadn't happened, we wouldn't have seen (as much) of the Effect". (This is a Must Be True task, though)
We know that a weirdly strong El Niño led to a big draught, which made forests more susceptible to fire.
So, on Most Supported, we can say "if there hadn't been a weirdly strong El Niño, the forests would have been less susceptible to fire."
But this goes too far in predicting "few, if any" large fires. We just know less susceptible, not barely susceptible at all.

Although we have some support for the idea that strong El Niño's lead to more drought and thus susceptibility to fire, we can't derive a Must Be True inference that in 51% or more of strong El Niño ears there have been larger and more intense tropical forest fires.
The causal information is presented as "susceptible to fire at that time because of drought and El Niño".

There's a recurring flaw LSAT sometimes goes back to in which we assume that someone believes an implication of one of their beliefs.
For example: 2 is a prime number. Tania believes that her brother Ricky's age is 2, so Tania believes that her brother Ricky's age is a prime number.
That's flawed since Tania might not even know what a prime number is. We have no way of inferring her other beliefs. We can't assume that she knows all relevant information or is capable of or inclined to make rational connections between her beliefs. (Like even if I know that alcohol is bad for my body and know that scotch is alcohol, I might not believe that scotch is bad for my body.)
Similarly, these scientists who believe that El Niño was exacerbated by global warming that was caused by pollution don't necessarily know that El Niño spurned a big drought which amped up the risk of fires.
So this answer is congratulating us for having seen the big causal chain, but they're using it against us. What some/many scientists believe only goes the first couple links in the chain.
Air Pollution → Global Warm → Big Niño → Drought → Fire risk ↑
[ many scientists believe ]

If it's as important → the book will be published
as he claims
This is similar, but notably different, from our prediction. They intended for that difference to short circuit us.
We were expecting "If as important and well written as claimed, will be published", or
A and B → C
This is giving us
A → C
Suppose we know that "If there's karaoke at a party, Josie will have fun".
If there's karaoke and Jenga at a party, do we know if Josie will have fun?
Yes! The rule we just read said, if there's karaoke, it's a 100% guarantee that Josie will have fun. So adding in Jenga doesn't make us question that original conditional. We already must believe that Josie will have fun, since a party with karaoke and Jenga still involves karaoke at a party.
On Sufficient Assumption (especially more modern examples), don't think about the correct answer needing to be the perfect missing link you solved for. Think about the answers flexibly. If we add them to the claims we were given in the evidence, can we derive the conclusion?
This answer allows to construct this chain:
If S's book is as important as he claims,
it gets published,
which means Nguyen recommends to dean,
which means dean promotes Skiff.
So have we proven our Conclusion, that says "If Skiff's book is as important and as well written as he claims, then he'll get promoted"?
Sure. If Skiff's book is as important and as well written as he claims, then it's as important as he claims, and thus the book will be published, Nguyen will recommend to the dean, and the dean will promote Skiff

Our only concern is establishing that Skiff's book will get published. This asserts a need Skiff has to have it published, but that barely, if at all, strengthens the notion that it will get published.
How badly Skiff wants / needs it to be published probably doesn't matter. The decision is out of Skiff's hands. It's about whether or not a publisher wants to publish it.

Since this answer contains no wording about Skiff's book getting published, we don't really need to examine it. As it turns out, it's bringing up something irrelevant, in the sense that Nguyen's role in this argument is just to recommend the promotion to the dean, assuming Skiff's book gets published.
We have no reason to think that Skiff's book getting published hinges in any way on Nguyen's evaluation of how well-written it is.

It's hard to do a Sufficient Assumption question without encountering an answer choice that has the correct ideas in the wrong logical sequence.
We wanted
if as imp and well-written → book will be
as Skiff claimed published
This gives us the illegal light switch version of that:
if not as important book will not
and well-written → be published
as Skiff claimed
This hurts the plausibility of passing "pesticide resistance" from the domesticated/GMO kind to the wild/weedy relative. According to this answer, that's the harder direction to pass.

This could be helpful info if we were trying to figure out how to speed up the passing of one trait from a domesticated plant to its wild relative.
But we don't want to hear more about what worked with radishes. We really need to know if the stuff that worked with radishes, and with flower color, would also work with other crops and with pesticide-resistance.

This is our nightmare. The author is extrapolating from the sample of what worked in the radish experiment. She's assuming that the radish experiment is a representative sample of what would generally work for crops / traits.
If we learn that radishes are an outlier, that it's unusually easy with radishes for traits to pass from one species to a relative species, then it becomes less likely that this same behavior would also work well with other crop plants.

One of the three differences we're worried about as we move from the experiment on radishes to the conclusion about other crop plants is that the radishes were domesticated (selectively bred to have a certain flower color) whereas the author is talking about genetically engineering the trait of pesticide resistance.
That difference could potentially mean that what worked for radishes doesn't work for the author's plan. If, however, we knew that the domesticated radish's flower color had been genetically engineered, that would strengthen the argument. We would know that a genetically engineered trait is definitely capable of passing.
This answer is saying that flower color was not genetically engineered, underscoring the potential difference between the author's Evidence and Conclusion.

This does not match the first sentence. It matches the premise.
Not only does this not match the first sentence, it was never said at all, so it can't possibly be the correct answer.

Roger seems to explicitly calling for other energy sources. He's saying we'll need to increase energy from new sources. If you start getting energy from solar panels, then your "production from energy sources other than hydroelectric" has been increased.
Pauline seems to be assuming that energy from other sources will not go up so much that it will stabilize electricity costs, but she's not assuming that energy cannot go up from other sources.

Roger is convinced that our existing supply will not suffice in the near future. Even if we keep all that hydroelectric power, we'll still need more energy (to meet growing demand, we presume).

and

Roger never discusses energy costs, so this answer is a non-starter. But Pauline might disagree with this; she thinks a drop in energy supply (by losing the hydroelectric energy supplied by the dam) would cause costs to go up.

We'll almost never see weak wording like "may" in the correct answer to Sufficient Assumption, since we're looking for an answer that guarantees the conclusion is true (follows logically / properly drawn / properly inferred).
Since we're trying to prove the idea that "the banking system will not be strengthened", and since we were provided a law that says
if X → banking system won't be strengthened
We need an answer to tell us "X", which is that "the former owners will buy back these banks".

This claim is the heart of the argument — it's what the author is trying to convince us of, and the "Thus..." at the end restates it. So it has a major logical role, not the trivial introducer role this answer describes.
This puts pressure on the publication not to openly challenge the veracity of the quoted claims.

We'll almost never see weak wording like "could" in the correct answer to Sufficient Assumption, since we're looking for an answer that guarantees the conclusion is true (follows logically / properly drawn / properly inferred).
Since we're trying to prove the idea that "the banking system will not be strengthened", and since we were provided a law that says
if X → banking system won't be strengthened
We need an answer to tell us "X", which is that "the former owners will buy back these banks".

The correct answer on Sufficient Assumption will almost never contain wording we haven't already used in the passage, since it's just trying to patch together loose ends (not create a new loose end by introducing new wording like "overall economy").

We're only here to judge / prove whether the banking system will / won't be strengthened.
Wording like "these banks will be weaker than other banks for some time" is a very wishy-washy idea. We need definitive understanding that the banking system isn't strengthened.

There's no analogy in the accountant's argument. I'm not even sure what a popular analogy would be.
There's a popular hypothesis from the newspaper industry about why profits are falling, but that's it.

There is some economic data presented, relating to the cost of newsprint.
But what would we match up with "a historically accepted approach"?
Historically, newspapers have used newsprint to print their papers? But the author certainly isn't suggesting that they stop using newsprint.

The accountant doesn't criticize a "newly developed method" or compare it to a conventional one.
There's no comparison between methods at all. The argument is about competing explanations for falling profits.

Nice, this gives us both parts of the author's argument. We challenge the "rising cost of newsprint" explanation by saying that the cost of newsprint hasn't actually risen, and then we introduce a different explanation (falling circulation / falling advertising) as the real explanation for the falling profits of the newspaper industry.

The author is calling into question an explanation for a phenomenon.
There isn't any justification for a practice. That would be like saying, "The reason we offer some articles for free and put others behind a paywall is ____ ."
The newspaper industry is trying to explain falling profits, but falling profits aren't a "practice". They're just something that's happening.
This answer alludes to a Faulty Implications move, where you show the author that they're wrong by showing how their same logic would lead to some undesirable / untrue outcome.
No analogy is used or reinterpreted in the accountant's argument.
The accountant challenges an explanation, not an approach's effectiveness.
No comparison of methods occurs in the accountant's argument.
The accountant challenges the newsprint-cost explanation and offers circulation/advertising as the alternative.
No reductio or extension to an undesirable practice is used.
There's no analogy in the accountant's argument. She's working with direct economic claims about costs and profits, not by analogy to anything else.

"Approach" is the wrong word for what the industry is doing. They're offering an explanation for why profits are falling. The accountant disputes that explanation, not the effectiveness of any approach.
There's no "newly developed method" being criticized, and no "conventional method" being held up as superior. The accountant is just disputing one explanation and proposing another.

This captures both moves. First, the accountant challenges the newsprint-costs explanation — pointing out that adjusted for inflation, newsprint hasn't gotten more expensive. Second, she offers a different explanation: circulation and advertising are falling.

The author hasn't mentioned anything about what people do / don't believe about alcohol or speculated in any way about why people drink, so the author hasn't committed to any assumptions about why people choose to drink alcohol.
If you negated this idea and said "people don't drink because they believe alcohol is beneficial", the author's argument wouldn't be weakened. She'd just say, "Cool, I never said that's WHY they drink; it just so happens to be an effect of them drinking."

Does the author draw a comparison? Nope.
Is there reference to a popular belief? Nope.
Is there a scientific opinion? Yeah, we could probably consider "recent evidence suggests" a scientific opinion.
So all three parts of this answer don't match.
Appealing to people's belief rather than actual scientific data is a famous flaw known as Inappropriate Appeal (to Opinion).

Does it hurt the author's argument if we say, "Yo, my dude — there are other ways to make your body an inhospitable environment than consuming alcohol", the author would just say "Sure, I know. I never said alcohol was the only substance that had these beneficial effects, just that it is a substance with these beneficial effects."

This says the claim supports a different conclusion (that cities are generally more polluted). But the cities-more-polluted line is the opening concession, not the conclusion. And the claim in question is the conclusion of the argument, not a premise.

Does this paragraph tell us whether less than 50% of people are aware of the recommended daily intake of vitamins A and D?
No. We know that many people are unaware of what constitutes a standard serving. But we don't know what people's awareness level is of the recommended daily intake of these vitamins.

Does the author draw a conclusion about alcohol consumption in general?
Sure, the conclusion just says "alcohol consumption is beneficial".
Is the author's premise about moderate alcohol consumption?
Yes — she says that moderate alcohol consumption has certain beneficial effects on health. But maybe light alcohol consumption or heavy alcohol consumption doesn't have those benefits. (perhaps light alcohol consumption is not enough to render your insides inhospitable to bacteria, whereas heavy alcohol consumption starts to be very damaging to your heart/liver)
By shifting from evidence about a subtype of alcohol consumption to a conclusion about all types of alcohol consumption, the author is making a Sampling assumption that what is true of moderate consumption is also true of light / heavy consumption.
We could object to the author by saying, "Even though moderate alcohol consumption can have beneficial effects, light alcohol consumption is totally neutral and heavy alcohol consumption is very damaging. Thus, we can't really just generalize that alcohol consumption is, on balance, beneficial."

This answer makes it seem like we're not dependent on these employee-training seminars for fostering creative thinking skills; the latter is taken care of for most employees by their high school education.
The whole selling point of implementing these new methods was their potential for teaching creative thinking, but if our workforce already comes to us with creative thinking skills, then that diminishes the incentive for using the new methods.

This answer is pretty tempting at first, because it seems to be saying something positive about these new methods that would strengthen Grodex's desire to conduct its employee-training seminars using these methods.
However, a compelling comparison would be "corporations that conduct training seminars using these methods are generally more successful than are corporations that conduct training seminars using other methods."
That sort of comparison would make it seem like these innovative methods might be better than the other options.
But the comparison here is between using these methods and doing no training seminars at all.
If you're trying to tell me that I should buy a certain LSAT resource because it's "better than not studying at all", then that's a weak testimonial for that resource.
Moreover, the correlation in this answer choice might really just be telling us that more successful corporations have the budget and scale to run training seminars. (In other words, it's not that the training seminar is causing the success; the success is allowing the training seminar to happen.)

This answer feel more like a weakener, because if hardly any employees show up to these training seminars, then who cares what educational methods our seminars employ.
Technically, it's not really a reason for or against using these new methods.

The author was Assuming a Similarity. She was thinking that, "If these new methods help children to think more creatively, then they will also help adults working for Grodex to think more creatively."
A potential objection to this conclusion could have been, "No, Grodex shouldn't use these methods. These are good for 5-10 year olds, but they wouldn't work on adults."
This answer rules out such an objection by telling us that the effects of these teaching methods are generally similar, whether it's kids or adults. So this gives Grodex reason to think that these methods generally would help an adult learn to think more creatively.

This is just a factual, mathematical claim. It isn't supported by any reasons. Supporting reasons for this claim would sound mathematical:
why would the density be 10 people / sq. meter in this hypothetical?
because ... there are currently 8 billion people at a growth rate of 10% per year. The habitable land mass of Earth is 20 billion square meters. (etc.)

We're not trying to draw an Inference or call out an unstated Assumption on Main Conclusion. We're trying to point at the explicit claim that is the author's conclusion and then find an answer that matches.
This answer choice was never stated.

The conclusion is the last claim in the paragraph only like 10% of the time on Main Conclusion questions, so be very suspicious any time you're picking an answer that says the last idea.
This is a premise, supporting our actual conclusion. There isn't any supporting reason offered for this claim. It's self-justifying math to say that, "If X doubles every 2 hours, then if you cut X in half, you'll be back to the original amount 2 hours later."

We're not trying to draw an Inference or call out an unstated Assumption on Main Conclusion. We're trying to point at the explicit claim that is the author's conclusion and then find an answer that matches.
