We know the committee's proposals are for upper-level courses (PRC -> UL), but this answer assumes the reverse: upper-level courses came from the committee (UL -> PRC). That is an illegal reversal. Dean Wilson's proposal could also be for an upper-level course. Additionally, the committee could have received proposals without approving them. Nothing guarantees that receiving a proposal leads to approval.
This restates the first sentence — the banking visionaries' optimistic view — not the author's conclusion. The conclusion pushes back against this view.

If more than one new course is approved, at least two proposals were submitted. Dean Wilson received only one proposal, so he can account for at most one approved course. Any additional approved courses must have had proposals submitted to the committee. All committee proposals are for upper-level courses, and all upper-level courses have prerequisites. Therefore, at least one of the approved courses (the one that came through the committee) will have prerequisites. This follows directly from combining the premises without any unsupported inferences.

This answer says if Dean Wilson's proposal is for an upper-level course, then all courses offered next year will have prerequisites. "All courses" goes far beyond what the premises support. The premises only tell us that new upper-level courses will have prerequisites — not that existing courses will have prerequisites. There could be many continuing lower-level courses on the schedule without prerequisites. This answer massively overgeneralizes from a rule about new upper-level courses to a claim about every course offered.

This answer says if no new upper-level courses are approved, then Dean Wilson's proposal will have been approved. There is no logical connection between the absence of upper-level courses and Dean Wilson's proposal being approved. If no upper-level courses are approved, the committee proposals were rejected. But that tells us nothing about whether Dean Wilson's proposal was accepted or rejected — those are independent decisions. Dean Wilson's proposal could be rejected regardless of what happens with the committee's proposals.
This assumes ~UL -> ~P, which is an illegal negation of UL -> P. Lower-level courses could also have prerequisites. The premises do not establish that only upper-level courses have prerequisites.
This reverses PRC -> UL into UL -> PRC. Upper-level courses could come through Dean Wilson too, not just the committee. And receiving a proposal does not guarantee approval.

Dean Wilson has only one proposal. If there are two or more new courses, at least one must come through the committee, making it upper-level with prerequisites. This follows directly from combining the premises.

"All courses offered next year" is far too broad. The prerequisite rule applies to upper-level courses, not to every course on the entire schedule. Existing lower-level courses could have no prerequisites.
There is no logical link between the committee's proposals being rejected and Dean Wilson's proposal being approved. These are independent decisions with no stated connection.

All upper-level courses have prerequisites. Does that mean non-upper-level courses do not? Not at all. "All dogs are animals" does not mean "all non-dogs are not animals." A lower-level course could easily have prerequisites too — the premises just do not discuss that possibility. This answer flips the conditional and pretends it works both ways.

Every committee proposal is upper-level, so every upper-level course came from the committee? That is like saying "every dog is an animal, so every animal is a dog." Dean Wilson could also have an upper-level course proposal. And even if the committee received proposals, who says they approved them all? This answer reverses the conditional and throws in an extra unsupported leap for good measure.

The Dean has one proposal in the drawer. If two new courses show up on the schedule, at least one of them did not come from the Dean — it had to go through the committee. And the committee's courses are all upper-level, and upper-level means prerequisites. So the second course (or third, or fourth) is guaranteed to have prerequisites. The Dean's one proposal might dodge the prerequisite requirement, but the committee's courses cannot. Two or more new courses means at least one gets prerequisites. The domino chain works perfectly.

"All courses offered next year will have prerequisites" — every single one? Intro to Basket Weaving now requires Calculus II? The premises say upper-level courses get prerequisites. Not all courses. Not lower-level courses. Not the ones that have been on the schedule for a decade. This answer takes a rule about a subset and applies it to the entire university catalog.

This answer identifies the argument's central flaw: it fails to consider that most mammals with short olecranon processes might not have been predators. The argument establishes that predators generally have short olecranon processes (predator -> short OP), but this does not mean that most mammals with short olecranon processes are predators (short OP -> predator). Many non-predatory mammals could have short olecranon processes for other reasons — digging, climbing, swimming, or defense. Without establishing that predation is the primary or dominant reason for this trait, the argument cannot conclude that Megatherium was probably a predator just because it had the trait. The answer correctly identifies the reversal of the conditional.

This answer says the argument assumes the only reason predators need to move forelimbs quickly is to attack prey. But the argument does not depend on this being the only reason. The argument's conclusion is based on the link between short olecranon processes and predation — not on whether predators also move fast for other reasons. Even if predators also use fast forelimbs for chasing, defending territory, or other activities, the argument's reasoning would be equally flawed (or not) because those additional uses do not affect the reversal problem. The flaw lies in the direction of the inference, not in whether predators have multiple uses for fast limbs.

This answer says the argument overlooks the possibility that Megatherium could have been a successful predator without a short olecranon process. But the argument is trying to prove that Megatherium was a predator because it had a short olecranon process. Whether Megatherium could have been a predator without this trait is irrelevant to whether having the trait indicates predation. To weaken the argument, we would need to show that having a short OP does not indicate predation — not that predation is possible without it. This answer addresses an alternative scenario that has no bearing on the argument's actual reasoning.

This answer suggests the argument assumes extinct mammals' olecranon processes were no shorter on average than those of living mammals. But the argument's premises speak about mammals generally, not specifically about living mammals. The claim that predatory mammals have short olecranon processes is presented as a general biological principle. There is no indication that this principle applies only to living mammals. Whether extinct mammals had shorter olecranon processes on average than living ones does not affect the argument's logic — the flaw is in reversing the conditional, not in making improper comparisons between extinct and living species.

This answer says the argument fails to consider that a longer olecranon process might confer advantages like greater strength. While this is biologically interesting, it is irrelevant to the argument's reasoning. The argument is about what a short olecranon process indicates, not about what a long olecranon process offers. The benefits of a long olecranon process do not affect whether a short one indicates predation. The argument's flaw is that it reverses the conditional between predation and short olecranon processes, and information about the advantages of long olecranon processes does not address this reversal.

The argument only shows predators tend to have short olecranon processes, not that most mammals with short olecranon processes are predators. Many non-predators could share this trait for other reasons, making the inference from trait to predation unjustified.

Whether predators also use fast forelimbs for other purposes does not affect the argument's flaw. The problem is reversing predator -> short OP, not whether predators have multiple reasons for fast forelimbs.
Whether Megatherium could have been a predator without a short OP is irrelevant. The argument's flaw is inferring predation from the trait, not assuming the trait is required for predation.
The argument's premises apply to mammals generally, not specifically living ones. There is no implicit comparison between extinct and living mammals that could constitute a flaw.
Benefits of a longer olecranon process are irrelevant. The argument is about what a short one indicates. Advantages of long processes do not address the reversal flaw in the argument.

Most basketball players are tall. Does that mean most tall people play basketball? Obviously not. Same logic problem here. Most predators have short olecranon processes, but maybe most mammals with short olecranon processes are diggers, climbers, or something else entirely. Megatherium — a giant ground sloth, for what it is worth — might have used those fast arms for tearing branches off trees. The argument never checked whether having the trait actually predicts predation, and this answer calls out that exact blind spot.

Maybe predators also use fast arms for chasing or wrestling — so what? That just gives predators more reasons to have short olecranon processes, which actually makes the predator-to-short-OP link stronger. The argument's problem is not about what predators do with their arms. It is about whether having short olecranon processes means you are a predator. This answer is looking at the wrong side of the equation.

Could Megatherium have hunted even without fast arms? Maybe, but who cares? The argument is not saying "you need a short olecranon process to be a predator." It is saying "you have a short olecranon process, so you are a predator." Those are completely different claims, and this answer is attacking the wrong one. It is like hearing someone say "you must be a doctor because you wear a white coat" and responding with "but some doctors do not wear white coats." True, irrelevant.

Were extinct mammals' arm bones different from living ones' on average? The argument does not care. It says "predatory mammals have short olecranon processes" — all mammals, living or extinct. The argument's problem is not that it compared the wrong groups. It is that it saw a trait common in predators and assumed anything with that trait must be a predator. This answer is looking for the flaw in the wrong neighborhood.

This answer says anything morally neutral either has outlasted its justification or deserves no praise. Diagrammed: morally neutral -> outlasted or no praise. The argument needs the opposite direction: outlasted or no praise -> morally neutral. This answer starts with moral neutrality and derives characteristics from it, but the argument needs to start with characteristics (some commitments deserve no praise) and derive moral neutrality. The conditional runs backward relative to the argument's needs.

This answer says commitment is virtuous when, and only when, the relationship or career is good. This limits when commitment is virtuous but does not support the conclusion that commitment is morally neutral. If the relationship is bad, this answer tells us commitment is not virtuous — but "not virtuous" could mean bad, harmful, or neutral. The answer does not specifically support moral neutrality. It also does not address the general category of commitment; it only addresses commitment to relationships and careers. The conclusion requires all commitments to be morally neutral, and this answer points in an indeterminate direction when the commitment is to something bad.

This answer says if a commitment deserves no praise, it is morally neutral. Diagrammed: deserves no praise -> morally neutral. This does connect one piece of evidence (some commitments deserve no praise) to the conclusion (morally neutral). However, the evidence only identifies one type of praiseworthy-less commitment: commitment to a relationship benefiting no one. This principle would only establish that this specific type of commitment is morally neutral, not that all commitments are. The conclusion is universal — all commitments are morally neutral — and this answer only supports the neutrality of a subset. The correct answer must bridge the gap for all commitments, not just the unpraiseworthy ones.
This paraphrases the conclusion: home banking benefits banks more than customers. It matches the second sentence's meaning in different words, which is standard for correct Main Conclusion answers.
This restates the evidence from the third sentence — the supporting reason for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

This answer says if a commitment has outlasted its original justification, it cannot be virtuous. The evidence states that commitment "often" is involvement that has outlasted its justification, but not always. So this principle only covers commitments that have outlasted their justification, not all commitments. And "cannot be virtuous" does not equal "morally neutral" — a commitment that is not virtuous could still be morally negative rather than neutral. Like answer C, this gets the direction right but lacks the scope and precision needed to support the universal conclusion.

This answer states that all commitments are morally neutral if there are any commitments that are undeserving of praise. Diagrammed: any commitment deserves no praise -> all commitments are morally neutral. The evidence establishes that at least one type of commitment deserves no praise (commitment to a relationship benefiting no one). Applying this principle: since at least one commitment is undeserving of praise, all commitments are morally neutral. This is the only answer that bridges the gap between evidence about some commitments and a conclusion about all commitments. The principle's structure is designed to generalize from the existence of any unpraiseworthy commitment to universal moral neutrality — exactly what the essayist's reasoning requires.
This says: morally neutral -> outlasted or no praise. The argument needs: outlasted or no praise -> morally neutral. Wrong conditional direction.

This says commitment is virtuous only when the career or relationship is good. But when it is bad, commitment could be harmful, negative, or neutral — this does not specifically support moral neutrality.
This connects "deserves no praise" to "morally neutral," but only covers one type of commitment. The conclusion says all commitments are neutral, not just the ones that deserve no praise.

This covers only commitments that outlasted their justification (not all commitments), and "not virtuous" does not specifically mean "morally neutral." Too narrow in scope and imprecise in conclusion.

If any commitment deserves no praise, then all commitments are morally neutral. The evidence shows at least one commitment deserves no praise. Therefore, all commitments are morally neutral. This perfectly bridges the some-to-all gap.

If something is morally neutral, it either outlasted its justification or deserves no praise? The argument is trying to prove things are morally neutral, not figure out what follows from being morally neutral. This answer starts where the argument ends. The evidence says some commitments deserve no praise. The conclusion says all commitments are neutral. This answer says neutral things deserve no praise. That is the road from B to A when the argument needs the road from A to B.

So commitment is virtuous when the thing you are committed to is good, and not virtuous when it is bad? That is a reasonable-sounding principle, but it does not land on "morally neutral." Not virtuous could mean bad, useless, harmful — lots of things besides neutral. And what about commitment to something good? This answer says that is actually virtuous, which contradicts the essayist's claim that all commitments are morally neutral. This answer argues for a sliding scale; the essayist wants a flat line.

Deserves no praise means morally neutral? Okay, that handles the bad commitments. But what about commitment to a relationship that is wonderful? That commitment presumably deserves praise, so this principle says nothing about it. The essayist wants all commitments to be neutral — the good ones, the bad ones, the ones that outlasted their welcome, all of them. This answer only neutralizes the losers and leaves the winners untouched. It is half a bridge.

Commitment that has hung around too long cannot be virtuous? Sure, but "not virtuous" and "morally neutral" are different destinations. Not virtuous could mean actively bad. And "often" outlasted justification is not "always." The essayist needs a principle that covers every commitment, not just the ones that should have ended three years ago. This answer knocks some commitments off the virtuous pedestal but does not land them in the morally neutral zone, and it only addresses some commitments anyway.

This answer says no children who spend free time reading stories fail to develop a lifelong interest in literature. Cutting through the double negative: children who read -> lifelong interest. This makes reading sufficient for developing interest, but the argument needs reading to be necessary for interest, not sufficient. The argument's gap is: few read -> few develop interest. To validate this, we need: developing interest requires reading (interest -> read). This answer instead says: reading guarantees interest (read -> interest). Knowing that readers always develop interest does not tell us anything about whether non-readers might also develop interest through other means. This is the classic sufficient-necessary confusion.

This answer says only those who currently spend their free time reading stories will develop a lifelong interest in literature. The word "only" establishes reading as a necessary condition: lifelong interest -> currently reads stories. Contrapositive: does not currently read -> will not develop lifelong interest. The evidence tells us few children currently read. Combined with this assumption: few children read, and only readers develop lifelong interest, therefore few children will develop lifelong interest. The conclusion follows directly. This is the precise bridge needed: reading during childhood is the only pathway to lifelong literary interest.

This answer says children growing up without a television in the household do not fail to read stories. Parsing the double negative: no TV -> reads stories. This describes what happens in TV-free homes but says nothing about developing a lifelong interest in literature. The conclusion is about lifelong literary interest, and this answer never mentions that concept. Even if we know that TV-free children read, we still have no link between reading and developing lifelong interest. The assumption needs to connect reading behavior to the conclusion's outcome, and this answer stops at the reading step without reaching the literary interest step.

This answer says few people who watch a great deal of television develop lifelong literary interest. The evidence states that children prefer TV over reading because of its visual appeal, but it does not say children watch "a great deal" of television. A child might watch only a small amount of TV but still find it more appealing than reading. This answer addresses heavy TV watchers, while the evidence describes a broader group — children who simply do not read, regardless of how much TV they watch. The assumption does not accurately connect to the evidence's population. Additionally, this answer does not establish reading as necessary for literary interest; it only says heavy TV watching prevents it.

This answer says few children who spend free time reading stories watch television. This describes reading children's TV habits but says nothing about developing lifelong literary interest. The conclusion is about whether children will develop a lifelong interest in literature, and this answer never addresses that concept. Whether young readers watch TV is irrelevant to bridging the gap between "few read" and "few will love literature." Like answer C, this answer operates entirely in the reading-and-TV-watching domain without ever reaching the literary-interest domain that the conclusion requires.

This says: reads -> develops interest (reading is sufficient). The argument needs: develops interest -> reads (reading is necessary). Wrong conditional direction — this does not prevent non-readers from developing literary interest through other means.

"Only those who read" makes reading necessary for lifelong interest. Contrapositive: not reading -> no lifelong interest. Since few children read, few will develop lifelong interest. The conclusion follows directly.
This says TV-free children read, but never connects reading to developing lifelong literary interest. The conclusion's key concept — lifelong interest in literature — is completely unaddressed.

The evidence says children prefer TV over reading, not that they watch "a great deal" of television. This answer targets heavy TV watchers, a narrower group than the argument addresses. It also does not establish reading as necessary for literary interest.
This describes reading children's TV habits but never mentions lifelong literary interest. The conclusion's key concept is completely absent from this answer.

Every kid who reads develops a lifelong love of literature? Heartwarming, but not what the argument needs. The argument says few kids read, so few will love literature. That only works if reading is required for loving literature. This answer says reading is sufficient for loving literature. Big difference. Under this answer, reading kids always become book lovers, but kids who never read could still discover literature later through some other path. The non-readers are the argument's concern, and this answer says nothing about them.

"Only" is the LSAT's favorite word for establishing necessary conditions, and it does its job perfectly here. Only readers become lifelong literature fans. Not reading? Not becoming a literature fan. Most kids are not reading. Therefore, most kids will not become literature fans. Chain complete. This is the exact assumption that turns "few read" into "few will love literature" — no other pathway to literary interest exists if reading is the only way in.

Kids without TVs read stories. Okay, nice to know, but the argument is not struggling to explain why kids do or do not read — the TV-ubiquity premise already covered that. The argument's problem is connecting "does not read" to "will not love literature forever." This answer addresses the wrong gap. It talks about the input (who reads) without connecting it to the output (who develops lifelong interest).

The stimulus says kids prefer TV over books, not that they are binge-watching eight hours a day. A kid might watch thirty minutes of TV and still not bother reading. This answer targets the heavy-TV-watching population when the argument is about the non-reading population. Those might overlap a lot, but they are not the same group. And even within the right group, this answer does not provide the missing link: that reading is required for lifelong literary interest.

This answer says a documentary with no purpose other than authentically depicting human behavior can be "legitimate." Two problems. First, the filmmaker's documentary is not described as having "no purpose other than" depicting behavior — it might serve additional purposes. Second, the conclusion is about documentaries being "worthwhile," not "legitimate." Legitimacy and worthiness are different evaluative standards; a documentary can be legitimate without being worthwhile, and vice versa. This answer uses the wrong evaluative term and describes a narrower category of documentary than the filmmaker's.

This answer says a documentary can be authentic only if subjects do not speak directly to the camera. This addresses documentary authenticity, not documentary worthwhileness. Even if we established that the filmmaker's documentary is authentic and others are not, we still would not know that authenticity makes a documentary more worthwhile. The conclusion's key concept — being "more worthwhile" — is absent from this answer. Additionally, this answer addresses documentary-level authenticity, while the evidence discusses subject-level behavior (acting naturally). Being authentic as a documentary and having subjects who act naturally are related but distinct concepts.

This answer addresses whether filmmakers have a moral obligation to reveal camera locations. The argument is not about the ethics of hidden cameras — it is about the relative worthwhileness of documentaries. Whether the filmmaker's practice is morally permissible is a separate question from whether it produces better documentaries. This answer defends the filmmaker's method against an ethical critique that the argument never raises. The argument's gap is between natural behavior and documentary worth, not between hidden cameras and moral permissibility.
This captures only the bank-benefit half of a comparative conclusion. It misses the crucial comparison — that customers benefit less than banks — and focuses too narrowly on branch closures.

This answer states that the more authentically a documentary depicts its subjects, the more worthwhile it is. The filmmaker's evidence establishes that subjects act naturally when filmed with hidden cameras, meaning the documentary depicts them authentically. This principle bridges directly from authentic depiction to worthwhileness: more authentic depiction equals more worthwhile documentary. Since the filmmaker's subjects act more naturally than subjects who speak directly to the camera, the filmmaker's documentaries depict subjects more authentically, and therefore — by this principle — are more worthwhile. This is the precise bridge between the evidence (natural behavior / authentic depiction) and the conclusion (more worthwhile).

This answer says documentary subjects should not try to discover hidden camera locations. The argument does not discuss what subjects should or should not do regarding camera locations. The argument is about the relative worthwhileness of documentaries based on how naturally subjects behave. Whether subjects should or should not search for cameras is an entirely different issue from whether documentaries featuring natural behavior are more worthwhile. This answer addresses subject behavior regarding camera discovery, not the relationship between natural behavior and documentary quality.

The filmmaker's documentary is not limited to "no purpose other than" depicting behavior, and "legitimate" is different from "worthwhile." Both the evidence category and the evaluative standard fail to match.

This connects camera-awareness to documentary authenticity but never addresses worthwhileness. The conclusion is about documentaries being more worthwhile, and this answer does not mention that concept.

The argument is about documentary worthwhileness, not the ethics of hidden cameras. Moral obligation to reveal camera locations is a different question entirely from whether the resulting documentary is more worthwhile.

More authentic depiction means more worthwhile. The filmmaker's hidden cameras produce more authentic depiction (subjects act naturally). Therefore the filmmaker's documentaries are more worthwhile. This bridges the exact gap between naturalness and documentary value.

Whether subjects should try to find hidden cameras is irrelevant. The argument is about whether natural behavior makes documentaries more worthwhile, not about what subjects should do about camera locations.

"No purpose other than" depicting behavior? The filmmaker never said that was the only goal. And "legitimate" is not "worthwhile." A documentary about paint drying could be legitimate without being worthwhile. This answer describes the wrong kind of documentary and evaluates it on the wrong scale. Two swings, two misses.

Documentaries where people talk to the camera are not authentic? Maybe. But so what? The filmmaker is not trying to prove the documentary is authentic — the filmmaker is trying to prove it is more worthwhile. "My documentary is authentic" and "my documentary is more worthwhile" are different claims. This answer helps with the first claim but completely ignores the second, which happens to be the actual conclusion.

Is it okay to hide cameras? That is an ethics question, and nobody asked it. The filmmaker is arguing that hidden cameras produce better documentaries, not that hidden cameras are morally acceptable. Getting permission to hide the camera does not make the documentary more or less worthwhile. This answer is preparing for a debate about filmmaking ethics when the actual debate is about filmmaking quality.

More real equals more worthwhile. The filmmaker's subjects act naturally (real behavior), other documentaries have people performing for the camera (less real behavior). By this principle, real beats performative on the worthwhileness scale. The word "authentically" is the bridge between "act naturally" (the evidence) and "more worthwhile" (the conclusion). Simple, clean, and exactly the principle the argument was missing.

This answer says only a few corporations currently give bonuses that provide strong enough incentives. The argument is about what highly profitable corporations could do to save money, not about what corporations currently do. Whether many or few corporations already use effective bonuses does not affect whether the strategy would work if implemented. The argument makes a prescriptive claim about a potential policy, and the current adoption rate of that policy is irrelevant to its potential effectiveness. Additionally, this answer does not specify whether the bonuses are expensive or whether the corporations are highly profitable.

This answer says if a corporation can save money by giving bonuses, it is because bonuses reduce monitoring time. Diagrammed: saves money via bonuses -> reduces monitoring. This uses the conclusion as the trigger (sufficient condition) and provides an explanation for why it works. But the argument needs to establish that the conclusion is true, not explain why it would be true if it were. A necessary assumption should be something that, if false, would destroy the argument. This answer, if negated ("it is not necessarily because of reduced monitoring"), does not destroy the argument — the argument has already established the monitoring-reduction mechanism in its premises.

This answer says the more valuable managers' time is, the less likely the corporation will have managers monitor employees. At highly profitable corporations (where managers' time is most valuable), this suggests monitoring is already minimal. If monitoring is already low, there is little monitoring to reduce, which means less potential savings from the bonus strategy. This weakens rather than supports the argument. The argument depends on highly profitable corporations currently spending substantial manager time on monitoring, so there is something to save by reducing it. An answer suggesting they already do not monitor much undermines the premise that monitoring savings are available.
This mixes language from the evidence and the opposing view into a causal claim the author never makes. The conclusion is about relative benefit, not about what home banking enables.
The argument is not trying to question this claim — it is using it as ammunition. Calling something into question means attacking it. The argument puts this claim on its team.

This answer states that for employees of highly profitable corporations where monitoring is reduced, expensive bonuses constitute strong incentives to keep working hard. This is the precise bridge the argument needs. The evidence says corporations can save money by reducing monitoring if employees get strong incentives. The conclusion says they can save money by giving expensive bonuses. This assumption connects the two by establishing that expensive bonuses are strong incentives for the relevant employees. Negation test: if expensive bonuses do not constitute strong incentives for these employees, then giving bonuses would not replace the need for monitoring, and no money would be saved. The argument collapses.

This answer says corporations can save money by reducing monitoring only if employees receive expensive bonuses. The word "only" makes expensive bonuses the sole method for saving money through reduced monitoring. The argument only needs bonuses to be one effective method, not the only method. Maybe strong incentives could also come from stock options, promotions, or other rewards. The argument does not need to assume bonuses are the exclusive solution — it only needs to assume they are an effective one. Negation test: "Corporations can also save money through reduced monitoring using incentives other than expensive bonuses." This does not destroy the argument because bonuses can still work even if alternatives also work.
How many corporations currently give effective bonuses does not affect whether the strategy would work if adopted. The argument is about potential savings, not current practices.

This uses the conclusion (saving money via bonuses) as the trigger and explains why it works. The argument needs an assumption that helps prove the conclusion, not one that starts from the conclusion being true.

If valuable manager time means less monitoring already happens, there is little monitoring to cut and little money to save. This weakens the argument by suggesting the savings opportunity is already minimal.

Expensive bonuses are strong incentives for these employees. This bridges "strong incentives save money" (evidence) to "expensive bonuses save money" (conclusion). Without this, bonuses might not motivate employees, and monitoring would still be needed.
The argument only needs expensive bonuses to be one effective method, not the only method. "Only if" makes bonuses exclusively necessary, which is stronger than what the argument requires.

Only a few companies currently do this? So what? The argument is not about what companies do — it is about what they could do. The fact that most companies have not tried expensive-bonuses-instead-of-monitoring does not mean it would not work. Maybe most companies just have not thought of it yet. Current adoption rates reveal nothing about theoretical effectiveness.

If bonuses save money, it is because of reduced monitoring? The argument already explained that. The premises lay out the whole chain: managers' time is expensive, monitoring wastes it, bonuses replace monitoring. This answer just restates the argument's own logic as if it were an assumption. What the argument actually needs is the link it skipped: that expensive bonuses would actually motivate these employees. This answer starts where the argument ends.

So profitable companies with expensive managers already skip the monitoring? Then there is nothing to save by replacing monitoring with bonuses — the monitoring was already reduced on its own. This answer is like saying "the more valuable your time, the less you waste it." If that is true, these corporations have already solved the monitoring problem without bonuses, and the bonuses would just be an unnecessary expense. This hurts the argument, not helps it.

The argument says "strong incentives" and the conclusion says "expensive bonuses." This answer says those are the same thing for these particular employees. Expensive bonuses motivate the workers at profitable companies to keep hustling even when the boss is not watching. Without this assumption, you could hand out gold-plated bonuses and employees might still slack off the moment monitoring stops. The bonuses have to actually work as motivation, and this answer confirms they do. Negation test: "Expensive bonuses do not motivate these employees" — argument destroyed.

This answer describes a correlation-to-association flaw: inferring two things are associated merely because they often co-occur. The columnist's argument does not involve any claim of association or correlation between two phenomena. Instead, the columnist uses evidence about one attitude (pre-test acceptance) to cast doubt on a different attitude (post-test resentment). The reasoning error is about conflating two different time points and mental states, not about inferring association from co-occurrence. This is the wrong flaw category for this argument.

This answer says the argument uses opinions from people unqualified to judge the scientific value of placebos. But the argument does not rely on subjects' understanding of placebos' scientific value. The evidence is about subjects' willingness to accept risk, not about their scientific expertise. The conclusion is about whether subjects feel resentment, not about whether placebos have scientific value. The argument would be equally flawed if every subject had a PhD in pharmacology — the problem is the gap between pre-test acceptance and post-test resentment, not the subjects' qualifications.

This answer says the argument uses an unrepresentative sample. But the evidence states that "almost all subjects" accept the risk, and the subjects described are the same people the conclusion discusses — test subjects in experimental medicine trials. There is no indication that the sample is different from or unrepresentative of the relevant population. The people filling out consent forms are the same people who may or may not feel resentment later. The argument's problem is not about who was surveyed but about what the survey measures (pre-test acceptance) versus what the conclusion claims (post-test resentment).
The stimulus describes technology, not consumer demand. Whether people want thin TVs with large screens is not addressed.

This answer identifies the argument's central flaw: it takes for granted that subjects who accept the risk of receiving ineffective substances before the test will not change their attitudes once the substances they receive turn out to be ineffective. The consent forms measure pre-test willingness to accept a risk. The resentment claim is about post-test emotional reaction to an actual outcome. These are psychologically distinct states. A subject can rationally accept a 50% chance of receiving a placebo while simultaneously feeling deep resentment when they actually receive one — especially when dealing with a serious disease. The argument assumes attitudinal consistency across the pre-test/post-test boundary, and this answer correctly identifies that unwarranted assumption.

This answer says the argument draws a moral conclusion from purely factual evidence. But the conclusion is not a moral claim. The conclusion says the evidence "casts doubt" on the claim that subjects feel resentment — this is an empirical dispute about whether subjects experience a particular emotional state, not a moral judgment about whether they should or should not feel resentment. Both the evidence (subjects accept risk) and the conclusion (subjects probably do not resent outcomes) are factual/empirical claims. The argument stays within the empirical domain throughout. There is no is-ought transition.
The argument does not infer an association between two phenomena. It uses one attitude (pre-test acceptance) to dispute a different attitude (post-test resentment). Wrong flaw category entirely.

The argument does not depend on subjects' scientific expertise. The flaw is about conflating pre-test risk acceptance with post-test emotional response, not about the qualifications of the people providing evidence.
The sample is the test subjects themselves — the same population the conclusion discusses. There is no sampling problem. The flaw is about what the evidence measures, not about who it measures.

The argument assumes pre-test risk acceptance means subjects will not resent the actual outcome. Accepting a risk in the abstract is psychologically different from experiencing the negative outcome. This answer correctly identifies the temporal/attitudinal gap.
The conclusion is empirical (subjects probably do not feel resentment), not moral. Both evidence and conclusion are factual claims about subjects' attitudes. There is no fact-to-value transition.

This describes a "things happen together so they must be connected" flaw. But the columnist's argument is not about two things happening together. It is about one attitude (accepting risk) being used to disprove a different attitude (feeling resentment). There is no correlation being drawn, no association being inferred. The flaw is about confusing "I am okay with the possibility" with "I am okay with the reality." Wrong flavor of bad reasoning.

Are the subjects unqualified to accept risk? They are the ones taking the risk — they are uniquely qualified to say whether they are okay with it. The issue is not "these people do not understand placebos." The issue is "being okay with a risk before it happens is not the same as being happy about it after it happens." The subjects could be Nobel Prize-winning pharmacologists and the flaw would be identical.

Unrepresentative sample? The evidence is about medical test subjects and the conclusion is about medical test subjects. Same people. The problem is not who was asked but when they were asked and what the answers actually prove. "I accept the risk" on a form before the test does not tell you whether "I resent the outcome" after the test. The sample is fine; the measurement is the issue.

Before the coin flip: "Sure, I accept a 50-50 chance." After losing the coin flip while suffering from a serious disease: "This is outrageous." Sound familiar? That is exactly what this argument ignores. Signing a form that says "I know I might get a sugar pill" is a very different emotional experience from actually getting the sugar pill while your condition worsens. The argument assumes that pre-game acceptance means post-game contentment, which is about as psychologically realistic as assuming that agreeing to play Monopoly means you will not flip the board when you land on Boardwalk with a hotel.

An increased use of organic farming methods does not establish that organic orchards are more profitable. There could be many reasons for the trend — environmental concerns, government subsidies, consumer pressure — none of which necessarily connect to profitability. More importantly, this answer does nothing to strengthen the specific link the argument needs: that better-tasting apples generate more revenue. The argument's gap is between taste and profit, and an industry trend toward organic methods does not bridge that gap.

This answer introduces a relationship between short-term and long-term profitability. Even if orchards that are profitable in the short term tend to remain profitable in the long term, this does not help the argument. The argument never discusses short-term profitability, and we have no information about whether organic orchards are more profitable in the short term. Without that information, this answer has no clear connection to the argument's conclusion. The gap the argument needs to bridge is between taste and profit, not between short-term and long-term profitability.

This answer directly bridges the argument's gap. The argument establishes that organic and conventional orchards have equal costs and equal productivity, with the only difference being that organic apples taste better. The conclusion that organic orchards are more profitable requires an assumption that better taste leads to higher revenue. If demand for apples is primarily based on flavor, then better-tasting organic apples will generate more demand and therefore more revenue. With equal costs and higher revenue, organic orchards would indeed be more profitable. This answer provides exactly the missing link between taste and profit.
The stimulus describes size-brightness tradeoffs at one thickness, not how changing thickness affects brightness. This unbounded claim is unsupported.

Price sensitivity among consumers does not help the argument. The argument does not provide any information about the price of organic versus conventional apples. If most people prefer the lowest price, organic orchards would need to price their apples competitively. But we do not know whether organic apples cost more, less, or the same as conventional apples at retail. This answer fails to connect to the taste-to-profit link that the argument requires. Even if organic apples were cheaper, this answer still would not explain why they are more profitable — lower prices could mean lower revenue per unit.

Consumer preferences about the appearance of apples are not directly relevant to the argument. The argument is about taste, not appearance. There might be some relationship between how an apple looks and how it tastes, but neither the argument nor this answer establishes that connection. Without knowing whether appearance influences purchasing decisions more than taste does, or whether appearance correlates with taste, this information does not clearly strengthen or weaken the link between the superior flavor of organic apples and higher profitability. If anything, by suggesting conventional apples look better, it might slightly weaken the argument — but that depends on assumptions not provided.
A trend toward organic farming does not prove organic orchards are more profitable. The argument needs a link between taste and profit, and this answer does not provide one.

The argument says nothing about short-term profitability. Even if short-term profits predict long-term profits, we do not know whether organic orchards are more profitable in the short term. This does not help.

If consumers buy apples primarily based on flavor, better-tasting organic apples will generate more demand and revenue. With equal costs and higher revenue, organic orchards are more profitable — exactly what the conclusion claims.
Price preferences do not help because the argument gives no information about apple prices. The argument needs a link between taste and profit, not between price and purchasing behavior.
Apple appearance is a different attribute from taste. The argument is about flavor driving profit, and consumer preferences about looks do not address that link.

More people are going organic — cool. But "popular" and "profitable" are not synonyms. People might switch to organic farming because they care about the environment, because regulations pushed them, or because organic sounds trendy at dinner parties. None of that establishes whether better-tasting apples actually make more money. The argument needs a taste-to-cash pipeline, and this answer is still stuck at the farm gate.

Short-term profits predicting long-term profits — fine, but who said anything about the short term? The argument is laser-focused on one thing: organic apples taste better, therefore organic orchards make more money. This answer wanders off into a different economic relationship entirely. It is answering a question nobody asked.

There it is — the missing link. If people buy apples based on flavor above all else, then the better-tasting organic apples will fly off the shelves. Same costs, same output, but more demand? That is a recipe for higher profits. The argument was one premise short of making sense, and this answer is that premise. Flavor drives demand, demand drives revenue, and revenue minus equal costs equals more profit for the organic orchard.

If everyone is bargain-hunting for the cheapest apple, then who cares how good the organic ones taste? This answer might actually hurt the argument more than help it. But setting that aside, the fundamental problem is that the argument says nothing about apple prices. The argument needs evidence that flavor sells apples, and this answer is talking about price tags instead.

This answer restates the opposing view presented in the first sentence of the argument — the banking industry's optimistic vision of home banking. The author introduces this view only to push back against it with "but." The conclusion is the author's own position, not the position being challenged. This answer captures the setup, not the punchline.

This answer accurately paraphrases the author's conclusion from the second sentence. The author states that home banking "may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers." This answer restates that idea: enabling home banking "may be more beneficial to banks than to their customers." The wording is different but the meaning is identical — a comparative claim that home banking disproportionately serves banks' interests. This is exactly what a correct Main Conclusion answer should do: capture the same idea in slightly different language.

This answer restates the evidence from the third sentence of the argument. The fact that customers will serve as their own tellers and pay more fees is the reason the author believes home banking benefits banks more than customers. It is the support for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. In the argument's structure, this information explains why the author holds the view expressed in the second sentence.

This answer captures only half of the conclusion. The author's point is comparative — home banking benefits banks more than customers. This answer only addresses the bank side: eliminating branches would benefit banks. It omits the customer side entirely and drops the crucial comparison. The conclusion is not just that banks will benefit; it is that banks will benefit more than customers will. Additionally, the conclusion is about the broader phenomenon of home banking, not just about eliminating branch offices specifically.

This answer cobbles together language from different parts of the argument without accurately representing any single claim the author makes. It connects home banking to the elimination of branches and employees, blending the opposing view (home banking) with the evidence (eliminating branches) into a causal claim the author never explicitly states. The conclusion is about who benefits more from home banking, not about what home banking enables banks to do. This answer sounds like it could be part of the argument, but it does not match the actual conclusion.

This is the banking industry's sales pitch — the shiny brochure version of the future. But the author is not selling this vision; the author is poking holes in it. The conclusion comes after the "but," where the author says, essentially, "nice for the banks, not so nice for you." Picking this answer is like reading a movie review that says "some people loved this film, but it was terrible" and concluding the reviewer loved the film.

Ding ding ding. "More beneficial to banks than to their customers" is just a dressed-up version of "more of a paradise for banks than for their customers." Same idea, fancier suit. The LSAT loves to rephrase conclusions in slightly different language to see if test-takers actually understood the point rather than just memorized the words. This answer understood the assignment.

This is the "here is why" part of the argument, not the "here is what the conclusion claims" part. Customers doing their own banking and paying more fees is the evidence supporting the conclusion. It is the engine, not the destination. The conclusion is "home banking is better for banks than for customers." This answer explains why that is the case.

"Banks will benefit from closing branches." Sure, that is part of the picture, but it is like summarizing Romeo and Juliet as "a guy from Verona had a bad week." The actual conclusion is about the comparison — banks win, customers lose. This answer only covers the first half and zooms in on branch closures when the conclusion is about the whole home-banking arrangement.

The word "always" makes this answer too strong to attribute to either speaker. Bernard argues that Carl's views should not be legitimized, but his argument is specifically about Carl's case. We cannot conclude that Bernard believes one should "always" avoid legitimizing views whose adoption one opposes. Furthermore, even if Bernard did hold this absolute position, Ayla might agree with the general principle — she just thinks that allowing Carl to speak will not actually legitimize his views but rather expose them. Their disagreement is about the consequences of public expression, not about whether one should avoid legitimizing harmful views as a general rule.

The word "every" makes this answer too strong. Ayla suggests that public scrutiny at the forum will produce convincing arguments against Carl's views, allowing people to see them for what they are. But we cannot conclude that Ayla believes this works for "every" dangerous idea. She may only believe this about Carl's particular views or about the particular forum being discussed. Additionally, Ayla calls Carl's views "false" but never calls them "dangerous" — that is Bernard's characterization. We do not know whether Ayla considers Carl's views dangerous, so any answer involving "dangerous" ideas is at best a half-scope match for Ayla's position.

This answer captures the core disagreement. Bernard believes that allowing Carl to speak at the forum would legitimize and help spread his views — meaning public expression of erroneous ideas is counterproductive. Ayla believes the opposite: "the best way to combat false views is to challenge them in public," which requires allowing their public expression. Bernard opposes public expression of false views as a means of fighting them; Ayla endorses it. This is a clean disagreement where both speakers hold clear, opposing positions on whether allowing public expression of erroneous ideas is an effective strategy for combating them.

Bernard says Carl's views are "false, and worse, dangerous," but this does not mean he believes there is a general tendency for people with false views to pose a danger to society. He is making a specific claim about Carl, not a generalization about all people with false views. Even if we could attribute this general belief to Bernard, we do not know Ayla's position on it. Ayla acknowledges that Carl's views are false but never addresses whether false views generally make their holders dangerous to society. Without clear positions from both speakers, this cannot be the point at issue.

Both Bernard and Ayla appear to agree with this statement, or at least neither clearly disagrees. Bernard argues against legitimizing and promulgating Carl's views "since we wish not to support their adoption," which aligns with not encouraging adoption of dangerous views. Ayla discusses combating "false views" and seeing them "for what they are," which also suggests she opposes their adoption. Since both speakers appear to be on the same side of this proposition, it is not a point of disagreement. Additionally, Ayla never uses the word "dangerous" — she discusses "false views" — so attributing a position about "dangerous" views to her is unsupported.

"Always" is too strong. Bernard's argument is about Carl's specific case, and even if he holds a broader principle, Ayla might agree with it while disagreeing about whether speaking at the forum actually legitimizes views.
"Every" is too strong for Ayla's position, and "dangerous" is Bernard's word, not Ayla's. Ayla discusses "false views" and may not consider Carl's views dangerous at all.

Bernard thinks public expression of Carl's views legitimizes them. Ayla thinks public expression lets people refute them. They directly disagree about whether allowing public expression of erroneous ideas is an effective way to fight them.

Bernard says Carl's views are false and dangerous, but that is specific to Carl — not a claim about people with false views generally. And Ayla never addresses whether false views make people dangerous to society.

Both speakers likely agree that adoption of dangerous views should not be encouraged. Ayla also discusses "false views," not "dangerous" ones, so her position on dangerous views specifically is unclear.

"Always" is the answer's downfall. Bernard says not to legitimize Carl's views in this situation, but he never declared a universal law of anti-legitimization. And Ayla might completely agree with the principle — she just thinks a public forum is where bad ideas go to die, not where they get legitimized. Their fight is about strategy, not about whether legitimizing bad views is generally undesirable.
Compound screens are thin, each tile is bright, and unlimited tiles can be joined without losing brightness or gaining thickness. Result: thin TVs can now be both bright and very large.

"Every dangerous idea" — whoa, slow down. Ayla said public scrutiny would work on Carl's views at this forum. She did not declare a universal law covering every bad idea in existence. Plus, "dangerous" is Bernard's label, not Ayla's. She called them "false," which is a different complaint. For all the passage reveals, Ayla thinks Carl's views are as dangerous as a kitten with a yarn ball — just wrong, not threatening.

This is the debate in a nutshell. Bernard says "keep Carl off the stage — public expression legitimizes bad ideas." Ayla says "put Carl on the stage — public expression demolishes bad ideas." Same question, opposite answers. Should false views be aired publicly to fight them? Bernard says absolutely not. Ayla says it is literally the best strategy available. Clean disagreement, no ambiguity.

Bernard thinks Carl's views are dangerous. That is about Carl specifically — not a thesis statement about everyone who has ever been wrong posing a threat to civilization. And Ayla? She never touches the "dangerous" question at all. She is focused on "false," which is a different word with a different meaning. No clear positions from both speakers means no point at issue.

Using the camera "extensively" to record family members does not establish that James got all the use he intended from it. Extensive use is not the same as complete intended use. He might have bought the camera for a different purpose entirely, and the family recordings were just a bonus. Or he might have intended to use the camera extensively for many different occasions over a long period, making the family recordings only a fraction of his intended use. This answer provides evidence of significant use but not evidence that his intended use was fulfilled — which is what the principle requires.

This answer establishes exactly what the principle requires. James bought the camera specifically to avoid hiring a videographer for his sister's graduation party. He returned the camera immediately after the party. This means James's entire intended use — recording the graduation party — was complete before the return. He got all the use he ever planned to get from the camera and then returned it, which satisfies all three conditions of the principle: purchase, fulfillment of intended use, and return. The return is therefore unethical under the stated principle.

This answer does not tell us whether James got all his intended use from the camera. He used it several times, but the return was prompted by dropping it and discovering broken features — not by having completed his intended use. If anything, this suggests James returned the camera because it no longer worked properly, which is a legitimate reason for a return that falls outside the principle's scope. The principle addresses returns after getting full intended use, not returns due to product malfunction. The ethics of returning a damaged item is a separate question the principle does not address.

James returned the camera because he found a lower price at another store, not because he completed his intended use. This does not tell us whether James used the camera at all, let alone whether he got all his intended use from it. The ethics of returning an item to repurchase it at a lower price is an entirely different question from the one the principle addresses. The principle is about returning items after getting full intended use, not about price-matching strategies.

This answer is cleverly worded but falls short. "Used the camera in the manner for which he bought it" is not the same as "got all the use from it that he ever intended to get." Consider someone who buys a camera to record an entire YouTube series. Recording one episode is using it "in the manner intended," but it is not getting all the intended use. The principle requires that the full scope of intended use be completed, not merely that the item was used for its intended purpose. James used the camera as intended but thought a different one would work better — suggesting he planned to continue using a camera, meaning his intended use was not fulfilled.
Extensive use does not mean James got all his intended use. He could have planned to use the camera for much more than just recording family activities.
James bought the camera specifically for the graduation party and returned it right after. His intended use was completely fulfilled before the return, satisfying all conditions of the principle.
James returned the camera because it broke after being dropped, not because he finished his intended use. Returning a malfunctioning product falls outside this principle's scope.
James returned the camera for a price reason, not because he completed his intended use. This does not satisfy the principle's conditions and raises a different ethical question entirely.

"Used in the manner intended" is not the same as "got all intended use." James could have intended much more use of the same type. The fact that he wants a different camera suggests ongoing intended use that was not fulfilled.

James recorded his family doing funny things — extensively. Good for James. But "used it a lot" and "got everything I wanted from it" are different claims. Maybe James bought the camera for a year-long vlogging project and the family videos were just the appetizer. Extensive use is not the same as mission accomplished.

James bought the camera for one reason: film his sister's graduation party without paying a videographer. Party happens, James films it, James returns the camera the next morning. That is textbook "got all the use I intended and then returned it." He essentially rented a camera for free using the store's return policy as his personal equipment library. The principle was practically written for this exact scenario.

James dropped the camera and it broke. Then he returned it. That is a completely different ethical question from the one the principle addresses. The principle is about people who use something for exactly what they wanted and then return it like they are running a free rental service. James is returning a broken product, which is just normal consumer behavior. Wrong ethical dilemma entirely.
The stimulus describes advantages but never claims zero disadvantages. Silence on drawbacks does not prove their absence.

James found the same camera cheaper at another store and returned the first one. Savvy shopping, maybe. Relevant to this principle? Not remotely. The principle cares about whether James got all his intended use before returning the camera, and this answer does not reveal whether James even turned the camera on. Price-hunting and use-fulfillment are completely different conversations.

The word "it" at the end of this answer refers back to "efficiency." This answer claims that some measures that appear to promote efficiency are actually harmful to efficiency itself. But the stimulus does not claim that Taylorism harms efficiency — quite the opposite. The stimulus explicitly states that Taylorism resulted in "greater efficiency" and "increased productivity." The negative consequence of Taylorism described in the stimulus is reduced intrinsic worth of work, not reduced efficiency. This answer misidentifies what was harmed.

This answer perfectly captures the dual nature of Taylorism as described in the stimulus. Taylorism was a "development in industry" that benefited workers "financially" by increasing their standard of living, while simultaneously making their work "less rewarding in other respects" by stripping it of creativity and intrinsic worth. The phrase "in other respects" correctly identifies that the negative impact was non-financial — it was about the quality and meaningfulness of the work itself. This generalization fits the specific situation described in the stimulus like a glove.

This answer claims that increased efficiency is "sometimes accompanied by decreases in the amount of effort workers devote to their jobs." But the stimulus does not describe workers devoting less effort — it describes their jobs becoming routine and repetitive. These are different things. A job can be routine and repetitive while still requiring significant effort. The stimulus says Taylorism changed the character of the work, not the effort workers put into it. Additionally, this answer frames the decreased effort as something workers choose, which is not how the stimulus describes the situation — Taylorism changed the nature of the jobs, not the workers' level of engagement.

This answer claims that an increase in workers' standard of living "will likely involve" a decrease in how much they value their jobs. But the stimulus describes a more specific causal structure: both the increased standard of living and the decreased intrinsic worth of work were caused by a third factor — Taylorism. This answer frames the relationship as direct causation between the two outcomes, omitting the common cause. Additionally, "how much they value their jobs overall" is broader than what the stimulus describes — the stimulus identifies a specific reduction in intrinsic worth related to creativity and talent, not a general decrease in job valuation.

The stimulus does not compare creative workers to non-creative workers in terms of their efficiency. It states that Taylorism reduced the role of creativity and talent in workers' jobs. That is a change in the nature of work over time, not a comparison between different types of workers at the same time. Nothing in the stimulus supports the claim that more creative workers are less efficient than average workers. The stimulus is about a tradeoff between financial benefit and intrinsic work quality, not about relative efficiency levels of different worker types.
The stimulus does not claim Taylorism harmed efficiency — it explicitly says efficiency increased. The negative consequence was to the intrinsic worth of work, not to efficiency itself.
Taylorism benefited workers financially (higher standard of living) while making work less rewarding (routine, repetitive, less creative). This answer captures both sides of that tradeoff perfectly.
The stimulus says jobs became routine and repetitive, not that workers put in less effort. Routine work can still require significant effort. This answer mischaracterizes the nature of the change.

In the stimulus, both effects — higher pay and less rewarding work — were caused by Taylorism. This answer incorrectly suggests a direct causal link between higher standards of living and lower job valuation, missing the common cause.
The stimulus does not compare creative workers' efficiency to average workers' efficiency. It describes a historical change in the nature of work, not a comparison between types of workers.

This answer says efficiency measures can backfire and actually reduce efficiency. But Taylorism did not reduce efficiency — it supercharged it. The problem is that efficiency came at the cost of meaningful work, not that efficiency failed. This answer is describing a boomerang effect that simply did not happen in the stimulus. Wrong target for the criticism.

Nailed it. Taylorism made workers richer but their jobs duller. This answer says exactly that in general terms: some industrial developments pad the wallet while draining the soul. Financial benefit, check. Less rewarding work, check. "In other respects" correctly identifies that the downside was not about money — it was about the work itself becoming a creativity desert. Clean match, no loose ends.

This answer says workers started putting in less effort. The stimulus says their jobs became boring. Those are not the same thing. A factory worker doing the same motion 10,000 times a day is exerting plenty of effort — the work is just mind-numbingly repetitive. Taylorism changed what the work looked like, not how hard people were working. This answer confuses "the job got duller" with "workers got lazier."

This answer says getting a raise makes people like their jobs less. That is not what happened. Taylorism did both things simultaneously — it was the common cause of both the financial improvement and the creative decline. The higher standard of living did not cause the boring work; Taylorism caused both independently. This answer draws a direct causal arrow between the two effects when it should be pointing both arrows back at their shared origin.
Reciprocal treatment of injurious people is outside the argument's scope. The argument is about reasonable behavior reducing the need for government.

If many residents never use the branch libraries because of irregular hours, this actually supports closing them. Residents who are not using the branches have nothing to lose from their closure and might gain access to a larger library with more consistent hours. This answer strengthens the argument for consolidation by suggesting that the branch libraries are already failing to serve some residents.

If residents are already complaining about the book selection at branch libraries, this supports the argument for a larger library with better selection. The complaints validate the argument's premise that branch libraries are inadequately supplied and suggest residents would welcome a better-stocked alternative.

This answer identifies the key unintended consequence of consolidation. If the only possible site for a new library is not readily accessible to most Winchester residents, then the improved book selection becomes irrelevant for the majority of the community. A library that people cannot easily reach does not meet their needs regardless of how well-stocked it is. The branch libraries, despite their limited selections, at least provided convenient local access. Replacing accessible but poorly supplied libraries with an inaccessible but well-supplied library could easily leave residents worse off overall.

The argument already accounts for the financial dimension by stating that closing branches would allow Winchester to afford a larger library. The word "significant" does not tell us whether the cost would exceed the savings from closing branch libraries. Without information about whether the cost exceeds available resources, this answer does not clearly weaken the argument.

The phrase "attempts to cater" significantly weakens this answer. If each branch library merely attempts to serve the entire township's tastes, that does not mean it succeeds. The branch libraries could be attempting and failing to meet diverse tastes, which would actually support the argument for a larger, better-stocked library. This answer would be stronger if it said each branch library successfully caters to local neighborhood tastes.
If residents are not using branches due to irregular hours, closing them causes less disruption. This supports rather than undermines the consolidation plan.
Complaints about branch library selections support the case for a larger library with a better collection. This strengthens the argument.

If the only possible location for the new library is hard for most residents to reach, better books do not matter — people cannot use a library they cannot get to. This directly undermines the claim that consolidation would better meet needs.
The argument already says closing branches would fund the new library. "Significant" cost does not tell us whether it exceeds available resources.
"Attempts to cater" is too weak — attempting is not succeeding. The branch libraries could be trying and failing, which would support rather than undermine consolidation.

People are not using the branch libraries anyway because the hours are all over the place. So closing them is... a problem? This is practically an argument for consolidation. "The branch libraries are so inconvenient that nobody goes there" is not a compelling reason to keep them open.

Residents are already complaining about the books at the branch libraries. So the argument says "let us build a bigger library with better books" and this answer replies "people hate the current book selection." That is not a weakness — that is the argument's best supporting evidence.

The beautiful new library with its magnificent collection of current titles is located in... the one spot nobody can get to. What good is the world's greatest library if most residents need a GPS and a packed lunch to reach it? The branch libraries might have had dusty old books, but at least people could actually walk in the door.

"It would cost a lot" — but the argument already said Winchester could afford it if the branches close. "Significant" sounds alarming but reveals nothing specific. Maybe it costs a lot but still less than running several branch libraries.
Nothing suggests compound screen technology is inappropriate for small screens. The ability to go large does not mean small is impossible. A few tiles would make a small, bright screen.
The stimulus describes technological capability but says nothing about consumer demand. Whether consumers want these TVs is a market question the stimulus does not address.

The stimulus describes the size-brightness relationship at one thickness. It does not describe how changing thickness affects brightness. "The thicker the set, the brighter the screen" asserts an unbounded correlation the stimulus cannot support. Maybe thickness helps to a point, maybe not.

This follows directly from combining premises. Compound screens are a few inches thick. Each tile is bright. Unlimited tiles can be added without losing brightness or gaining thickness. Therefore: thin TVs can now have screens that are both bright and very large. Each element of this answer corresponds to a supported proposition, and the conjunction follows without additional assumptions.

The stimulus describes advantages of compound screens but never claims they have no disadvantages. There could be many drawbacks not mentioned: higher cost, lower resolution, visible seams, shorter lifespan. Silence on disadvantages does not prove their absence.
The stimulus says compound screens can be very large, not that they must be. Nothing prevents using the technology for small screens.

The stimulus describes a cool technology. This answer says people want to buy it. Just because you can build a TV screen the size of a billboard does not mean consumers are lining up for one. The stimulus is a science article, not a market research report.

The stimulus says thin screens get dimmer as they get bigger. This answer concludes that making any screen thicker will make it brighter — forever. Maybe after six inches of thickness the brightness plateaus and you just have a very heavy, very thick TV. Wild extrapolation from one relationship to a completely different one.

Add tiles: bigger screen. Each tile stays bright: still bright. Adding tiles does not add thickness: still thin. Thin plus bright plus unlimited size equals a TV that is the size of a wall, blazingly bright, and thinner than a textbook. This answer just reads the instruction manual and states the obvious result.

The quoted statement supports the main conclusion and is itself supported by another premise (disease, injury, diet evidence). The LSAT's description — "a premise for which another premise is offered as support" — accurately captures both relationships. While we might call this an "intermediate conclusion," calling it a "premise" is not technically wrong since it does support the main conclusion.

The statement plays a direct logical role — it supports the main conclusion and is supported by evidence. Background information would be a neutral fact that sets the scene without participating in the argument's logic.

This claims no support is offered for the quoted statement. But the second sentence — increased disease, injury, and a less nutritious diet — directly supports the claim that the transition was traumatic. Support is clearly offered.
The main conclusion is the final sentence, introduced by "thus." The quoted statement supports this conclusion but is not the conclusion itself.

The argument supports and builds upon the "traumatic" claim rather than seeking to rebut it. An opposing viewpoint would be contested by the argument, but this statement is firmly integrated into the argument's reasoning.
The quoted statement supports the main conclusion and is supported by the disease/diet evidence. This answer correctly identifies both relationships.
The quoted statement is not background — it actively supports the conclusion and is supported by evidence. It plays a direct logical role.
Support is offered — the evidence about disease, injury, and diet directly supports the "traumatic" claim.
The main conclusion is the final sentence about groups being motivated by benefits. The "traumatic" claim supports the conclusion; it is not the conclusion.
The argument supports the "traumatic" claim and builds on it — it does not attempt to rebut it.

A premise that gets backed up by another premise — exactly right. "The transition was traumatic" supports the main conclusion and gets support from the disease-and-diet evidence. A supported supporter. The LSAT calling it a "premise" instead of "intermediate conclusion" is loose with terminology, but the description is accurate.

"Plays no logical role" — the statement that holds the entire argument together? The "traumatic transition" claim is the bridge between evidence and conclusion. Calling this background is like calling the foundation of a house "decorative."

"No support is offered" — did the second sentence take the day off? More disease, more injuries, worse diet — that is direct support for "traumatic." This answer ignores the evidence sitting right there.
"Thus" in the last sentence is the LSAT's neon sign saying "main conclusion here." The traumatic claim supports the conclusion — it is the supporting act, not the headliner.

The argument does not claim cyberspace property is "widely considered to be real estate." It draws an analogy based on shared terminology. This answer addresses a stronger claim than the argument makes.

No premise presupposes the conclusion. The premises about shared terminology and trespass law's real estate application are factual claims independent of whether trespass law should apply to cyberspace. The flaw is a weak analogy, not circular logic.
